vce-bio12-cell-theory-and-cell-size: bio12a1-ct-1
Which statement is a principle of cell theory?
All cells contain a nucleus.
All cells arise from pre-existing cells.
All living things are made of many cells.
Cells can arise spontaneously from non-living matter.

Cell theory states that all living things are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, and spontaneous generation was disproved.
bio12a1-ct-2
A cube-shaped cell has a side length of 2 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
SA = 6 × 2² = 24 µm²; V = 2³ = 8 µm³; SA:V = 24:8 = 3:1. A 6:1 ratio would be a 1 µm cube.
bio12a1-ct-3
As a cell grows larger while keeping the same shape, which change occurs?
Its volume increases more slowly than its surface area.
Its SA:V ratio increases.
Its rate of diffusion across each square micrometre of membrane decreases.
Its SA:V ratio decreases, so exchange per unit volume becomes less efficient.
Volume scales with the cube of length and surface area with the square, so SA:V falls as a cell grows. Less membrane is available per unit of cytoplasm to supply materials and remove wastes.
bio12a1-ct-4
Agar cubes of three sizes (1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm sides) containing a pH indicator were placed in acid for 5 minutes. Which result would be expected?
The 3 cm cube would show the greatest percentage of its volume changed colour.
All cubes would show the same percentage of volume changed colour.
The 1 cm cube would show the greatest percentage of its volume changed colour.
The acid would penetrate a greater distance into the 3 cm cube.
Acid diffuses inward at about the same rate (same penetration depth) in all cubes, but the smallest cube has the highest SA:V, so the largest fraction of its volume changes colour.
bio12a1-ct-5
Which feature helps a large cell overcome the limits of a low SA:V ratio?
A spherical shape
Microvilli or a flattened, elongated shape
A thicker cell wall
Fewer membrane transport proteins
Folding the membrane into microvilli or flattening the cell increases surface area without much increase in volume, raising SA:V. A sphere has the lowest SA:V of any shape for a given volume.
bio12a1-ct-6
Explain why most cells are microscopic in size. (2 marks)

Cells exchange materials (nutrients, O₂, wastes) across their plasma membrane; small cells have a high SA:V ratio so the membrane area can supply the volume quickly enough / diffusion distances to the centre stay short; large cells would have too little membrane relative to volume and could not meet metabolic demands.
bio12a1-ct-7
Cell X is a cube of side 4 µm and cell Y is a cube of side 8 µm. Calculate the SA:V ratio of each and state which cell would exchange materials more efficiently. (3 marks)
X: SA = 6 × 16 = 96 µm², V = 64 µm³, SA:V = 1.5:1; Y: SA = 6 × 64 = 384 µm², V = 512 µm³, SA:V = 0.75:1; cell X is more efficient because it has the higher SA:V ratio (twice that of Y).
bio12a1-ct-8
Describe how the development of the light microscope contributed to cell theory. (2 marks)

Microscopes allowed cells to be observed for the first time (e.g. Hooke's cork cells, van Leeuwenhoek's microorganisms); repeated observation of cells in all plant and animal tissues, and of cells dividing, provided the evidence that all organisms are made of cells and that cells come from pre-existing cells.
bio12a1-ct-9
In Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment, broth in a flask with a long curved neck stayed free of microbial growth while the neck remained intact. What did this result support?
Microorganisms arise spontaneously from the nutrient broth itself.
Microorganisms need light to grow in nutrient broth.
Microorganisms in the broth came from pre-existing microorganisms carried into it from the air.
Heating the broth creates new microorganisms within it.

Broth in the intact swan-neck flask stayed sterile while air could still reach it, so the microbes must have come from pre-existing microbes rather than arising spontaneously in the broth. Spontaneous generation is the tempting but incorrect idea that the experiment disproved.
bio12a1-ct-10
Which cube-shaped cell has the highest surface area to volume ratio?
A cube with a side length of 1 µm
A cube with a side length of 5 µm
A cube with a side length of 10 µm
A cube with a side length of 20 µm
For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length, so the 1 µm cube has 6:1 while the 20 µm cube has only 0.3:1. Choosing the largest cube because it has the most surface area ignores that its volume grows faster.
bio12a1-ct-11
A student claims that doubling the side length of a cube-shaped cell doubles its surface area to volume ratio. Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?
The claim is correct, because the surface area and the volume both double.
The claim is incorrect, because the SA:V ratio halves when the side length doubles.
The claim is incorrect, but only because the shape of the cell has changed.
The claim is incorrect, because the SA:V ratio is multiplied by four when the side length doubles.

For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length, so doubling the side length halves the ratio. Surface area rises by a factor of four and volume by a factor of eight, so they do not increase together. The shape of the cell stays the same when it is scaled up.
bio12a1-ct-12
A cube-shaped cell has a surface area of 54 µm². What is its surface area to volume ratio?

A surface area of 54 µm² gives 6s² = 54, so the side length is 3 µm and the volume is 27 µm³. Then 54 ÷ 27 = 2:1. A 6:1 ratio is the constant from the surface area formula, 1:2 inverts the ratio, and 3:1 is the side length rather than the ratio.
bio12a1-ct-13
A cube-shaped cell has a volume of 0.125 µm³. What is its surface area to volume ratio?

A volume of 0.125 µm³ gives a side length of 0.5 µm, so the surface area is 6 × 0.5² = 1.5 µm² and 1.5 ÷ 0.125 = 12. The 24:1 result comes from not squaring the side length in the surface area, and 1:12 inverts the ratio.
bio12a1-ct-14
A cube-shaped cell grows in side length from 2 µm to 6 µm while keeping its shape. By what factor does its volume increase?
Volume scales with the cube of the side length, so the increase is (6 ÷ 2)³ = 3³ = 27 times. Multiplying by 9 treats volume as if it scaled with area, while 3 uses only the linear increase in length.
bio12a1-ct-15
Which value is the best estimate of the diameter of a typical animal cell?
100 nm
1 mm
10 cm
Typical eukaryotic cells are around 10–100 µm across, so 10–30 µm is a good estimate. A diameter of 100 nm is about the size of a virus, while 1 mm is large enough to see without a microscope.
bio12a1-ct-16
A cell measures 0.02 mm across. What is its diameter in micrometres?
2 µm
200 µm
20 µm
There are 1000 µm in 1 mm, so 0.02 mm × 1000 = 20 µm. Dividing by 1000 gives 2 µm, leaving the number unchanged gives 0.02 µm, and multiplying by 10 000 gives 200 µm.
bio12a1-ct-17
A rectangular box-shaped cell measures 1 µm × 1 µm × 10 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?

The surface area is 2(1 × 1 + 1 × 10 + 1 × 10) = 42 µm² and the volume is 1 × 1 × 10 = 10 µm³, so SA:V = 4.2:1. Counting each pair of faces only once gives 2.1:1, treating the box as a 1 µm cube gives 6:1, and inverting the ratio gives 0.24:1.
bio12a1-ct-18
Which development allowed scientists to see fine internal structures of cells, such as membranes and ribosomes, in detail?
The compound light microscope
The electron microscope
The simple magnifying lens used by van Leeuwenhoek
The X-ray diffraction camera

Light microscopes cannot resolve structures smaller than about 200 nm, which includes membranes and ribosomes, while electron microscopes can. The light microscope was essential for cell theory but cannot show these details, and X-ray diffraction is used to study molecular structure rather than to image cells.
bio12a1-ct-19
Which of these cells is typically the smallest in diameter?
A human egg cell
A human red blood cell
A typical bacterium
A typical plant palisade cell

Typical bacteria are about 1–5 µm across, which is smaller than a human red blood cell (around 7–8 µm) or a plant palisade cell (tens of micrometres). A human egg cell is one of the largest human cells, at about 100 µm in diameter.
bio12a1-ct-20
Which two scientists, working in 1838 and 1839, proposed that plants and animals are both made of cells?
Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek
Redi and Pasteur
Watson and Crick
Schleiden and Schwann

Schleiden studied plants and Schwann studied animals, and together they proposed that living things are made of cells. Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek made the first observations of cells and microorganisms, Redi and Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation, and Watson and Crick described the structure of DNA in 1953.
bio12a1-ct-21
A single cube of side 2 µm and eight separate cubes of side 1 µm have the same total volume. Which statement is correct?
The eight 1 µm cubes have a total surface area of 48 µm² and a combined SA:V of 6:1, twice the 3:1 of the single cube.
The single 2 µm cube has a total surface area of 48 µm² and an SA:V of 6:1, because it is one larger object.
Both arrangements have an SA:V of 3:1, because their total volumes are the same.
The eight 1 µm cubes have a total surface area of 24 µm², the same as the single cube.

Each 1 µm cube has 6 µm² of surface, so the eight cubes have 48 µm², while the single 2 µm cube has 24 µm². Dividing by the shared total volume of 8 µm³ gives 6:1 and 3:1 respectively, so dividing a cell into smaller pieces increases the membrane available per unit of cytoplasm.
bio12a1-ct-22
Which tool is used to calibrate the scale of an eyepiece graticule so that cell dimensions can be measured?
A thermometer
A stage micrometer
A pH meter
A digital balance

A stage micrometer is a slide with a known scale, and comparing it with the eyepiece graticule at each magnification gives the size of each graticule unit. A thermometer, a pH meter and a balance do not measure length under a microscope.
bio12a1-ct-23
Cell P is a cube of side 2 µm. Cell Q is a box measuring 1 µm × 2 µm × 4 µm. Which statement about their surface area to volume ratios is correct?
Cell P has the greater SA:V, because cubes have the highest SA:V of any shape.
The two cells have equal SA:V, because both have a volume of 8 µm³.
Cell Q has the greater SA:V, at 3.5:1 compared with 3:1 for cell P.
Cell P has the greater SA:V, at 3:1 compared with about 2.9:1 for cell Q.

Cell Q has a surface area of 28 µm² against 24 µm² for cell P, while both have a volume of 8 µm³, giving 3.5:1 against 3:1. Equal volumes do not mean equal SA:V ratios, and a cube does not have the highest SA:V of all shapes for a given volume.
bio12a1-ct-24
A rectangular prism-shaped cell measures 2 µm × 3 µm × 5 µm. Calculate its surface area, its volume and its surface area to volume ratio, showing your working. (3 marks)
bio12a1-ct-25
A student claims that a large cell is more efficient at exchanging materials with its surroundings than a small cell because it has more membrane. Evaluate this claim. (2 marks)
The claim is incorrect [1]; the large cell has more total membrane but a lower SA:V, so less membrane is available per unit of cytoplasm to exchange materials [1]
bio12a1-ct-26
Distinguish between the magnification and the resolution of a light microscope. (2 marks)
Magnification is how many times larger the image appears than the specimen [1]; resolution is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate points [1]
bio12a1-ct-27
A cell measures 60 mm long in a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×1500. Calculate the actual length of the cell in µm. (2 marks)
bio12a1-ct-28
Describe the contribution of Rudolf Virchow to cell theory. (2 marks)
Stated that all cells arise only from pre-existing cells, by cell division [1]; this completed cell theory by explaining how new cells, and therefore growth and repair, are produced [1]
bio12a1-ct-29

Cube-shaped cells with side lengths of 1.5 µm, 6 µm, 9 µm and 12 µm have surface area to volume ratios of 4:1, 1:1, 0.67:1 and 0.5:1 respectively. Describe the relationship between side length and SA:V ratio, and explain it using surface area and volume. (3 marks)

As side length increases, the SA:V ratio decreases, so the two are inversely proportional [1]; for a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length [1]; surface area increases with the square of the side length while volume increases with the cube, so volume increases faster [1]
vce-bio12-cs-c1
A cube-shaped cell doubles its side length. Its surface area to volume ratio:
Doubles
Stays the same
Increases eightfold
Halves
Surface area grows by 2² = 4 and volume by 2³ = 8, so SA:V is multiplied by 4/8 = 1/2. Large cells struggle to exchange materials fast enough.
vce-bio12-prokaryotic-and-eukaryotic-cel: bio12a1-pe-1
Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
Ribosomes
Mitochondria
Nuclear envelope
Golgi apparatus
All cells have ribosomes (prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes, eukaryotes 80S in the cytosol). The other structures are membrane-bound organelles found only in eukaryotes.
bio12a1-pe-2
A newly discovered single-celled organism has a cell wall, circular DNA in the cytosol, plasmids and no membrane-bound organelles. It is best classified as
a plant cell.
a fungal cell.
a protist.
a prokaryote.
Circular DNA in a nucleoid region, plasmids and the absence of membrane-bound organelles are defining features of prokaryotes. Fungi and plants have cell walls but are eukaryotes with nuclei.
bio12a1-pe-3
Which feature would distinguish a plant cell from an animal cell under a light microscope?
Presence of a nucleus
Presence of a cell wall and large central vacuole
Presence of a plasma membrane
Presence of cytoplasm
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, a large central vacuole and often chloroplasts. Both cell types have a nucleus, plasma membrane and cytoplasm.
bio12a1-pe-4
The typical size range of prokaryotic cells compared with eukaryotic cells is
prokaryotes 10–100 µm; eukaryotes 1–10 µm.
prokaryotes 0.1–5 µm; eukaryotes 10–100 µm.
both 10–100 µm.
prokaryotes 0.1–5 nm; eukaryotes 10–100 nm.
Most prokaryotes are about 0.1–5 µm, while most eukaryotic cells are about 10–100 µm. Nanometre values are far too small for whole cells.
bio12a1-pe-5
Which statement about the DNA of prokaryotes is correct?
It is linear and wrapped around histones inside a nucleus.
It is enclosed in a double membrane.
It is found only in plasmids.
It is a single circular chromosome located in the nucleoid region, often with plasmids.
Prokaryotes have one main circular chromosome in the nucleoid (not membrane-bound) and may carry small circular plasmids. Linear, histone-bound DNA in a nucleus is eukaryotic.
bio12a1-pe-6
State two structural differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. (2 marks)

Any two: eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus while prokaryotes have a nucleoid region; eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles (e.g. mitochondria, ER) while prokaryotes do not; prokaryotic DNA is circular while eukaryotic DNA is linear; prokaryotes have smaller (70S) ribosomes; prokaryotes are generally much smaller.
bio12a1-pe-7
A student examines a cell with an electron microscope and sees a nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts and a cell wall. Identify the type of cell and justify your answer. (2 marks)

A plant (eukaryotic, photosynthetic) cell; the nucleus and mitochondria show it is eukaryotic, and the chloroplasts and cell wall together indicate a plant cell (animal cells lack both; fungi lack chloroplasts).
bio12a1-pe-8
Explain why compartmentalisation by membrane-bound organelles is an advantage to eukaryotic cells. (2 marks)

Organelles separate incompatible reactions and keep enzymes and substrates concentrated in specific compartments (e.g. hydrolytic enzymes in lysosomes); this increases the efficiency of metabolism and allows eukaryotic cells to be larger and more complex than prokaryotes.
bio12a1-pe-9
The cell wall of most bacteria is made mainly of which substance?
cellulose.
chitin.
peptidoglycan.
lignin.

Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids. Plant walls are made of cellulose and fungal walls of chitin, while lignin is a strengthening material added to some plant walls rather than a bacterial component.
bio12a1-pe-10
Which of the following structures in a eukaryotic cell contains 70S ribosomes, similar to those of prokaryotes?
Lysosome.
Golgi apparatus.
Plasma membrane.
Mitochondrion.

Mitochondria carry their own 70S ribosomes, consistent with their bacterial origin. The Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and plasma membrane do not contain 70S ribosomes, and the ribosomes in the cytosol are 80S.
bio12a1-pe-11
Which statement best describes the function of plasmids in prokaryotic cells?
They carry the main chromosome that controls cell division.
They carry small extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance, that can be passed between bacteria.
They store glycogen as an energy reserve.
They are the site of aerobic respiration.

Plasmids are small, separate circles of DNA that can carry extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance, and can be transferred between bacteria. The main chromosome is the nucleoid DNA rather than a plasmid, and glycogen storage and aerobic respiration are not plasmid functions.
bio12a1-pe-12
A cell appears 2.5 mm long in a light microscope image taken at ×500 magnification. What is its actual length?
50 µm.
5 µm.

Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. The image is 2.5 mm = 2500 µm, and 2500 ÷ 500 = 5 µm. Leaving the value as 2500 µm ignores the magnification, 50 µm comes from dividing by 50 instead of 500, and 0.005 µm comes from treating 2.5 mm as 2.5 µm.
bio12a1-pe-13
Why can a transmission electron microscope reveal structures such as ribosomes that a light microscope cannot resolve?
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, giving much higher resolution.
Electron microscopes use coloured stains that light cannot pass through.
Electron microscopes can view living cells in their natural state.
Electron microscopes magnify only about ×2 but keep the specimen in full colour.

The electron beam has a much shorter wavelength than visible light, so resolution is far higher and tiny structures can be seen. The other options are false: electron micrographs are black and white (or false colour), and specimens are prepared in a vacuum, so living cells cannot be viewed.
bio12a1-pe-14
Which observation provides the strongest evidence for the endosymbiotic theory of the origin of mitochondria?
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, similar to bacteria.
Mitochondria are found only in animal cells.
Mitochondria contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
Mitochondria are surrounded by a single membrane, like lysosomes.

Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, features they share with bacteria. This supports the idea that they were once free-living prokaryotes engulfed by a larger cell. Mitochondria are found in plant and animal cells, have no chlorophyll and are surrounded by a double membrane.
bio12a1-pe-15
Which bacterial structure is a sticky outer layer that can help the bacterium resist attack by the host's immune cells?
Flagellum.
Ribosome.
Nucleoid.
Capsule.

A capsule is a sticky layer of polysaccharide outside the cell wall that can help bacteria evade the immune system and adhere to surfaces. A flagellum is used for movement, ribosomes make proteins and the nucleoid holds the chromosome.
bio12a1-pe-16
Most prokaryotes reproduce by binary fission. Which statement best explains why bacterial populations can grow rapidly?
Meiosis produces four genetically different cells, increasing variation.
Mitosis divides chromosomes within a membrane-bound nucleus to make two identical cells.
Binary fission produces two genetically identical cells, and under favourable conditions this can happen quickly.
Cells fuse together to form one larger cell, so the number of cells shrinks.

Binary fission copies the single chromosome and splits the cell into two genetically identical daughter cells, without mitosis or meiosis. Under favourable conditions it can be very rapid, so populations can double quickly. Fusion would reduce cell numbers rather than increase them.
bio12a1-pe-17
Which of the following organisms is a eukaryote?
Escherichia coli.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast).
Streptococcus.
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).

Yeast is a single-celled fungus with a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. E. coli, Streptococcus and cyanobacteria are all prokaryotes, even though cyanobacteria are often called blue-green algae.
bio12a1-pe-18
A eukaryotic cell is 40 µm across and a bacterium is 2 µm across. How many bacteria, placed end to end, would span the diameter of the eukaryotic cell?
40 ÷ 2 = 20 bacteria. Subtracting the sizes (38) or multiplying them (80) does not count how many fit along a length, and 2 is simply the bacterium's diameter in µm.
bio12a1-pe-19
Which statement about the cytoplasm of a prokaryotic cell is correct?
It contains membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.
It contains free 70S ribosomes and the nucleoid region.
It is enclosed by a nuclear envelope.
It contains no ribosomes.

Prokaryotic cytoplasm holds free 70S ribosomes and the nucleoid, with no membrane-bound organelles. Mitochondria are eukaryotic, the nuclear envelope surrounds a eukaryotic nucleus, and ribosomes are present in all cells.
bio12a1-pe-20
Which organelle is found in plant cells and some protists, but not in animal or fungal cells, and contains its own circular DNA?
Chloroplast.
Lysosome.
Centriole.
Vacuole.

Chloroplasts are photosynthetic organelles with their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, and they are absent from animal and fungal cells. Lysosomes and centrioles are found in animal cells, and a vacuole is a membrane-bound sac with no DNA of its own.
bio12a1-pe-21
Penicillin kills bacteria by interfering with the synthesis of their cell walls, but it does not harm human cells. Which statement best explains this?
Human cells have peptidoglycan cell walls that penicillin cannot penetrate.
Human cells do not make peptidoglycan, so penicillin has no target in them.
Penicillin acts only on viruses, which are not cells.
Human cells have 70S ribosomes, which penicillin cannot bind.

Penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, a compound that human cells do not make, so there is no target in human cells. The option about 70S ribosomes is wrong because human cells have 80S ribosomes, and penicillin does not act on ribosomes.
bio12a1-pe-22
Which structure is found in many prokaryotes, is absent from eukaryotic animal cells, and is used by bacteria to attach to surfaces?
Pili.
Mitochondria.
Nucleus.
Centrioles.

Pili are short, hair-like protein projections on bacteria used for attachment to surfaces, and some are used to transfer DNA between cells. Mitochondria, the nucleus and centrioles are all found in eukaryotic animal cells.
bio12a1-pe-23
A cube-shaped cell with sides of 1 µm has a surface area to volume ratio of 6:1. Which change would give a ratio of 3:1?
Halving the side length to 0.5 µm, which doubles the ratio to 12:1.
Halving the side length to 0.5 µm, which halves the ratio to 3:1.
Doubling the side length to 2 µm, which halves the ratio to 3:1.
Doubling the side length to 2 µm, which doubles the ratio to 12:1.

For a cube, surface area to volume ratio = 6 ÷ side length, so doubling the side length from 1 µm to 2 µm halves the ratio to 3:1. Halving the side length to 0.5 µm doubles the ratio to 12:1, so the options claiming a 3:1 ratio from halving are wrong.
bio12a1-pe-24
State the function of ribosomes in a cell. (1 mark)
Site of protein synthesis (translation) [1]
bio12a1-pe-25
Explain how the large central vacuole of a plant cell helps the cell stay firm. (2 marks)
The vacuole takes up water, creating turgor (internal) pressure [1]; this pushes the plasma membrane against the cellulose cell wall, which resists expansion and keeps the cell firm [1].
bio12a1-pe-26
A bacterium with an actual length of 2 µm appears 10 mm long in a light microscope image. Calculate the magnification. Show your working. (2 marks)
Image size = 10 mm = 10 000 µm [1]; magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 10 000 ÷ 2 = ×5000 [1].
bio12a1-pe-27
Describe the role of the plasma membrane in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. (2 marks)
Controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell (selectively permeable) [1]; separates the cell's contents from its external environment [1].
bio12a1-pe-28
A cube-shaped cell has sides of 3 µm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, and explain how a larger ratio affects the efficiency of exchange of substances with the environment. (3 marks)

Surface area = 6 × 3² = 54 µm² and volume = 3³ = 27 µm³ [1]; ratio = 54 ÷ 27 = 2:1 [1]; a larger ratio gives more membrane per unit volume, so exchange of substances with the environment is more efficient [1].
bio12a1-pe-29

A student uses an eyepiece lens of ×10 and an objective lens of ×40 to view a cell. The image of the cell measures 8 mm across. Calculate the actual diameter of the cell in micrometres. Show your working. (3 marks)
Total magnification = 10 × 40 = ×400 [1]; image size = 8 mm = 8000 µm [1]; actual size = 8000 ÷ 400 = 20 µm [1].
bio12a1-pe-30
Compare a bacterial cell with a human liver cell with respect to: the location of DNA, the size of ribosomes, the presence of membrane-bound organelles, and typical cell size. (4 marks)

DNA: bacterium in a nucleoid (not membrane-bound), liver cell in a membrane-bound nucleus [1]; ribosomes: bacterium 70S, liver cell 80S [1]; membrane-bound organelles: absent in the bacterium, present in the liver cell (e.g. mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus) [1]; size: bacterium typically 0.1–5 µm, liver cell typically 10–100 µm [1].
bio12a1-pe-31
Explain why offspring produced by binary fission are genetically identical to the parent cell, yet bacterial populations can still show genetic variation. (2 marks)

Binary fission replicates the single circular chromosome and the cell divides, so each daughter receives identical DNA [1]; variation arises from mutations and from the transfer of plasmids between bacteria [1].
bio12a1-pe-32
Describe how plasmids carrying antibiotic resistance genes can spread through a bacterial population during antibiotic treatment. (3 marks)

Plasmids carry genes for antibiotic resistance [1]; plasmids can be transferred from resistant to non-resistant bacteria [1]; bacteria that have received the plasmid survive treatment, reproduce and increase the proportion of resistant bacteria in the population [1].
vce-bio12-pe-c1
A newly discovered cell has a cell wall, ribosomes and a plasma membrane. Which further observation would show it is prokaryotic?
A cell wall made of cellulose surrounding the plasma membrane
Circular DNA in a nucleoid region and no membrane-bound organelles
Ribosomes free in the cytoplasm as well as on internal membranes
A plasma membrane made of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins
Cell walls, ribosomes and membranes are found in both kinds of cell. Lacking a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles is what defines a prokaryote.
vce-bio12-organelles-and-their-functions: bio12a1-or-1
Which organelle is the site of aerobic cellular respiration stages that produce most of the cell's ATP?
Chloroplast
Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
The mitochondrion carries out the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, which produce most ATP. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
bio12a1-or-2
Cells of the pancreas that secrete large amounts of the protein enzyme amylase would be expected to have large amounts of
smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
lysosomes only.
chloroplasts.
rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.
Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes of the rough ER and modified and packaged by the Golgi apparatus as part of the secretory pathway. Smooth ER synthesises lipids.
bio12a1-or-3
The correct order of organelles in the secretory pathway for an exported protein is
Golgi apparatus → rough ER → vesicle → plasma membrane
nucleus → lysosome → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane
ribosome on rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
mitochondrion → rough ER → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane
Proteins are synthesised by ribosomes on the rough ER, carried in vesicles to the Golgi for modification and packaging, then secretory vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane (exocytosis).
bio12a1-or-4
A cell treated with a drug that disrupts lysosome membranes would most likely
stop producing ATP.
be unable to synthesise proteins.
lose its cell wall.
be damaged by released hydrolytic enzymes digesting its own components.
Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes. If released into the cytosol they can break down cell components. ATP production and protein synthesis depend on other organelles.
bio12a1-or-5
Which organelle is correctly matched to its function?
Smooth ER: synthesis of lipids and detoxification
Ribosome: packaging proteins into vesicles
Vacuole: site of photosynthesis
Nucleolus: production of ATP
Smooth ER makes lipids (including steroids) and detoxifies drugs, e.g. in liver cells. Ribosomes synthesise polypeptides, the Golgi packages them, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
bio12a1-or-6
Describe the structure and function of the chloroplast. (3 marks)

Double membrane-bound organelle; contains stacks of thylakoid membranes (grana) containing chlorophyll, surrounded by fluid stroma; site of photosynthesis, converting light energy into chemical energy in glucose (light-dependent reactions on thylakoids, light-independent reactions in stroma).
bio12a1-or-7
Muscle cells in the flight muscles of birds contain many more mitochondria than skin cells. Explain this difference. (2 marks)

Flight muscle contracts repeatedly and has a very high energy demand; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration producing ATP, so more mitochondria supply the large amounts of ATP needed for contraction, whereas skin cells require far less.
bio12a1-or-8
Explain the role of the nucleus in controlling cell activities. (2 marks)

The nucleus contains the DNA (chromosomes) holding the genetic instructions; genes are transcribed into mRNA which leaves through nuclear pores to ribosomes, so the nucleus controls which proteins (including enzymes) are made and hence cell activities.
bio12a1-or-9
A plant cell is placed in pure water and becomes firm. What is the main reason?
The cell wall absorbs water and swells until it stretches
The central vacuole takes up water, pressing the cytoplasm against the cell wall
The chloroplasts absorb water and swell
The lysosomes release water into the cytosol

Water enters the central vacuole by osmosis, creating turgor pressure against the rigid cell wall, which keeps the cell firm. The cell wall does not swell, and chloroplasts and lysosomes do not store water.
bio12a1-or-10
Which structure is present in plant cells but absent from animal cells?
A nucleus
A cell membrane
A cell wall made mainly of cellulose
Ribosomes
Plant cells have a rigid cell wall of cellulose outside the cell membrane, which animal cells lack. Nuclei, cell membranes and ribosomes are found in both cell types.
bio12a1-or-11
Centrioles are most directly involved in which process?
Photosynthesis
Storage of starch
Digestion of bacteria
Organising spindle fibres during cell division

Centrioles, found in animal cells, help organise the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes during mitosis. Photosynthesis, starch storage and digestion of bacteria are not centriole functions; the last is a lysosome function.
bio12a1-or-12
Which function is performed by the Golgi apparatus but not by the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
Sorting, modifying and packaging proteins into vesicles
Synthesising polypeptides on attached ribosomes
Breaking down hydrogen peroxide
Producing ATP by aerobic respiration

The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles, while the rough ER synthesises polypeptides on its ribosomes. Hydrogen peroxide is broken down in peroxisomes and ATP is made in mitochondria.
bio12a1-or-13
Which structure gives an animal cell its shape and moves organelles through the cytoplasm?
Cell wall
Cytoskeleton
Nuclear envelope
Central vacuole

The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres that supports cell shape and moves organelles and vesicles. Animal cells have no cell wall, the nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus, and the large central vacuole is a plant cell feature.
bio12a1-or-14
What distinguishes rough endoplasmic reticulum from smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
It contains chlorophyll
It is surrounded by a double membrane
It has ribosomes attached to its outer surface
It is the main site of lipid synthesis

Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface, which is why it is the main site of protein synthesis for export. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is the site of lipid synthesis, while chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts.
bio12a1-or-15
A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium and fuses the resulting vesicle with an organelle containing digestive enzymes. Which organelle is this?
Ribosome
Chloroplast
Nucleolus
Lysosome
Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest engulfed material such as bacteria. Ribosomes make proteins, chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
bio12a1-or-16
What is the main advantage of the inner mitochondrial membrane being folded into cristae?
It increases the surface area for electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase
It stores the mitochondrion's genetic material
It allows glycogen to be stored for later use
It prevents oxygen from entering the matrix

Folding increases the membrane surface area, so more electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase can be packed in, increasing ATP production. The other options describe functions that do not relate to cristae.
bio12a1-or-17
In which region of the chloroplast do the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
Thylakoid membranes
Stroma
Outer membrane
Cristae

The light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the fluid stroma, using ATP and NADPH made in the light-dependent reactions. Thylakoid membranes are where the light-dependent reactions occur, and cristae are found in mitochondria.
bio12a1-or-18
What are the main components of chromosomes in a eukaryotic cell?
RNA and lipid
Glucose polymers and ribosomes
ATP and phospholipids
DNA wound around histone proteins
Chromosomes are DNA bound to histone proteins, which package the DNA within the nucleus. RNA, lipids, glucose polymers, ribosomes and ATP are not the main components of chromosomes.
bio12a1-or-19
Which statement about both mitochondria and chloroplasts is correct?
Both contain their own DNA and ribosomes
Both are surrounded by a single membrane
Both produce oxygen as a by-product
Both are found only in animal cells

Both organelles contain their own DNA and ribosomes, which is consistent with the endosymbiotic theory. Both have a double membrane, only chloroplasts release oxygen, and mitochondria occur in plant cells as well as animal cells.
bio12a1-or-20
Lysosomes are formed by vesicles budding off which organelle?
Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Chloroplast
Nucleolus
Lysosomes form from vesicles that bud off the Golgi apparatus. Mitochondria and chloroplasts do not give rise to lysosomes, and the nucleolus is located inside the nucleus.
bio12a1-or-21
State the function of ribosomes. (1 mark)
Site of protein synthesis (translation of mRNA into a polypeptide) [1]
bio12a1-or-22
State the function of the nucleolus. (1 mark)
Production of ribosomal subunits, including synthesis of ribosomal RNA [1]
bio12a1-or-23
Mature mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus and mitochondria. Explain how this is an advantage for their function in transporting oxygen. (2 marks)

Lack of a nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried per cell [1]; without mitochondria the cell does not use oxygen for its own respiration, so more oxygen is delivered to the tissues [1]
bio12a1-or-24
Explain how the cell wall prevents a plant cell from bursting when it takes in large amounts of water. (2 marks)
The cell wall is rigid and strong, made of cellulose [1]; it resists the outward pressure (turgor pressure) generated by the vacuole and cytoplasm, so the cell does not burst [1]
bio12a1-or-25
Describe the structure and function of lysosomes. (3 marks)

Membrane-bound sacs (vesicles) containing hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes [1]; the enzymes break down materials taken into the cell, such as food particles [1]; they also digest worn-out organelles so their components can be recycled [1]
bio12a1-or-26
Describe the structure of a mitochondrion, naming three parts. (3 marks)
Double membrane: a smooth outer membrane and an inner membrane [1]; the inner membrane is folded into cristae [1]; a fluid matrix containing enzymes, mitochondrial DNA and ribosomes [1]
bio12a1-or-27
A drug stops the nuclear pores from functioning. Explain the likely effect on protein synthesis in the cytoplasm. (4 marks)

mRNA is made in the nucleus by transcription of DNA [1]; mRNA cannot pass through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm [1]; ribosomes in the cytoplasm cannot receive the mRNA template for translation [1]; so fewer proteins (including enzymes) are made, disrupting cell activities [1]
bio12a1-or-28
Compare the structure and function of the chloroplast and the mitochondrion. (4 marks)

Both have a double outer membrane [1]; the chloroplast has thylakoids stacked in grana containing chlorophyll and a stroma, while the mitochondrion has cristae and a matrix [1]; the chloroplast carries out photosynthesis, converting light energy into chemical energy in glucose [1]; the mitochondrion carries out aerobic respiration, releasing energy from glucose to make ATP [1]
bio12a1-or-29
A student claims that all living cells contain a nucleus. Evaluate this claim using one example. (2 marks)
The claim is incorrect [1]; prokaryotic cells such as bacteria have no nucleus, and their DNA lies in a nucleoid region in the cytoplasm [1]
vce-bio12-or-c1
A cell type has unusually large amounts of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. It most likely:
Stores large amounts of fat, such as the cells of adipose tissue
Carries out photosynthesis, such as the palisade cells of a leaf
Secretes large amounts of protein, such as digestive enzymes or antibodies
Divides very rapidly, such as the cells at the tip of a growing root
Rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins for export and the Golgi packages them into secretory vesicles.
vce-bio12-plasma-membrane-structure: bio12a1-pm-1
In the fluid mosaic model, the 'mosaic' refers to
the ability of phospholipids to move laterally.
the scattered pattern of proteins embedded in the phospholipid bilayer.
the carbohydrate layer inside the cell.
the two layers of the cell wall.
'Mosaic' describes the varied proteins dotted through the bilayer; 'fluid' describes the lateral movement of phospholipids and proteins.
bio12a1-pm-2
Phospholipids form a bilayer in water because
their tails are hydrophilic and face the water.
they are attracted to cholesterol in the cytosol.
they are held together by covalent bonds between molecules.
their phosphate heads are hydrophilic and their fatty acid tails are hydrophobic.
The amphipathic phospholipids orient with hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous fluid on both sides and hydrophobic tails facing inward, away from water.
bio12a1-pm-3
Which component of animal plasma membranes helps maintain fluidity across a range of temperatures?
Cholesterol
Glycoproteins
Cellulose
Channel proteins
Cholesterol reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents tight packing of phospholipids at low temperatures. Glycoproteins are involved in cell recognition.
bio12a1-pm-4
A cell-surface molecule that allows immune cells to recognise a cell as 'self' is most likely a
phospholipid.
glycoprotein.
cholesterol molecule.
fatty acid.
Glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer surface act as recognition markers (e.g. MHC markers). Phospholipids and cholesterol are structural.
bio12a1-pm-5
Researchers found that a membrane from an Antarctic fish has a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acid tails than that of a tropical fish. The most likely reason is that unsaturated tails
pack more tightly, making the membrane more rigid in cold water.
have kinks that prevent tight packing, keeping the membrane fluid at low temperatures.
are hydrophilic and attract water.
act as transport proteins.
Double bonds create kinks in unsaturated tails, so phospholipids cannot pack closely, which maintains fluidity in cold conditions.
bio12a1-pm-6
Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. (3 marks)

A phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing outward and hydrophobic tails inward; proteins (integral/transmembrane and peripheral) are embedded in or attached to the bilayer in a mosaic pattern, with cholesterol and glycoproteins/glycolipids present; components can move laterally, so the membrane is fluid.
bio12a1-pm-7
Explain why small non-polar molecules such as O₂ can cross the plasma membrane freely but ions such as Na⁺ cannot. (2 marks)

O₂ is small and non-polar so it dissolves in and passes through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer; Na⁺ is charged and is repelled by the hydrophobic tails, so it needs channel or carrier proteins to cross.
bio12a1-pm-8
State two functions of membrane proteins. (2 marks)

Any two: transport (channel or carrier proteins); receptors for signalling molecules such as hormones; enzymes; cell recognition (glycoproteins); attachment/adhesion to other cells or the cytoskeleton.
bio12a1-pm-9
The part of a transmembrane protein that passes through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer is made mainly of
nonpolar amino acids whose side chains interact with the fatty acid tails.
amino acids with polar or charged side chains.
phosphate groups.
sugar residues.

Nonpolar side chains interact favourably with the fatty acid tails in the core. Polar or charged residues would be repelled by the core, so they are found at the ends of the protein facing the aqueous fluid.
bio12a1-pm-10
Which of these is a glycolipid's distinguishing feature compared with a phospholipid?
A phosphate group in each fatty acid tail.
No fatty acid tails at all.
A carbohydrate head group in place of a phosphate-containing head group.
A protein chain attached to its head group.

Glycolipids have a sugar head group instead of the phosphate-containing head found in phospholipids, and they are located on the outer surface of the membrane. A protein chain is not part of a glycolipid, which is why the last option is wrong.
bio12a1-pm-11
Phospholipids rarely move from one layer of the bilayer to the other. The main reason is that
the two layers are joined by covalent bonds between their heads.
the phosphate heads would have to pass through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.
cholesterol binds each phospholipid in one fixed position.
the fatty acid tails are too short to reach the other layer.

Moving a charged, hydrophilic head through the nonpolar core is energetically unfavourable, so flip-flop is rare while sideways movement within one layer is common. The layers are held together by hydrophobic interactions, not covalent bonds, which makes the first option wrong.
bio12a1-pm-12
Which observation best shows that membrane proteins can move laterally within the bilayer?
Proteins are found on both the inner and outer surfaces of the membrane.
Membrane proteins appear as particles when the membrane is viewed by electron microscopy.
Fluorescent markers on proteins of two fused cells spread over the whole combined membrane over time.
The phospholipid tails in one cell are saturated and in another cell they are unsaturated.
Labelled proteins that mix across a fused membrane show that they are free to move sideways in the bilayer. The other options describe the distribution or structure of proteins, not their movement.
bio12a1-pm-13
A channel protein allows Na⁺ ions to cross the membrane. Which feature of the channel is essential for this?
A hydrophilic lining that forms a water-filled pathway through the bilayer, so Na⁺ does not contact the hydrophobic core.
A hydrophobic lining that matches the fatty acid tails, so the ion dissolves in it.
Covalent bonds that attach the channel to the phospholipid tails.
A large cytosolic tail that holds the ion outside the membrane.
Charged ions need a hydrophilic pathway through the membrane, which a water-filled pore provides. A hydrophobic lining would repel the charged ion rather than let it pass.
bio12a1-pm-14
Compared with a membrane made of phospholipids with long fatty acid tails, a membrane made of phospholipids with short fatty acid tails (same degree of saturation) would be
less fluid, because short tails pack more closely together.
more fluid, because short tails form stronger hydrogen bonds with water.
less fluid, because short tails form more hydrogen bonds with each other.
more fluid, because short tails have fewer contacts between neighbouring tails.

Shorter tails have less contact (van der Waals attraction) between neighbouring tails, so they pack less tightly and the membrane is more fluid. The option claiming closer packing is tempting, but it reverses the effect of shorter tails.
bio12a1-pm-15
How does a carrier protein differ from a channel protein?
A carrier protein forms a continuous water-filled pore, while a channel protein changes shape.
A carrier protein binds a specific substance and changes shape to move it across, while a channel protein forms a pore.
A carrier protein is always peripheral, while a channel protein is always inside the cytosol.
A carrier protein always uses ATP, whereas a channel protein never moves substances.

Channel proteins form open pores, whereas carrier proteins bind a specific solute and change shape to move it. Some carriers use ATP but many do not, so the option saying carriers always use ATP is wrong.
bio12a1-pm-16
Which of the following is NOT a component of an animal plasma membrane?
Cholesterol
Cellulose
Glycoproteins
Phospholipids
Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide found in plant cell walls and is absent from animal plasma membranes. Cholesterol, glycoproteins and phospholipids are all found in animal plasma membranes.
bio12a1-pm-17
Membrane fluidity increases as temperature rises. The best explanation is that
cholesterol melts and becomes a liquid between the phospholipids.
the phosphate heads lose their charge, so they pack more tightly.
the phospholipids gain kinetic energy, so they move more and the bilayer becomes looser.
the bilayer absorbs heat and becomes covalently cross-linked.
Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of the phospholipids, so they move more and pack less tightly. Cholesterol does not melt; it actually reduces fluidity changes at high temperatures.
bio12a1-pm-18
A receptor protein in the membrane responds to one particular hormone and ignores other hormones. The most likely explanation is that its binding site
is made of phospholipid, so it attracts only lipid-soluble molecules.
is located inside the hydrophobic core, away from other molecules.
is the same as the binding site of every other membrane receptor.
has a shape and chemical properties complementary to that hormone.
Specific binding depends on a complementary shape and chemistry, so only the matching hormone fits the site. Receptors are proteins, not phospholipids, which makes the lipid-soluble option wrong.
bio12a1-pm-19
Where in the plasma membrane are cholesterol molecules located?
Dissolved in the cytosol, away from the bilayer.
Among the phospholipid fatty acid tails, with its small hydroxyl group near the phospholipid heads.
Attached covalently to the tips of membrane proteins.
Between the phosphate heads, with its ring structure in the aqueous fluid.

Cholesterol inserts between phospholipids, with its hydroxyl group near the polar heads and its rigid ring and hydrocarbon body among the fatty acid tails. The option placing the ring in the aqueous fluid is wrong because the ring is hydrophobic.
bio12a1-pm-20
Why is membrane fluidity important for vesicle transport?
It allows membranes to bend, fuse and mix their components during vesicle budding and fusion.
It keeps the membrane rigid so that vesicles can hold their shape.
It stops proteins from moving so that receptors stay in place.
It prevents phospholipids from forming a bilayer.

A fluid bilayer lets membranes bend and fuse, and lets lipids and proteins rearrange as vesicles bud from and fuse with membranes. A rigid membrane would make these changes difficult, which is why the rigidity option is wrong.
bio12a1-pm-21
Which statement about the asymmetry of the plasma membrane is correct?
Carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids are found only on the extracellular (outer) surface.
Carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids are found only on the cytosolic (inner) surface.
The inner and outer leaflets of the bilayer have identical lipid and protein composition.
Cholesterol is found only in the inner leaflet of the bilayer.

The plasma membrane is asymmetric, and its carbohydrate chains are always on the outer surface. Cholesterol occurs in both leaflets, and the two leaflets differ in composition, so the other options are wrong.
bio12a1-pm-22
Which of these is the main lipid making up the plasma membrane?
Triglycerides
Cholesterol
Waxes
Phospholipids

Phospholipids form the bilayer and are the most abundant lipid in the membrane. Cholesterol is present but in smaller amounts, and triglycerides are energy-storage lipids that do not form membrane bilayers.
bio12a1-pm-23
Peptide hormones such as insulin cannot pass through the plasma membrane, yet they can still change the activity of a target cell. Explain how. (3 marks)

Peptide hormones are polar and charged, so they cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer [1]; they bind to a specific receptor protein on the outer surface of the membrane [1]; the binding causes a change in the receptor that triggers a response inside the cell, such as a second messenger [1].
bio12a1-pm-24
Several enzymes that catalyse consecutive steps of a metabolic pathway are embedded close together in a membrane. Explain how this arrangement can increase the rate of the pathway. (2 marks)
The product of one enzyme is passed directly to the next enzyme in the sequence [1]; this reduces the time for intermediates to diffuse away, so the pathway runs faster [1].
bio12a1-pm-25
A small tear forms in a phospholipid bilayer in an aqueous environment. Explain why the bilayer tends to reseal itself. (2 marks)
Hydrophobic tails exposed at the edges of the tear are unfavourable in water [1]; the phospholipids rearrange so the tails are shielded and the heads face the water, closing the gap [1].
bio12a1-pm-26
A membrane contains 3 200 cholesterol molecules and 12 800 phospholipid molecules. Express the ratio of cholesterol to phospholipid molecules in simplest form. (2 marks)
bio12a1-pm-27

A transmembrane α-helix rises about 0.15 nm per amino acid residue. Calculate the length of a 20-residue transmembrane helix, and state whether it could span a hydrophobic core about 3.0 nm thick. (2 marks)
20 × 0.15 nm = 3.0 nm [1]; this equals the thickness of the hydrophobic core, so the helix can just span the bilayer [1].
bio12a1-pm-28
Beetroot cells were placed in water at 20 °C and in water at 60 °C for 10 minutes. The water at 60 °C turned red, but the water at 20 °C stayed colourless. Explain this result. (3 marks)

The high temperature damages the membranes, disrupting their structure and denaturing their proteins [1]; the membranes lose their selective permeability [1]; the red betalain pigment stored in the cells diffuses out into the water [1].
vce-bio12-pm-c1
Glucose cannot diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer mainly because it is:
Too small to be detected by the membrane, so it needs a channel protein to guide it
Non-polar, so it is attracted to the hydrophobic tails and becomes trapped in the membrane
Large and polar, so it cannot pass between the hydrophobic tails; it needs a carrier protein
Always moving against its gradient, so it can only cross the membrane by active transport
Small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass through the bilayer. Large or polar molecules need channel or carrier proteins.
vce-bio12-passive-transport-across-membr: bio12a1-pt-1
Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because facilitated diffusion
requires ATP.
moves substances against their concentration gradient.
only moves water.
requires membrane channel or carrier proteins.
Facilitated diffusion is passive (no ATP) and occurs down a concentration gradient but needs a protein channel or carrier. Moving against a gradient is active transport.
bio12a1-pt-2
A red blood cell is placed in a solution that is hypertonic to its cytoplasm. What will happen?
Water leaves the cell and it shrinks (crenates).
Water enters the cell and it bursts (lyses).
There is no net movement of water.
Solute moves into the cell by osmosis.
In a hypertonic solution the solute concentration outside is higher, so water moves out by osmosis and the cell shrinks. Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute.
bio12a1-pt-3
Plant cells placed in pure water do not burst because
they have no aquaporins.
the cell wall resists expansion, so the cell becomes turgid.
water cannot cross the plasma membrane of plant cells.
the vacuole pumps water out by active transport.
Water enters by osmosis, but the rigid cellulose wall exerts pressure back, so the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting.
bio12a1-pt-4

A student measured the mass of potato cylinders after 24 hours in sucrose solutions. The cylinders gained mass at 0.0 and 0.2 mol L⁻¹, showed no change at 0.3 mol L⁻¹ and lost mass at 0.4 and 0.6 mol L⁻¹. What can be concluded?
The potato cells are isotonic to about 0.3 mol L⁻¹ sucrose.
Sucrose entered the cells at low concentrations.
The potato cells are hypertonic to 0.6 mol L⁻¹ sucrose.
Water moved into the cylinders at 0.4 mol L⁻¹.
No net mass change means no net water movement, so the cell sap is approximately isotonic to 0.3 mol L⁻¹. At 0.6 mol L⁻¹ the solution is hypertonic to the cells, so they lost water.
bio12a1-pt-5
Increasing the temperature of a solution generally increases the rate of diffusion because
molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster.
the concentration gradient is reversed.
more ATP is available.
the membrane becomes less permeable.
Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles, so they move and collide more, increasing diffusion rate. Diffusion does not use ATP.
bio12a1-pt-6
Define osmosis. (2 marks)

The net movement of water molecules across a selectively (partially) permeable membrane; from a region of lower solute concentration (higher free water concentration) to a region of higher solute concentration.
bio12a1-pt-7
People with cystic fibrosis have faulty CFTR channel proteins, so chloride ions do not move out of lung epithelial cells. Explain why this results in thick, sticky mucus. (3 marks)

Cl⁻ ions normally diffuse out through CFTR channels into the mucus (facilitated diffusion); without this, solute concentration outside the cell stays low; so less water follows by osmosis into the mucus, leaving it dehydrated, thick and sticky.
bio12a1-pt-8
Explain why glucose enters most body cells by facilitated diffusion rather than simple diffusion. (2 marks)

Glucose is a relatively large, polar molecule that cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer; it needs specific carrier (GLUT) proteins to move down its concentration gradient.
bio12a1-pt-9
Which molecule is most likely to cross a phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion?
oxygen (O₂)
glucose
sodium ions (Na⁺)
amino acids

Small non-polar molecules such as O₂ dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuse directly. Glucose, charged ions and amino acids are too large or too polar to cross the core without a carrier or channel protein.
bio12a1-pt-10
A cell is placed in an isotonic solution. Which statement is correct?
Water moves rapidly out of the cell, so the cell shrinks.
Water moves in and out at equal rates, so there is no net change in cell volume.
Solute moves out of the cell until the solute concentrations are equal.
The solution has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so the cell shrinks.

An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm, so water moves in and out at equal rates and there is no net change. The option describing lower solute outside the cell describes a hypotonic solution, which makes the cell swell, not shrink.
bio12a1-pt-11
Which factor does NOT directly affect the rate of simple diffusion across a membrane?
the concentration gradient
the surface area of the membrane
the amount of ATP in the cell
the temperature

Simple diffusion is passive, so its rate depends on the concentration gradient, surface area, diffusion distance, temperature and molecular size. ATP is used only in active transport. Temperature is a tempting wrong answer because it does change the kinetic energy of particles.
bio12a1-pt-12
Which of the following is an example of active transport rather than passive transport?
oxygen moving into a respiring cell down its concentration gradient
water entering a root hair cell through aquaporins, down its gradient
carbon dioxide leaving a respiring cell by simple diffusion
sodium ions pumped out of a cell against their gradient by the sodium–potassium pump

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP, as the sodium–potassium pump does. The other three move down a concentration gradient without ATP, so they are passive.
bio12a1-pt-13
A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sucrose solution and its cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall. What is this process called?
plasmolysis
lysis
crenation
turgidity

Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell loses water to a hypertonic solution and the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall. Lysis is bursting and crenation is shrinking, both of animal cells; turgidity is the firm state of a plant cell in a hypotonic solution.
bio12a1-pt-14
Which feature of a small cell most helps simple diffusion supply all of its needs?
a low surface area to volume ratio
a high surface area to volume ratio
a thick plasma membrane
a rigid cell wall around the cell

A high surface area to volume ratio means the membrane is large relative to the cell's contents, so diffusion can reach every part of the cell quickly. A low ratio, or a thick membrane that slows diffusion, makes supply harder. A cell wall does not improve diffusion into the cell.
bio12a1-pt-15

A dialysis bag made of partially permeable tubing contains glucose solution and starch solution and is placed in distilled water. After 30 minutes, which substance or substances would be found in the water outside the bag?
starch only
neither glucose nor starch
glucose only
both glucose and starch

Glucose molecules are small enough to pass through the pores of the tubing and diffuse out, while starch molecules are too large and stay inside. The starch-only option reverses the effect of pore size, and the both option ignores the size limit.
bio12a1-pt-16
The rate of glucose uptake by facilitated diffusion levels off as the external glucose concentration keeps increasing. Why does this happen?
glucose molecules begin to repel one another
the concentration gradient reverses
the cell starts to pump glucose out using ATP
all the carrier proteins are occupied, so transport is at its maximum rate

Facilitated diffusion depends on a limited number of carrier proteins. When all are occupied, adding more glucose cannot increase the rate. The gradient still exists and the process stays passive, so reversal and ATP-driven pumping are wrong.
bio12a1-pt-17
Which statement describes a hypotonic solution relative to the cytoplasm of a cell?
It has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water tends to move into the cell by osmosis.
It has a higher solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water tends to move out of the cell.
It has the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm, so there is no tendency for water to move.
It has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so solute tends to move into the cell by osmosis.

A hypotonic solution has less solute than the cytoplasm, so water moves into the cell by osmosis. The description of higher solute outside the cell is a hypertonic solution. Osmosis moves water, not solute, so the last option is wrong.
bio12a1-pt-18
The concentration of oxygen inside a cell is 0.02 mmol L⁻¹ and outside the cell it is 0.10 mmol L⁻¹. In which direction does oxygen move, and why?
Out of the cell, because the cell has a higher concentration of oxygen.
No net movement, because oxygen is non-polar.
Into the cell, down its concentration gradient from the higher outside concentration.
Into the cell, because active transport moves oxygen against its gradient.

Oxygen is at a higher concentration outside (0.10 mmol L⁻¹) than inside (0.02 mmol L⁻¹), so it diffuses into the cell down the gradient without ATP. Its non-polar nature allows it to cross, so there is net movement, and active transport is not needed for a downhill move.
bio12a1-pt-19
A potato cylinder with an initial mass of 5.00 g gains mass and reaches 5.60 g after 24 hours in pure water. What is the percentage change in mass?
Percentage change = (change in mass ÷ initial mass) × 100 = (0.60 ÷ 5.00) × 100 = 12.0%. Dividing by the final mass gives 10.7%, leaving out the ×100 gives 0.12%, and 0.60% is just the raw mass gain.
bio12a1-pt-20
In an experiment investigating osmosis using potato cylinders in sucrose solutions, which variable is the independent variable?
the sucrose concentration of the solutions
the change in mass of the cylinders
the length of the potato cylinders
the time the cylinders are left in the solution

The independent variable is the one the investigator deliberately changes, here the sucrose concentration. The change in mass is measured, so it is the dependent variable, and length and time are kept constant as controlled variables.
bio12a1-pt-21
Carrier proteins used in facilitated diffusion are specific to particular molecules. What explains this specificity?
they are made of phospholipid, so they only interact with fat-soluble molecules
each binding site has a shape that fits only particular molecules
they use ATP to change shape for each molecule they carry
they transport only water, which then carries other molecules along with it

Specificity comes from the shape of the binding site on the carrier protein, which is complementary to the shape of one type of molecule. Carrier proteins are not made of lipid, and facilitated diffusion does not use ATP. Water is moved by aquaporins, not carried along by carriers.
bio12a1-pt-22
If the thickness of a membrane is doubled, with all other factors kept the same, the rate of simple diffusion of a gas across it will most likely
double
stay the same
approximately halve
increase about four times

The rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance, so doubling the distance roughly halves the rate. Doubling the rate reverses the relationship, staying the same ignores distance, and a fourfold increase wrongly applies a squared relationship.
bio12a1-pt-23
Define diffusion. (2 marks)
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration [1]; down a concentration gradient, without the input of energy (ATP) [1].
bio12a1-pt-24
Explain why heating beetroot tissue in water causes red pigment to leak out into the surrounding water. (2 marks)

Heat denatures the membrane proteins and disrupts the phospholipid bilayer, making the membrane more permeable [1]; so the pigment molecules can diffuse out of the cell down their concentration gradient [1].
bio12a1-pt-25
Compare simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion, giving two similarities and two differences. (4 marks)

Similarity: both are passive and require no ATP [1]; both move substances down a concentration gradient [1]. Difference: simple diffusion needs no membrane protein, whereas facilitated diffusion requires channel or carrier proteins [1]; facilitated diffusion can become saturated when all carriers are occupied, whereas the rate of simple diffusion rises in proportion to the gradient [1].
bio12a1-pt-26

A dialysis bag containing starch solution is placed in a beaker of iodine solution. After 20 minutes the contents of the bag turn blue-black, but no starch is found in the beaker. Explain both observations. (3 marks)

Iodine molecules are small enough to pass through the pores of the dialysis tubing, moving down their concentration gradient into the bag [1]; the iodine reacts with starch to form a blue-black colour [1]; starch molecules are too large to pass through the pores and remain in the bag [1].
bio12a1-pt-27
Describe the role of aquaporins in the movement of water into a cell. (2 marks)
Aquaporins are channel proteins embedded in the membrane [1]; they allow water molecules to cross the membrane rapidly by facilitated diffusion, down the water concentration gradient [1].
bio12a1-pt-28

A patient is given an intravenous drip of 0.9% saline, and their red blood cells keep their normal shape. Explain why. A second patient is given an intravenous drip of distilled water, and their red blood cells burst. Explain why. (4 marks)

Saline is isotonic to the cytoplasm of the red blood cells [1]; so water moves in and out at equal rates, with no net water movement [1]. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm (lower solute concentration) [1]; so water moves into the cells by osmosis, causing them to swell and lyse (burst) [1].
bio12a1-pt-29
Explain why the net rate of diffusion decreases as a solution moves towards equilibrium. (3 marks)

The concentration gradient becomes smaller as particles spread out [1]; so there is a smaller difference between the rates of particles moving in each direction, reducing the net movement [1]; at equilibrium particles move in both directions at equal rates, so the net rate is zero [1].
vce-bio12-pt-c1
A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. After some time:
Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells until the cell wall bursts
Salt enters by osmosis and the cell swells until it becomes turgid
Nothing happens, because the cellulose cell wall stops water moving
Water leaves by osmosis and the cytoplasm pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis)
The solution is hypertonic, so water moves out down its concentration gradient. The cell wall stops the cell bursting in water, but it does not stop water leaving.
vce-bio12-active-transport-endocytosis-a: bio12a1-at-1
The sodium–potassium pump moves
3 Na⁺ into the cell and 2 K⁺ out, without ATP.
water into the cell against its gradient.
Na⁺ and K⁺ down their concentration gradients.
3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in, using ATP.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses one ATP per cycle to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, both against their concentration gradients.
bio12a1-at-2
A neutrophil engulfing a bacterium is an example of
exocytosis.
pinocytosis.
phagocytosis.
facilitated diffusion.
Phagocytosis ('cell eating') is a type of endocytosis in which large solid particles are engulfed in a vesicle. Pinocytosis takes in fluid.
bio12a1-at-3

Root hair cells were placed in a solution containing a respiratory inhibitor. Uptake of nitrate ions from soil, where nitrate concentration is lower than inside the cells, stopped. This shows that nitrate uptake
occurs by osmosis.
occurs by simple diffusion.
occurs by facilitated diffusion.
requires ATP from respiration and so is active transport.
Uptake against a concentration gradient that stops when respiration (ATP production) is blocked indicates active transport. Passive processes would not depend on ATP.
bio12a1-at-4
Which process releases insulin from beta cells of the pancreas?
Endocytosis
Exocytosis
Osmosis
Phagocytosis
Insulin is a protein packaged into secretory vesicles by the Golgi; the vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release their contents by exocytosis.
bio12a1-at-5

A graph shows the rate of uptake of a substance into cells increasing with external concentration and then levelling off, and the rate is zero in the absence of oxygen. The plateau is best explained by
the concentration gradient disappearing.
all carrier proteins being in use (saturated).
the membrane becoming impermeable.
osmosis stopping.
Carrier-mediated transport plateaus when all carrier proteins are occupied. Dependence on oxygen indicates ATP is needed, so it is active transport.
bio12a1-at-6
Compare active transport with facilitated diffusion. (3 marks)

Similarity: both use specific membrane proteins; difference: active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient whereas facilitated diffusion moves them down the gradient; active transport requires energy from ATP whereas facilitated diffusion is passive.
bio12a1-at-7
Describe the process of endocytosis. (2 marks)

The plasma membrane folds inward (invaginates) around the material outside the cell; the membrane pinches off to form a vesicle that carries the material into the cytoplasm; it requires energy (ATP) and is a form of bulk transport.
bio12a1-at-8
Explain why cells that carry out large amounts of active transport, such as kidney tubule cells, contain many mitochondria. (2 marks)
Active transport requires ATP to power protein pumps; mitochondria produce most ATP through aerobic respiration, so many mitochondria supply the energy needed for continuous active transport.
bio12a1-at-9
Which molecule is hydrolysed directly to release the energy used by the sodium–potassium pump?
Glucose
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
ATP

ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing the energy the pump uses to change shape. Glucose and oxygen are used in aerobic respiration to make ATP, so they are not the molecule that directly powers the pump.
bio12a1-at-10
Which is the best example of exocytosis?
Release of a neurotransmitter from a vesicle into the synapse
Entry of Na⁺ into a neurone through an open channel protein
Entry of water into a root hair cell by osmosis
Entry of glucose into a red blood cell by a carrier protein

In exocytosis a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell, as neurotransmitters are released into a synapse. The other options are passive movements through membrane proteins or osmosis, with no vesicle fusing with the membrane.
bio12a1-at-11
A cell takes in droplets of extracellular fluid containing dissolved proteins by forming tiny vesicles at its membrane. This process is called
phagocytosis.
exocytosis.
pinocytosis.
osmosis.

Pinocytosis ('cell drinking') is endocytosis of fluid and dissolved solutes in small vesicles. Phagocytosis takes in large solid particles, exocytosis releases material from the cell, and osmosis is the passive movement of water.
bio12a1-at-12
In one cycle, a sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. If 1200 Na⁺ are moved out of a cell, how many K⁺ are moved in?
1200 ÷ 3 = 400 cycles, and each cycle moves 2 K⁺ in, giving 400 × 2 = 800 K⁺. Dividing 1200 by 2 gives 600, which uses the K⁺ number in the wrong place, and 400 counts cycles rather than ions.
bio12a1-at-13
A cell's sodium–potassium pumps move 300 Na⁺ out of the cell. Assuming one ATP is hydrolysed per cycle and each cycle moves 3 Na⁺ out, how many ATP molecules are used?
300 ÷ 3 = 100 cycles, each using one ATP, so 100 ATP molecules are hydrolysed. Using 300 assumes one ATP per ion, and 150 divides by the K⁺ number instead of the Na⁺ number.
bio12a1-at-14
Which organelle fuses with a phagosome (the vesicle containing an engulfed bacterium) to digest its contents?
Lysosome
Ribosome
Centriole
Nucleolus

Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that fuse with the phagosome and break down the engulfed material. Ribosomes make proteins, centrioles organise microtubules, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
bio12a1-at-15
Which feature of the plasma membrane allows vesicles to fuse with it during exocytosis?
Its rigid cellulose layer
Its fluid phospholipid bilayer
Its impermeable protein layer
Its fixed, immobile proteins

The phospholipid bilayer is fluid, so the membrane can deform and merge with a vesicle membrane. Cellulose is a component of plant cell walls, not the plasma membrane, and membrane proteins can move within the bilayer.
bio12a1-at-16
Which description matches receptor-mediated endocytosis?
Random uptake of any fluid as the membrane folds
Engulfment of a bacterium by a white blood cell
Uptake of specific molecules bound to receptors in coated pits
Release of a hormone from a vesicle by fusion with the membrane

In receptor-mediated endocytosis, specific molecules bind to receptor proteins in clathrin-coated pits, which then pinch off as vesicles, making the process selective. Random fluid uptake is pinocytosis, engulfment of particles is phagocytosis, and hormone release is exocytosis.
bio12a1-at-17
Which statement about active transport is NOT correct?
It requires a membrane protein.
It requires energy from ATP.
It moves substances down their concentration gradients.
It can move substances against their concentration gradients.

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradients using membrane proteins and ATP. Moving substances down a gradient is passive transport, such as diffusion, and does not need ATP.
bio12a1-at-18
What happens to the membrane of a secretory vesicle during exocytosis?
It fuses with the plasma membrane, adding to the cell surface membrane.
It is digested by lysosomes before release.
It pinches off inside the cytoplasm to form a new vesicle.
It is broken down into amino acids.

When the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, its membrane becomes part of the cell surface membrane and its contents are released outside. Pinching off inside the cytoplasm describes endocytosis, the opposite process.
bio12a1-at-19
Which statement best distinguishes endocytosis from active transport?
Endocytosis moves individual ions, while active transport moves large droplets.
Endocytosis moves material in bulk inside vesicles, while active transport moves individual molecules or ions through membrane proteins.
Both processes move material only down concentration gradients.
Only endocytosis requires energy from ATP.

Endocytosis is bulk transport of material within membrane-bound vesicles, whereas active transport moves individual molecules or ions through membrane proteins. Both processes need ATP, so the last option is wrong, and active transport moves substances against gradients, not down them.
bio12a1-at-20
Name the organelle that packages proteins into vesicles before they are exported by exocytosis. (1 mark)
Golgi apparatus [1].
bio12a1-at-21
Describe two features of endocytosis that distinguish it from simple diffusion. (2 marks)

Endocytosis requires energy from ATP, whereas simple diffusion is passive [1]; endocytosis moves material in bulk inside a membrane-bound vesicle, whereas diffusion moves individual small molecules directly across the membrane [1].
bio12a1-at-22
Explain why a neutrophil must be able to change the shape of its plasma membrane when engulfing a bacterium. (2 marks)
The membrane must extend outwards to surround the bacterium [1]; the flexible phospholipid bilayer and cytoskeleton allow the membrane to deform and enclose the bacterium in a vesicle [1].
bio12a1-at-23
Describe how the sodium–potassium pump moves three Na⁺ out of the cell and two K⁺ into the cell during one cycle. (3 marks)

Three Na⁺ bind to the pump protein on the inside of the cell [1]; ATP is hydrolysed, the phosphate attaches to the pump and it changes shape, releasing the Na⁺ outside [1]; two K⁺ bind from outside, the phosphate is released and the pump returns to its original shape, releasing the K⁺ inside [1].
bio12a1-at-24
Describe the sequence by which a digestive enzyme made by a pancreatic cell is released from the cell. (3 marks)

The enzyme is synthesised on ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum [1]; it is transported to the Golgi apparatus, where it is packaged into vesicles [1]; the vesicles move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it and release the enzyme outside the cell by exocytosis [1].
bio12a1-at-25
Explain how endocytosis and exocytosis allow a cell to move large molecules across its plasma membrane, and identify one property of the membrane that makes both processes possible. (4 marks)

In endocytosis the membrane folds inwards around material outside the cell and pinches off a vesicle that carries it into the cytoplasm [1]; in exocytosis a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside [1]; both processes require energy from ATP [1]; the fluid phospholipid bilayer allows the membrane to deform and fuse with vesicle membranes [1].
vce-bio12-at-c1
Cells lining the gut absorb glucose against a concentration gradient. If a poison stops ATP production, this uptake will:
Stop, because active transport needs energy from ATP
Speed up, because diffusion takes over
Continue unchanged
Reverse by osmosis
Moving a substance against its gradient requires energy. Simple diffusion could only move glucose down its gradient.
vce-bio12-binary-fission: bio12a1-bf-1
Binary fission is the method of cell reproduction used by
plant cells.
animal cells.
prokaryotes such as bacteria.
fungal hyphae only.
Binary fission is how prokaryotes reproduce asexually. Eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis and cytokinesis.
bio12a1-bf-2
Which is the correct sequence of events in binary fission?
DNA replicates → copies move to opposite ends as the cell elongates → septum/cell wall forms → two cells separate
Cell elongates → DNA replicates → chromosomes condense → nuclear envelope breaks down
Spindle forms → chromosomes align → cytokinesis → DNA replicates
Cell divides → DNA replicates → plasmids form

The circular chromosome is copied, the copies separate as the cell elongates, then the membrane pinches in and a new wall (septum) forms between them. There is no spindle or nuclear envelope in prokaryotes.
bio12a1-bf-3
A bacterium divides every 20 minutes under ideal conditions. Starting with one cell, how many cells would be present after 2 hours?
2 hours = 120 min = 6 generations. 2⁶ = 64 cells.
bio12a1-bf-4
Why are the two cells produced by binary fission genetically identical (barring mutation)?
Because crossing over occurs.
Because the nucleus divides by meiosis.
Because they fuse with another bacterium.
Because each receives a copy of the replicated circular chromosome.
The single chromosome is replicated and one copy goes to each daughter cell, so they are clones. Crossing over and meiosis occur in sexual reproduction of eukaryotes.
bio12a1-bf-5
Which feature of mitosis is absent from binary fission?
DNA replication
Division of cytoplasm
Formation of a mitotic spindle
Production of genetically identical cells
Prokaryotes lack spindle fibres made from microtubules. Both processes involve DNA replication, cytoplasm division and produce identical cells.
bio12a1-bf-6
Describe the process of binary fission. (3 marks)
