The circular chromosome (and any plasmids) is replicated; the cell elongates and the two chromosome copies move to opposite ends; the plasma membrane pinches inward and a new cell wall (septum) forms, splitting the cell into two genetically identical daughter cells.
bio12a1-bf-7

Escherichia coli has a generation time of 30 minutes. Calculate the number of cells present after 4 hours starting from 10 cells, and suggest one reason why real populations do not continue to grow at this rate. (3 marks)
4 h = 8 generations; 10 × 2⁸ = 10 × 256 = 2560 cells; growth slows because nutrients run out / wastes accumulate / space becomes limited.
bio12a1-bf-8
Explain why bacterial infections can become serious within hours. (2 marks)

Binary fission is a simple, rapid process with short generation times (e.g. ~20 min); the number of cells doubles each generation, so the population grows exponentially and can reach very large numbers quickly.
bio12a1-bf-9
Plasmids are:
linear chromosomes that carry the cell's essential genes
small, circular DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome that can replicate independently
protein filaments that form the septum
ribosomes that synthesise the cell wall

Plasmids are small circles of DNA found in many bacteria, often carrying non-essential genes such as antibiotic resistance. Linear chromosomes are a eukaryotic feature, so that option wrongly applies eukaryotic structure to bacteria.
bio12a1-bf-10
How many generations of binary fission are needed for one bacterial cell to produce 4096 cells?
Each generation doubles the number of cells, so 2ⁿ = 4096 gives n = 12, because 2¹² = 4096. Choosing 4096 confuses the number of cells with the number of generations.
bio12a1-bf-11
Before dividing by binary fission, a bacterial cell typically grows to:
about half its original size
the same size as before, since it does not need to grow
about ten times its original size
about twice its original size
The cell must roughly double its size so that each daughter cell reaches a normal size after division. Halving the size describes the daughter cells, not the parent before it divides.
bio12a1-bf-12
How many chromosomes does a typical Escherichia coli cell contain?
1 circular chromosome
2 circular chromosomes
23 pairs of linear chromosomes
46 linear chromosomes
E. coli has one circular chromosome, which is replicated before division; two copies exist only briefly during replication. The 23 pairs and 46 options describe the human karyotype, not a bacterium.
bio12a1-bf-13
Which processes can introduce genetic variation into a bacterial population?
crossing over during meiosis
mutation and transfer of DNA between cells, such as plasmid exchange
independent assortment of chromosomes in meiosis I
fertilisation between two gametes

Bacteria do not undergo meiosis or fertilisation, so their variation comes from mutation and from transfer of DNA such as plasmids between cells. The other three options occur only in the sexual reproduction of eukaryotes.
bio12a1-bf-14
Mitochondria reproduce by a process most similar to:
mitosis
meiosis
binary fission
budding

Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA and divide in a way similar to binary fission, which supports the endosymbiotic theory. Mitosis is the nuclear division of eukaryotic cells, which mitochondria do not undergo.
bio12a1-bf-15
A bacterial culture doubles every 15 minutes. How many minutes does it take for one cell to produce 256 cells?
256 = 2⁸, so 8 generations are needed, and 8 × 15 = 120 minutes. The answer 240 comes from doubling the time again, while 90 comes from counting only 6 generations.
bio12a1-bf-16
Generation time for a bacterial population is best defined as:
the time taken for the population to double in number
the time taken for the chromosome to be copied
the time between formation of the septum and cell separation
the time a population spends in the lag phase

Generation time is the time the population takes to double, which under given conditions equals one cycle of binary fission. The other options describe single steps or phases rather than the doubling time.
bio12a1-bf-17
A bacterial population has unlimited nutrients and space. On a graph of cell number against time, with an arithmetic scale, its growth is best shown as:
a flat horizontal line
a J-shaped curve that becomes steeper over time
a straight line with a constant gradient
an S-shaped curve that falls after a peak

Each generation doubles the population, so each time interval adds more cells than the one before, making the curve steeper. A straight line would mean the same number of cells is added in every interval.
bio12a1-bf-18
A bacterial culture is kept at 10 °C instead of its optimum of 37 °C. The rate of binary fission falls mainly because:
the circular chromosome becomes linear at low temperature
plasmids are lost from the cell
enzymes involved in DNA replication and cell division work more slowly
the cell switches to meiosis to conserve energy
Binary fission depends on enzymes, and their rate falls as temperature drops below the optimum. The chromosome does not change shape with temperature, and bacteria do not undergo meiosis.
bio12a1-bf-19
Where does the septum form during binary fission?
in the middle of the cell, between the two chromosome copies
at both ends of the cell, close to each chromosome
at the outer surface of the cell wall
only after the daughter cells have separated
The membrane pinches inward and a new wall forms at the midpoint, between the separated chromosome copies. The septum forms before the daughter cells separate, so the last option is wrong.
bio12a1-bf-20

A single bacterium at 37 °C has a generation time of 20 minutes, and at 25 °C it has a generation time of 60 minutes. Both populations start from one cell. After 2 hours, the population at 25 °C compared with the population at 37 °C is:
four times larger
one-sixteenth the size
the same size
16 times larger
At 37 °C there are 2⁶ = 64 cells after 2 hours, and at 25 °C there are 2² = 4 cells, and 4 ÷ 64 = 1/16. Describing the population as 16 times larger inverts the ratio.
bio12a1-bf-21
A bacterial cell contains one circular chromosome and two plasmids. How many separate circular DNA molecules does it contain?
One chromosome plus two plasmids gives three separate circular DNA molecules. An answer of 1 ignores the plasmids, and an answer of 2 ignores the chromosome.
bio12a1-bf-22
A student states that after binary fission each daughter cell contains only half the DNA of the parent cell. Explain why this is incorrect. (2 marks)
The chromosome is replicated before division, so the parent has two copies of its DNA [1]; each daughter receives one complete copy, the same amount of DNA as the original parent cell [1].
bio12a1-bf-23
A bacterial culture grows from 250 to 8000 cells in 3 hours. Calculate the generation time, in minutes. (3 marks)
8000 ÷ 250 = 32 = 2⁵, so 5 generations occurred [1]; 3 hours = 180 minutes [1]; generation time = 180 ÷ 5 = 36 minutes [1].
bio12a1-bf-24
Explain how plasmids can allow a bacterial population to become resistant to an antibiotic within a few generations. (3 marks)

Some bacteria carry plasmids with genes for antibiotic resistance [1]; the plasmid can be transferred to other bacteria, spreading the resistance genes [1]; the surviving resistant cells divide by binary fission, so the resistant population grows rapidly [1].
bio12a1-bf-25
Compare binary fission in prokaryotes with mitosis in eukaryotes. Identify two similarities and two differences. (4 marks)

Similarity: the DNA is replicated before the cell divides [1]; similarity: both produce two genetically identical daughter cells [1]; difference: binary fission does not use a spindle of microtubules, whereas mitosis does [1]; difference: a prokaryote has one circular chromosome not enclosed in a nucleus, whereas a eukaryote has multiple linear chromosomes enclosed in a nucleus [1].
bio12a1-bf-26
Explain why the chromosome must be fully replicated before the two copies separate during binary fission. (2 marks)
Each daughter cell must receive one complete copy of the chromosome [1]; separating before replication is complete would leave a cell with incomplete genetic information [1].
vce-bio12-bf-c1
A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes in ideal conditions. Starting from one cell, about how many cells are there after 3 hours?
3 hours = 9 generations of 20 minutes. Cells = 2⁹ = 512. Growth is exponential, not linear.
vce-bio12-the-eukaryotic-cell-cycle-and-: bio12a1-cc-1
During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
G1
M
G2
S
DNA synthesis occurs in the S phase of interphase. G1 and G2 are growth phases, and M is mitosis.
bio12a1-cc-2
In which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
Prophase
Metaphase
Anaphase
Telophase
In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles. In metaphase chromosomes align at the equator.
bio12a1-cc-3
A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each daughter cell have after mitosis?
Mitosis produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent, each with the full diploid number of 46.
bio12a1-cc-4

In a root tip squash, 200 cells were counted: 180 in interphase, 10 in prophase, 4 in metaphase, 3 in anaphase and 3 in telophase. If the cell cycle takes 20 hours, approximately how long is spent in prophase?
0.4 hours
1 hour
2 hours
10 hours
Time is proportional to the fraction of cells in that stage: 10/200 × 20 h = 1 hour.
bio12a1-cc-5
Cytokinesis in plant cells differs from that in animal cells because in plant cells
a cell plate forms between the two nuclei.
a cleavage furrow forms.
no new membrane is produced.
the nucleus divides after the cytoplasm.
Plant cells have rigid walls, so vesicles from the Golgi form a cell plate that becomes the new wall. Animal cells pinch in by a cleavage furrow.
bio12a1-cc-6
Describe the events of prophase and metaphase of mitosis. (3 marks)

Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibres begin to form from the centrosomes; metaphase: chromosomes line up along the equator (metaphase plate) with spindle fibres attached to each centromere.
bio12a1-cc-7
Explain the role of the G1 and G2 checkpoints in the cell cycle. (2 marks)

Checkpoints are control points where the cell checks conditions before proceeding; G1 checks cell size, nutrients and DNA damage before replication, and G2 checks that DNA has been replicated completely and correctly before mitosis; if problems are detected the cycle is halted for repair or apoptosis.
bio12a1-cc-8
Explain why mitosis is important for multicellular organisms. (2 marks)
Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells; this allows growth, repair/replacement of damaged or worn-out cells, and asexual reproduction, while keeping the chromosome number constant.
bio12a1-cc-9
Which of the following gives the correct order of the stages of the cell cycle?
G1, S, G2, M
S, G1, M, G2
M, G1, S, G2
G1, M, S, G2
The cell cycle runs G1, S (DNA replication), G2 and then M (mitosis). Orders that put M before S misplace DNA replication, which must be completed before division.
bio12a1-cc-10
A cell at the start of metaphase has 8 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids. How many chromatids are present in the cell?
Eight chromosomes with two sister chromatids each gives 8 × 2 = 16 chromatids. Answering 8 counts chromosomes instead of chromatids, and 32 doubles the correct count again.
bio12a1-cc-11
Which statement about the centromere is correct?
It is the region of the chromosome that codes for spindle proteins.
It is a membrane-bound organelle that organises microtubules.
It is the region where sister chromatids are joined and where spindle fibres attach.
It is the site where the nuclear envelope reforms in telophase.
The centromere holds sister chromatids together and is the point where spindle fibres attach during mitosis. The structure that organises microtubules is the centrosome, which is not membrane-bound.
bio12a1-cc-12
Which event occurs during telophase?
Chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate.
Sister chromatids separate at their centromeres.
Chromosomes condense and become visible under the microscope.
Nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes at the poles.
In telophase the chromosomes reach the poles and decondense, and a nuclear envelope reforms around each set. Lining up is metaphase, centromere splitting is anaphase, and condensation is prophase.
bio12a1-cc-13
What is the role of the centrosomes in an animal cell during mitosis?
They organise the spindle microtubules that pull sister chromatids apart.
They produce the ATP needed to replicate DNA.
They attach sister chromatids to each other before replication.
They form the cell plate that divides the cytoplasm.

The centrosomes duplicate in interphase, move to opposite poles and nucleate the spindle microtubules. Mitochondria make ATP, and a cell plate is a plant cytokinesis structure rather than a centrosome role.
bio12a1-cc-14
What type of protein do spindle fibres consist of?
Actin
Tubulin
Collagen
Keratin
Spindle fibres are microtubules built from tubulin. Actin forms the contractile ring in animal cytokinesis, while collagen and keratin are structural proteins that are not part of the spindle.
bio12a1-cc-15
What is the function of cyclins in the cell cycle?
They are structural proteins that form the spindle fibres.
They are enzymes that cut DNA at the centromere.
They bind cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and regulate progression through the cell cycle.
They attach sister chromatids to the nuclear envelope.
Cyclins rise and fall in concentration through the cycle and activate cyclin-dependent kinases, which drive transitions between phases. Spindle fibres are made of tubulin, not cyclins.
bio12a1-cc-16
The mitotic index of a tissue sample is calculated as:
the number of cells in mitosis divided by the total number of cells observed
the total number of cells observed divided by the number in mitosis
the number of cells in interphase divided by the number in mitosis
the number of chromosomes divided by the number of cells observed
The mitotic index is the proportion of cells that are in mitosis, so the number in mitosis is divided by the total. Inverting the division gives a value above 1, which cannot be a proportion.
bio12a1-cc-17
Which statement correctly distinguishes mitosis from cytokinesis?
Mitosis divides the cytoplasm, while cytokinesis divides the nucleus.
Mitosis divides the nucleus, while cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to form two cells.
Mitosis produces four haploid cells, while cytokinesis produces two diploid cells.
Mitosis occurs in G1, while cytokinesis occurs during S phase.

Mitosis separates the duplicated chromosomes into two nuclei, and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to form two cells. The reversed option swaps the two processes, and the four-cell option describes meiosis, not mitosis.
bio12a1-cc-18
Which statement best describes the time a typical dividing cell spends in interphase compared with mitosis?
Mitosis occupies most of the cell cycle because cells divide continuously.
Interphase and mitosis last the same length of time in most cells.
Interphase lasts only a few minutes, as the cell spends most of its time dividing.
Interphase occupies most of the cell cycle, while mitosis is comparatively brief.
In most cells interphase (G1, S and G2) makes up the majority of the cycle, while mitosis is short. The options that make mitosis dominant or equal reverse the actual proportions.
bio12a1-cc-19
Why are the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome genetically identical?
They are copies made by DNA replication of the same chromosome.
They are the products of crossing over during prophase.
They were inherited from two different parents.
They are the same as the homologous chromosome of the pair.
S phase replicates each chromosome exactly, so sister chromatids carry identical DNA sequences. Crossing over, homologous pairing and parental origin relate to meiosis, not to sister chromatids.
bio12a1-cc-20
A cell in metaphase has one chromosome that is not yet attached to a spindle fibre. What happens at the spindle checkpoint?
The cell skips metaphase and moves straight into telophase.
Anaphase is delayed until all chromosomes are correctly attached to spindle fibres.
The cell proceeds to cytokinesis, producing a daughter cell with an extra chromosome.
The chromosomes replicate again during G2.

The checkpoint holds the cell at metaphase until every chromosome is attached, so sister chromatids separate only when correctly aligned. Proceeding early would be the tempting error, risking daughter cells with missing or extra chromosomes.
bio12a1-cc-21
A single cell undergoes three consecutive rounds of mitosis with no cell death. How many daughter cells are produced?

Each round of mitosis doubles the number of cells, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Six assumes each round adds two cells, and nine is 3 squared, which multiplies the number of rounds rather than doubling the cells.
bio12a1-cc-22
Name the structure that forms in an animal cell during cytokinesis to pinch the cytoplasm into two cells. (1 mark)
Cleavage furrow (formed by a contractile ring of actin filaments) [1]
bio12a1-cc-23
Define interphase. (1 mark)
The period of the cell cycle between divisions in which the cell grows, replicates its DNA and prepares for mitosis [1]
bio12a1-cc-24
Distinguish between a chromosome and a chromatid in a cell after S phase. (2 marks)
A chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere after S phase [1]; a chromatid is one of the two identical copies of DNA that make up a replicated chromosome [1]
bio12a1-cc-25
Describe the events of telophase and cytokinesis in an animal cell. (3 marks)

Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles and decondense [1]; a nuclear envelope reforms around each set of chromosomes [1]; cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow forms and pinches the cytoplasm into two separate daughter cells [1]
bio12a1-cc-26
Describe the key events of G1, S and G2 of interphase. (3 marks)

G1: the cell grows and makes proteins and organelles [1]; S: DNA is replicated so that each chromosome has two sister chromatids [1]; G2: the cell continues to grow, checks the replicated DNA and makes proteins needed for division, such as tubulin for spindle fibres [1]
bio12a1-cc-27
A student writes: 'Mitosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell.' Identify the two errors in this statement and correct them. (2 marks)
Mitosis produces two daughter cells, not four [1]; each daughter cell has the same (diploid) chromosome number as the parent, not half [1]
bio12a1-cc-28
Explain why a sample of rapidly growing embryonic tissue would have a higher mitotic index than a sample of mature liver tissue. (4 marks)

Embryonic cells divide rapidly to produce the cells needed for growth [1]; so a greater proportion of cells are in mitosis at any one time [1]; cells in mature liver tissue divide only rarely, so few are in mitosis [1]; the mitotic index is the proportion of cells in mitosis, so it is higher in the embryo [1]
bio12a1-cc-29
A cell cycle lasts 18 hours. G1 lasts 8 hours, S phase lasts 7 hours and G2 lasts 2 hours. Calculate the time spent in mitosis, and the percentage of the cycle spent in interphase. (3 marks)
Time in mitosis = 18 − (8 + 7 + 2) = 1 hour [1]; time in interphase = 8 + 7 + 2 = 17 hours [1]; 17 ÷ 18 × 100 = 94.4% (about 94%) of the cycle [1]
vce-bio12-mi-c1
A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. At metaphase of mitosis, how many chromatids does it contain?
DNA replicated in S phase, so each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids: 92 in total.
vce-bio12-apoptosis-and-cancer: bio12a1-ap-1
Apoptosis is best described as
uncontrolled cell death caused by injury.
programmed cell death that occurs in a controlled sequence.
division of a cell into two.
the spread of cancer cells to other tissues.
Apoptosis is programmed, controlled cell death. Uncontrolled death from injury is necrosis; spreading cancer is metastasis.
bio12a1-ap-2
Which event is characteristic of apoptosis?
Cell swelling and bursting, causing inflammation
Increased production of ATP by mitochondria
Rapid uncontrolled division
Formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are engulfed by phagocytes
In apoptosis the cell shrinks, its DNA fragments and the membrane blebs into apoptotic bodies that phagocytes engulf without inflammation. Swelling and bursting describe necrosis.
bio12a1-ap-3
Caspases are enzymes that
break down cell components during apoptosis.
replicate DNA during S phase.
form spindle fibres.
promote cell division.
Caspases are proteases activated in apoptosis that break down proteins and the cytoskeleton, leading to dismantling of the cell.
bio12a1-ap-4
A mutation that inactivates the tumour suppressor gene p53 increases cancer risk because
cells with damaged DNA are no longer halted at checkpoints or sent into apoptosis.
the cell can no longer replicate its DNA.
apoptosis occurs too often.
the cell becomes a stem cell.
p53 halts the cell cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger apoptosis. Without it, damaged cells keep dividing and accumulate mutations.
bio12a1-ap-5
During development of the human hand, the cells between the fingers are removed. This is an example of
necrosis.
mitosis.
apoptosis.
metastasis.
Webbing between digits is removed by apoptosis during embryonic development, which shapes structures without causing inflammation.
bio12a1-ap-6
Distinguish between the intrinsic (mitochondrial) and extrinsic (death receptor) pathways of apoptosis. (2 marks)

The intrinsic pathway is triggered by signals from within the cell (e.g. DNA damage) causing mitochondria to release cytochrome c, which activates caspases; the extrinsic pathway is triggered by external signal molecules (e.g. from immune cells) binding to death receptors on the plasma membrane, which activates caspases.
bio12a1-ap-7
Explain how a mutation in a proto-oncogene can lead to the formation of a tumour. (3 marks)

Proto-oncogenes code for proteins that promote normal cell division; a mutation can convert it into an oncogene that is permanently 'switched on' / overactive; cells divide uncontrollably regardless of signals, forming a mass of cells (tumour).
bio12a1-ap-8
Explain why a balance between mitosis and apoptosis is important in an adult organism. (2 marks)

Mitosis replaces cells while apoptosis removes old, damaged or unneeded cells; if apoptosis is too low, cells accumulate (e.g. cancer); if too high, tissue is lost (e.g. degenerative disease), so balance maintains a constant, healthy cell number.
bio12a1-ap-9
Tumour suppressor genes normally code for proteins that
stimulate cells to divide whenever growth factors are present.
inhibit cell division or trigger apoptosis when a cell is damaged.
break down the extracellular matrix so that cells can move.
form the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes in mitosis.

Tumour suppressors such as p53 slow division or trigger apoptosis when needed, so losing them removes a brake on growth. Stimulating division describes the normal role of proto-oncogenes, and spindle fibres are structures rather than regulatory proteins.
bio12a1-ap-10
During apoptosis, what change to the plasma membrane signals phagocytes to engulf the cell?
Phosphatidylserine moves to the outer surface of the membrane.
Glucose transporters are removed from the membrane.
The membrane ruptures and releases cytoplasm.
The membrane becomes completely impermeable to all molecules.

Exposed phosphatidylserine acts as an 'eat me' signal that phagocytes recognise, so apoptotic cells are cleared without spilling their contents. Rupture and release of cytoplasm happens in necrosis, not apoptosis.
bio12a1-ap-11
Cytotoxic T cells destroy virus-infected body cells mainly by
releasing viral particles to be neutralised by antibodies.
causing the infected cell to undergo necrosis and burst.
stimulating the infected cell to undergo mitosis more often.
triggering apoptosis in the infected cell.

Cytotoxic T cells trigger apoptosis in the infected cell, which removes it without releasing viral particles or causing inflammation. Bursting by necrosis would release virus into the tissue, so it is the wrong mechanism.
bio12a1-ap-12
Which of the following is a chemical carcinogen?
X-rays
Benzene in tobacco smoke
Ultraviolet-B radiation
Gamma rays from a radioactive source
Benzene is a chemical that damages DNA and is present in tobacco smoke. X-rays, UV-B and gamma rays are physical agents, so they are not chemical carcinogens.
bio12a1-ap-13
Why does the risk of many cancers increase with age?
Older cells divide less often, so fewer mutations are made.
Cells accumulate more mutations over time from repeated DNA copying and environmental exposure.
Caspases become more active in older tissues.
Older tissues produce fewer stem cells, so tumours cannot form.

Mutations build up with each cell division and each exposure to mutagens, and several are usually needed for cancer, so risk rises over decades. The option saying older cells divide less is wrong because many adult tissues keep dividing throughout life.
bio12a1-ap-14
A tumour starts with 500 cells and the cell number doubles every 2 days. If all cells keep dividing, how many cells are present after 6 days?
Three doublings occur in 6 days: 500 → 1 000 → 2 000 → 4 000. Adding 500 cells every 2 days gives 2 000, while 8 000 counts four doublings instead of three.
bio12a1-ap-15
A mutagen is best defined as an agent that
increases the rate of change in the base sequence of DNA.
kills cells by necrosis and causes inflammation.
activates caspases directly in healthy cells.
increases the rate of mitosis without affecting DNA.
A mutagen raises the rate of DNA mutation, which may or may not lead to cancer. Necrosis, caspase activation and faster mitosis are not defining features of a mutagen.
bio12a1-ap-16
Angiogenesis, which growing tumours stimulate, is the
breakdown of blood vessels by caspases during apoptosis.
division of blood cells in the bone marrow.
release of cytochrome c from mitochondria.
formation of new blood vessels that supply nutrients and oxygen to the tumour.

A tumour larger than a few millimetres needs its own blood supply, so it stimulates new vessel growth. The other options describe apoptosis, blood-cell production and the intrinsic apoptosis pathway rather than angiogenesis.
bio12a1-ap-17
Which statement correctly compares mitosis and apoptosis?
Apoptosis produces two daughter cells, whereas mitosis destroys the nucleus.
Both processes are triggered by the release of caspases from mitochondria.
Mitosis is a form of cell death, whereas apoptosis increases the number of cells.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, whereas apoptosis is a controlled way for a cell to die.

Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells, whereas apoptosis is a controlled way for a cell to die. The other options swap these roles or misattribute caspase activity and changes in cell number.
bio12a1-ap-18
Radiotherapy kills cancer cells mainly by
causing DNA damage that cells cannot repair, leading to cell death.
stimulating angiogenesis so that the tumour grows faster.
increasing the rate of mitosis so cells divide more quickly.
heating the tumour above 100 °C to denature its proteins.

Radiation breaks DNA strands, and cancer cells that cannot repair the damage stop dividing or undergo apoptosis. Increasing mitosis or angiogenesis would worsen the cancer, and radiotherapy does not work by boiling tissue.
bio12a1-ap-19
Which is a common cause of necrosis?
A programmed signal that activates caspases
Removal of the cells between developing fingers
Loss of blood supply to a tissue, so its cells run out of oxygen and ATP
Normal replacement of old cells in the stomach lining
Loss of oxygen and ATP makes cells swell and burst, releasing contents that trigger inflammation. The other options describe programmed, controlled cell death, which is apoptosis.
bio12a1-ap-20
Which cell is most likely to be removed by apoptosis?
A healthy skin cell that is functioning normally
A muscle cell that is actively contracting
A cell with DNA damage that cannot be repaired
A liver cell that has just been formed by mitosis
Apoptosis removes cells whose DNA damage cannot be repaired, which stops them passing mutations to daughter cells. The other cells are healthy and functioning, so the body keeps them.
bio12a1-ap-21
Which of the following best describes a tumour?
An abnormal mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division.
A group of cells that have been removed by apoptosis.
A cluster of phagocytes that have engulfed dead cells.
A mass of red blood cells that has formed in the bone marrow.
A tumour is an abnormal growth of cells, which may be benign or malignant. Apoptotic cells and phagocyte clusters are removed by the body, and red blood cells do not form tumours.
bio12a1-ap-22
Explain why a benign tumour is usually less dangerous than a malignant tumour. (2 marks)
A benign tumour stays in one place and does not invade surrounding tissue [1]; a malignant tumour invades nearby tissue and can spread to other parts of the body, disrupting organ function [1].
bio12a1-ap-23
Explain why chemotherapy drugs that target rapidly dividing cells also cause hair loss and nausea. (3 marks)

The drugs damage DNA or block mitosis, killing cells that divide rapidly [1]; hair follicle cells and the cells lining the digestive tract also divide rapidly [1]; so these healthy cells are damaged too, causing side effects [1].
bio12a1-ap-24

A tissue produces 12 000 new cells per day by mitosis and loses 9 500 cells per day by apoptosis. Calculate the net change in cell number per day and state whether the tissue is growing or shrinking. (2 marks)
12 000 − 9 500 = 2 500 cells gained per day [1]; the tissue is growing, as its cell number is increasing [1].
bio12a1-ap-25
In a biopsy of a tumour, 21 of 350 cells counted were in mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index as a percentage. (2 marks)
bio12a1-ap-26
Explain how exposure to ultraviolet radiation can lead to skin cancer. (3 marks)

UV radiation is absorbed by DNA, forming thymine dimers that distort the DNA [1]; if these are not repaired correctly, the DNA base sequence is changed (a mutation) [1]; mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle or apoptosis can cause cells to divide uncontrollably and form a tumour [1].
bio12a1-ap-27
Explain why a tumour can become more aggressive over time as further mutations accumulate. (3 marks)

Cells in a tumour continue to acquire mutations as they divide [1]; cells with mutations that increase division or help them escape apoptosis have a growth advantage and out-compete other cells [1]; this produces a more aggressive population that may spread to other tissues [1].
bio12a1-ap-28
Explain why cancer cells that have lost contact inhibition continue to divide when they touch neighbouring cells. (2 marks)
Normal cells receive a signal from neighbouring cells that halts division [1]; cancer cells do not respond to this signal, so they keep dividing and form a mass [1].
bio12a1-ap-29
Explain why a mutation in a gene that codes for a DNA repair enzyme can increase cancer risk. (2 marks)
Without a working enzyme, DNA errors and damage are not corrected [1]; mutations then accumulate in genes controlling cell division, increasing the likelihood of cancer [1].
bio12a1-ap-30
Describe how cancer cells spread from a primary tumour to form secondary tumours elsewhere in the body. (3 marks)

Cancer cells detach from the primary tumour and invade the surrounding tissue [1]; they enter the blood or lymphatic system [1]; they travel to a distant site, where they settle and divide to form a secondary tumour [1].
vce-bio12-ap-c1
A mutation disables a protein that normally triggers apoptosis when a cell's DNA is damaged. The most likely result is that:
All cells with damaged DNA die immediately by necrosis instead
Cells stop dividing completely, so the tissue can no longer repair itself
Cells with damaged DNA survive and keep dividing, which can lead to a tumour
The immune system can no longer detect any of the body's own cells
Apoptosis removes damaged cells. Losing this checkpoint lets mutations accumulate in a growing population of cells.
vce-bio12-stem-cells-and-specialisation: bio12a1-sc-1
A stem cell that can give rise to every cell type in the body, including the placenta, is described as
pluripotent.
multipotent.
totipotent.
unipotent.
Totipotent cells (e.g. the zygote) can form all cell types including extra-embryonic tissue. Pluripotent cells (embryonic stem cells) form all body cell types but not the placenta.
bio12a1-sc-2
Haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow can produce red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets but not nerve cells. They are
totipotent.
pluripotent.
fully differentiated.
multipotent.
Multipotent stem cells form a limited range of cell types within a particular tissue or lineage.
bio12a1-sc-3
Cells in the same organism become specialised for different functions because they
express different genes.
contain different genes.
have different numbers of chromosomes.
lose DNA during differentiation.
All somatic cells contain the same DNA, but differentiation involves switching specific genes on or off, producing different proteins.
bio12a1-sc-4
Embryonic stem cells are typically obtained from
the inner cell mass of a blastocyst.
adult bone marrow.
the umbilical cord only.
mature skin cells.
Embryonic stem cells come from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst (about 5 days after fertilisation) and are pluripotent.
bio12a1-sc-5
Which two properties define a stem cell?
It is specialised and cannot divide.
It is only found in embryos and carries out photosynthesis.
It contains no nucleus and can divide by meiosis.
It can self-renew by mitosis and can differentiate into specialised cells.
Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide repeatedly (self-renew) and differentiate into specialised cell types. Adult stem cells exist in many tissues.
bio12a1-sc-6
Describe one advantage and one ethical concern of using embryonic stem cells in medical research. (2 marks)

Advantage: they are pluripotent, so can potentially form any body cell type to treat many diseases (e.g. replace damaged nerve or heart cells); concern: obtaining them destroys an embryo, which some people believe has the moral status of a person.
bio12a1-sc-7
Explain how a red blood cell is specialised for its function. (2 marks)

Function is to transport oxygen; it lacks a nucleus and most organelles so there is more room for haemoglobin, and its biconcave disc shape gives a high SA:V for rapid diffusion of O₂ (and flexibility to pass through capillaries).
bio12a1-sc-8
Explain the hierarchy of organisation from cells to organ systems, using an example. (3 marks)

Specialised cells of a similar type form tissues (e.g. cardiac muscle cells form cardiac muscle tissue); different tissues work together to form an organ (e.g. the heart contains muscle, nervous and connective tissue); organs work together in an organ system (e.g. heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system).
bio12a1-sc-9
Plant growth continues throughout life in regions called meristems, such as the root and shoot tips. The cells in these regions are best described as
stem cells that keep dividing and can differentiate into specialised plant cells.
fully differentiated cells that have lost the ability to divide.
gametes that fuse during fertilisation to form a new plant.
cells that have lost their genes during differentiation.

Meristem cells are stem cells that divide by mitosis and differentiate, so plants can keep growing. Fully differentiated cells have generally lost the ability to divide, and gametes do not form plant tissue in a meristem.
bio12a1-sc-10
Which feature of a root hair cell most directly increases the rate at which it absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil?
A thick, lignified cell wall.
A long, thin extension that greatly increases surface area.
Many chloroplasts that supply energy for water uptake.
A large central vacuole that fills most of the cell.

The long extension increases the surface area to volume ratio, speeding up absorption. A thick lignified wall would be rigid and slow movement of water, and chloroplasts are of little use in roots that are underground.
bio12a1-sc-11
Mature xylem vessel elements transport water up a plant. Which combination of features is characteristic of them?
Living cells with an intact nucleus and end walls.
Thin walls with cytoplasmic strands and no lignin.
Hollow, dead cells with lignified walls and no end walls.
Cells with flagella that push water upwards.

At maturity, xylem vessels are dead hollow tubes with lignin-strengthened walls, and their end walls have broken down to form a continuous channel. The option describing living cells with nuclei does not match xylem vessels.
bio12a1-sc-12
Motor neurons carry impulses over long distances, such as from the spinal cord to the leg muscles. Which feature is an adaptation for this function?
A very short axon, so impulses travel quickly.
Many chloroplasts in the cell body.
A membrane that is freely permeable to all ions.
A long axon, often insulated by a myelin sheath.

A long axon covered in myelin allows fast conduction over long distances, as the impulse jumps between the gaps in the sheath. Animal neurons do not contain chloroplasts, and a freely permeable membrane could not maintain the ion gradients needed for an impulse.
bio12a1-sc-13
Skeletal muscle fibres are long cells that contain many nuclei. This feature is an advantage because the nuclei
store energy as ATP for the whole fibre.
stop the cell from dividing during contraction.
together direct the large amount of protein synthesis needed for contraction.
allow the fibre to exchange gases more rapidly.

Each nucleus controls a region of the cytoplasm, so many nuclei support the high rate of protein synthesis needed for contraction. Nuclei do not store energy, and the number of nuclei does not change how quickly gases diffuse.
bio12a1-sc-14
The epithelial cells lining the small intestine have microvilli on their surface. What is the main function of this feature?
To secrete mucus that protects the intestinal wall.
To make the cells contract so food is pushed along the gut.
To pump oxygen into the blood.
To increase surface area for absorption of digested nutrients.

Microvilli greatly increase the surface area of the cell membrane, speeding up the absorption of digested food. Mucus is made by other cells, and the cells lining the intestine do not contract to move food along.
bio12a1-sc-15
Guard cells surround each stoma in a leaf. When guard cells take in water and become turgid, the stoma
opens, allowing carbon dioxide to enter the leaf.
closes, reducing water loss from the leaf.
stays the same size, because water does not move into guard cells.
closes permanently and stops all gas exchange.

When guard cells take in water and become turgid, they bend apart and open the stoma, letting carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis. The stoma closes when guard cells lose water, so the option describing closure on turgidity has the direction reversed.
bio12a1-sc-16
The trachea is lined with ciliated epithelial cells. What is the function of the cilia?
To produce surfactant that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
To sweep mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat.
To absorb oxygen from the air into the cell.
To contract and push air into the lungs.
Cilia beat in a coordinated wave to move mucus, with trapped dust and microbes, up and away from the lungs. Surfactant is made by other cells in the alveoli, and cilia do not contract to move air.
bio12a1-sc-17

In therapeutic cloning, the nucleus of a patient's body cell is placed into an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed, and stem cells are harvested from the resulting embryo. What is the main advantage of this approach?
The stem cells will be totipotent, so they can form a placenta.
The stem cells will be identical to the egg donor, so they cannot be rejected.
The stem cells are genetically matched to the patient, which reduces the risk of immune rejection.
No embryo is created, so the procedure raises no ethical concerns.

The nucleus comes from the patient's own cell, so the stem cells are a genetic match and are less likely to be rejected. The stem cells are pluripotent rather than totipotent, and the method does create an embryo, which is why it is ethically contested.
bio12a1-sc-18
Adult skin cells can be reprogrammed to become induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Which property do iPSCs share with embryonic stem cells?
They can form extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.
They are totipotent and can form a whole organism on their own.
They are fully specialised and can no longer divide.
They can differentiate into all the cell types of the body.

iPSCs are pluripotent, like embryonic stem cells, so they can form all body cell types but not extra-embryonic tissue. Totipotency is a feature of very early embryonic cells, and iPSCs are not specialised.
bio12a1-sc-19
Companion cells are closely associated with phloem sieve tubes. Why do companion cells contain many mitochondria?
They produce ATP to power active transport of sugars into the sieve tubes.
They store the water needed by the xylem vessels.
They synthesise lignin to strengthen the sieve tubes.
They carry out photosynthesis to supply energy to the sieve tubes.

Companion cells respire aerobically to make ATP, which powers the active loading of sugars into the sieve tubes. Lignin is found in xylem rather than phloem, and storing water is not a role of companion cells.
bio12a1-sc-20
Palisade mesophyll cells in a leaf are packed with chloroplasts and lie just beneath the upper epidermis. This arrangement is an adaptation for
storing starch for the plant's roots.
absorbing light energy for photosynthesis.
transporting water from the roots to the leaf.
reducing gas exchange with the atmosphere.

Palisade cells sit near the leaf surface and contain many chloroplasts, so they capture the most light for photosynthesis. Starch storage occurs in other tissues, water is carried by xylem rather than palisade cells, and gas exchange is needed for photosynthesis.
bio12a1-sc-21
Name the process by which a cell becomes structurally and functionally specialised for a particular role. (1 mark)
Differentiation [1]
bio12a1-sc-22
Give one advantage of collecting stem cells from umbilical cord blood rather than from bone marrow. (1 mark)
Collection is non-invasive, so the donor does not need surgery or experience pain [1].
bio12a1-sc-23
Explain why multicellular organisms contain specialised cells rather than every cell performing all functions. (2 marks)

Division of labour means each cell type can be structurally and functionally adapted to carry out one role efficiently [1]; cells can be grouped into tissues and organs that perform complex tasks no single cell could carry out [1].
bio12a1-sc-24
Explain why embryonic stem cells are more potent than adult stem cells. Refer to the stage of development at which each is found. (3 marks)

Embryonic stem cells come from the early embryo, before cells have committed to a lineage, so they can form all body cell types (pluripotent) [1]; adult stem cells are found in mature tissues and have become restricted to forming the cell types of that tissue (multipotent) [1]; as development proceeds, the genes for other cell types are progressively switched off [1].
bio12a1-sc-25
Explain how the lining of the small intestine is continually replaced, using the terms 'stem cell' and 'differentiation'. (3 marks)

Stem cells at the base of intestinal crypts divide by mitosis to produce new daughter cells [1]; some daughter cells differentiate into specialised cells, such as absorptive cells, by switching on particular genes [1]; older cells move up to the tip of the villus, where they are shed, so the lining is replaced about every few days [1].
bio12a1-sc-26
Explain how a small piece of plant tissue can be used to grow many genetically identical plants. Refer to undifferentiated cells in your answer. (3 marks)

Cells in the tissue are undifferentiated, stem-like cells that can still divide and form new tissues [1]; hormones in the growth medium stimulate them to divide, forming an undifferentiated mass called a callus [1]; cells in the callus then differentiate into roots and shoots, producing genetically identical plants (clones) [1].
vce-bio12-st-c1
Which correctly matches each cell with its potency?
Zygote: pluripotent; embryonic stem cell: totipotent; bone marrow stem cell: multipotent
Zygote: totipotent; embryonic stem cell: pluripotent; bone marrow stem cell: multipotent
Zygote: multipotent; embryonic stem cell: pluripotent; bone marrow stem cell: totipotent
All three are totipotent
Totipotent cells can form a whole organism (including the placenta); pluripotent cells can form any body cell; multipotent cells form a few related types.
vce-bio12-plant-transport-systems: bio12a1-pl-1
Xylem tissue in flowering plants transports
water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves.
sugars from leaves to roots.
hormones only.
oxygen from leaves to roots.
Xylem carries water and mineral ions upward from roots. Phloem carries sugars (mainly sucrose) in both directions.
bio12a1-pl-2
Which force is mainly responsible for pulling water up the xylem of a tall eucalyptus tree?
Root pressure
Gravity
Active transport by xylem vessels
Transpiration pull, relying on cohesion and adhesion of water molecules

Evaporation from leaves through stomata creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water up, held together by cohesion (hydrogen bonds) and adhesion to xylem walls. Xylem vessels are dead and cannot actively transport.
bio12a1-pl-3
The movement of sucrose from a source to a sink through phloem is called
transpiration.
translocation.
guttation.
osmosis.
Translocation is the movement of sugars and other organic compounds in phloem from sources (e.g. leaves) to sinks (e.g. roots, fruits).
bio12a1-pl-4
A potometer experiment showed that water uptake by a leafy shoot was greatest when a fan was blowing on it. The best explanation is that moving air
closes stomata.
lowers the temperature, slowing transpiration.
increases humidity around the leaf.
removes water vapour near the leaf, increasing the concentration gradient for evaporation.
Wind removes the humid layer around the leaf, steepening the water vapour gradient between the air spaces and the atmosphere, so transpiration and water uptake increase.
bio12a1-pl-5
Which statement about phloem sieve tube elements is correct?
They are dead cells with lignified walls.
They are living cells with sieve plates, supported by companion cells.
They transport water only upward.
They contain many chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Sieve tube elements are living but lack a nucleus; companion cells supply their metabolic needs. Lignified dead cells describe xylem vessels.
bio12a1-pl-6
Describe how water moves from the soil into the xylem of a root. (3 marks)

Water enters root hair cells by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential / higher solute concentration than the soil (minerals are actively transported in); water moves across the cortex via the cell walls and cytoplasm; at the endodermis the Casparian strip forces water through the cytoplasm before it enters the xylem.
bio12a1-pl-7
Explain why the rate of transpiration of a plant decreases on a hot day when it begins to wilt. (2 marks)
When water loss exceeds uptake, the plant closes its stomata (guard cells lose turgor) to conserve water; less water vapour can diffuse out of the leaf, so transpiration rate decreases.
bio12a1-pl-8
Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem. (3 marks)

Xylem consists of dead, hollow, lignified vessels while phloem consists of living sieve tube elements and companion cells; xylem transports water and minerals while phloem transports sugars (sucrose) and other organic compounds; xylem flow is upward only (from roots) while phloem transports sugars in both directions from sources to sinks.
bio12a1-pl-9
Stomata open in the light mainly because guard cells take up potassium ions (K⁺). This causes
water to enter the guard cells by osmosis, increasing turgor and bowing the cells apart.
water to leave the guard cells, making them flaccid and opening the pore.
the guard cells to lose their chloroplasts and collapse inwards.
the xylem to pull the guard cells apart by cohesion.

Active uptake of K⁺ lowers the water potential inside the guard cells, so water enters by osmosis, the cells become turgid and the pore opens. Water leaving the cells would make them flaccid and close the pore.
bio12a1-pl-10
Guttation, the loss of drops of liquid water from the leaf margins of some plants, usually occurs at night because
transpiration is at its highest rate, forcing water out of the hydathodes.
root pressure pushes xylem sap out through hydathodes when transpiration is low and humidity is high.
phloem sieve tubes leak sugar solution onto the leaf surface.
stomata are fully open, so water is forced out through them.

Root pressure builds when transpiration is low, such as on humid nights, and pushes xylem sap out through hydathodes. Guttation is not caused by high transpiration, and the liquid is xylem sap, not phloem sap.
bio12a1-pl-11
Water moving through the cell walls and intercellular spaces of the root cortex, without crossing a plasma membrane, is following which pathway?
Symplast pathway, through the cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata.
Transpiration pathway, through the stomata of the leaf.
Apoplast pathway, through cell walls and intercellular spaces.
Phloem loading pathway, driven by active transport of sucrose.

The apoplast pathway moves water through non-living cell walls and spaces. The symplast pathway passes through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata, and the Casparian strip at the endodermis forces water into the symplast before it reaches the xylem.
bio12a1-pl-12
Which set of conditions gives the fastest rate of transpiration?
Cool, humid, still and dark.
Cool, dry, still and dark.
Warm, humid, still and dark.
Warm, dry, windy and bright.

Warmth, low humidity, wind and light all increase transpiration, because they speed evaporation, steepen the water vapour gradient and keep stomata open. Each of the other sets includes at least one factor that slows transpiration.
bio12a1-pl-13
Sucrose is moved into sieve tube elements at a leaf (the source). This loading is usually done by
active transport, with companion cells using ATP.
diffusion down a concentration gradient from the xylem.
osmosis into the xylem vessels, pulled upward by transpiration.
root pressure forcing sugar into the phloem.

Companion cells use ATP to pump sucrose into sieve tube elements against a concentration gradient. Xylem and the transpiration pull are not involved in loading phloem, and root pressure acts on xylem sap, not on phloem loading.
bio12a1-pl-14
In the pressure flow hypothesis, sap moves through phloem from a source to a sink because
transpiration pulls sap up the sieve tubes from the roots.
loading sucrose at the source lowers water potential, water enters by osmosis and pressure rises; unloading at the sink lowers the pressure, so sap flows down the gradient.
sieve plates act as pumps, moving sap in both directions.
sucrose diffuses passively from the sink to the source.

Water entering by osmosis at the source raises hydrostatic pressure, while unloading at the sink lowers it. This pressure gradient moves sap by mass flow. Transpiration drives the xylem, not the phloem, and sieve plates are not pumps.
bio12a1-pl-15
Which feature allows water to move sideways between neighbouring xylem vessels?
Sieve plates at the ends of the vessels.
Plasmodesmata linking companion cells.
Pits in the lignified walls, where the wall is thin and unlignified.
Living cytoplasm lining the vessel walls.
Pits are thin, unlignified areas of the vessel walls that let water pass sideways between vessels. Sieve plates belong to phloem, and xylem vessels have no living cytoplasm.
bio12a1-pl-16
A plant cell is placed in a solution with a lower water potential than the cell sap. The cell will
gain water and become more turgid.
stay the same, because water potential does not affect movement of water.
gain solutes from the solution, increasing its water potential.
lose water and become flaccid.

Water moves by osmosis from higher to lower water potential, so the cell loses water, loses turgor and becomes flaccid. The cell would gain water only if the solution had a higher water potential than the cell sap.
bio12a1-pl-17
A leafy shoot takes up 4.5 mL of water in 3 hours. What is the average rate of water uptake?
1.5 mL h⁻¹
7.5 mL h⁻¹
13.5 mL h⁻¹
0.67 mL h⁻¹
Rate = volume ÷ time = 4.5 mL ÷ 3 h = 1.5 mL h⁻¹. Adding the numbers gives 7.5, multiplying gives 13.5, and dividing time by volume gives about 0.67, so these are all wrong.
bio12a1-pl-18
Which feature of root hair cells increases the rate at which they absorb water?
Thick, lignified walls.
A large surface area from many long, thin extensions.
Many chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
A waxy cuticle over the cell surface.

Root hairs are long, thin extensions of epidermal cells, which give a large surface area for absorbing water and ions. Lignified walls and a waxy cuticle would restrict uptake, and root cells generally lack chloroplasts.
bio12a1-pl-19
Most water lost from a leaf on a typical sunny day is lost through
the cuticle, as liquid water droplets.
lenticels in the stem.
root hairs.
stomata, as water vapour.

Stomata account for most transpiration because they are open to the air and are numerous. The cuticle is waterproof and loses little water, lenticels are minor in stems, and root hairs take in water rather than losing it.
bio12a1-pl-20
Stomata usually close at night because
without light, guard cells stop actively taking in K⁺, so water leaves them and they lose turgor.
the xylem stops transporting water at night.
guard cells absorb sucrose and become rigid.
the leaf temperature rises sharply at night.

Light drives ATP production in guard cells that powers K⁺ uptake. Without light, guard cells lose K⁺ and turgor, so the pore closes. Xylem transport does not simply stop at night, and leaf temperature usually falls.
bio12a1-pl-21
Which sequence correctly shows the pathway of water from the soil to the atmosphere?
Soil → xylem → root hair → stomata → atmosphere.
Soil → root hair → root cortex → endodermis → xylem → leaf mesophyll → air spaces → stomata → atmosphere.
Soil → root hair → phloem → leaf mesophyll → stomata → atmosphere.
Soil → root cortex → phloem → xylem → stomata → atmosphere.

Water enters root hairs, crosses the cortex and endodermis into the xylem, then moves through the leaf mesophyll and air spaces to leave through stomata. Phloem does not carry water to the leaves, and water does not enter the xylem before the root hairs.
bio12a1-pl-22
Define transpiration and state where most of it occurs in a plant. (2 marks)
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant [1]; most of it occurs through the stomata in the leaves [1].
bio12a1-pl-23
Explain why xylem vessels are described as dead at maturity, and state one consequence of this for water transport. (2 marks)

Xylem vessels lose their cytoplasm and nucleus at maturity, leaving hollow, lignified tubes [1]; with no living contents to obstruct flow, water moves continuously through the vessels as a column [1].
bio12a1-pl-24
Explain why a plant growing in dry soil may have reduced rates of photosynthesis. (3 marks)

Dry soil reduces the water available for uptake by the roots, so less water reaches the leaves [1]; stomata close to conserve water, reducing the entry of CO₂ into the leaf [1]; the lower CO₂ concentration in the leaf reduces the rate of photosynthesis [1].
bio12a1-pl-25
Explain how the waxy cuticle reduces water loss from a leaf, and state what happens to the rate of transpiration if the cuticle is damaged. (3 marks)

The waxy cuticle is waterproof, so it reduces evaporation from the leaf epidermis [1]; most water loss therefore occurs through the stomata [1]; if the cuticle is damaged, water loss through the epidermis increases and the rate of transpiration rises [1].
bio12a1-pl-26
Name the cells that surround each stoma and control its opening. (1 mark)
Guard cells [1].
bio12a1-pl-27
Explain why mineral ion uptake by root cells requires energy, while water uptake does not. (3 marks)

Mineral ions are often at a lower concentration in the soil than in root cells, so they must be moved against a concentration gradient [1]; this requires ATP from cellular respiration, as the process is active transport [1]; water moves down its water potential gradient by osmosis, which requires no energy input [1].
bio12a1-pl-28
Outline two advantages and two disadvantages to a plant of transpiration. (4 marks)

Advantage: the transpiration pull moves water and dissolved minerals up the xylem [1]; advantage: evaporation of water from the leaf cools the leaf [1]; disadvantage: water loss can cause wilting if uptake cannot keep pace [1]; disadvantage: stomata must be open for CO₂ uptake, so water is lost at the same time [1].
bio12a1-pl-29
Describe two adaptations of xerophytic plants that reduce water loss. (2 marks)
Small or needle-shaped leaves reduce the surface area available for transpiration [1]; sunken stomata in pits trap humid air around the pores, reducing water loss [1].
bio12a1-pl-30
Explain how a potometer can be used to estimate the rate of transpiration, and state one assumption made. (3 marks)

The cut shoot takes up water, so the movement of an air bubble along the capillary tube measures water uptake [1]; the distance moved by the bubble per unit time gives the rate [1]; assumption: water taken up equals water lost by transpiration, so water used in photosynthesis or growth is negligible [1].
vce-bio12-ps-c1
A complete ring of bark, including the phloem, is removed from a tree trunk. Over the following weeks:
Water stops moving to the leaves at once, because the xylem is part of the bark
The leaves wilt within minutes, because sugars can no longer reach them
Sugars build up above the ring and the roots starve, although water still moves up the xylem
Nothing changes, because the phloem only carries water and minerals
Phloem carries sugars from leaves to roots; the inner xylem still carries water up. Eventually the roots die without sugars.
vce-bio12-digestive-system: bio12a2-dig-1
In humans, most chemical digestion is completed and most nutrients are absorbed in the
stomach.
small intestine.
large intestine.
oesophagus.

The small intestine receives pancreatic enzymes and bile, and its villi absorb the products of digestion. The stomach begins protein digestion but absorbs very little, apart from substances such as alcohol.
bio12a2-dig-2
The main function of the villi and microvilli lining the small intestine is to
secrete hydrochloric acid to kill pathogens.
move food along by peristalsis.
store bile until it is needed.
increase the surface area available for absorption.
Villi and microvilli greatly increase the surface area of the intestinal lining, which increases the rate of absorption. Peristalsis is done by the smooth muscle layers, not the villi.
bio12a2-dig-3
A person has had their gallbladder removed. Which statement about bile is correct?
Bile is produced by the liver, stored in the gallbladder and emulsifies lipids, increasing their surface area for lipase.
Bile is produced by the gallbladder and chemically breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
Bile is produced by the pancreas and neutralises acid in the stomach.
Bile is an enzyme that digests proteins in the duodenum.

The liver makes bile and the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it, so bile still flows after removal. Bile contains no enzymes; it emulsifies fats mechanically so lipase can act on a larger surface area.
bio12a2-dig-4
Researchers measured the activity of a digestive enzyme at different pH values. Activity peaked at pH 2 and was negligible above pH 5. The enzyme is most likely
salivary amylase, secreted in the mouth.
pancreatic lipase, active in the duodenum.
pepsin, secreted in the stomach.
maltase, located on the microvilli of the small intestine.
The stomach is highly acidic (about pH 1.5–3), and pepsin works best in these conditions. Amylase, lipase and maltase work in roughly neutral to slightly alkaline conditions.
bio12a2-dig-5
Which of the following is the main role of the large intestine?
Absorbing water and some minerals and vitamins, and forming faeces
Digesting starch into maltose
Absorbing amino acids into the blood capillaries of villi
Producing bile salts

Undigested material entering the large intestine is mostly water and fibre. The colon reabsorbs water and electrolytes, gut bacteria produce some vitamins (such as vitamin K), and faeces are formed. Amino acid absorption happens in the small intestine.
bio12a2-dig-6
Distinguish between mechanical digestion and chemical digestion, giving one example of each from the human digestive system. (2 marks)

Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces without changing its chemical make-up, e.g. chewing by teeth or churning in the stomach; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break the bonds in large molecules to form smaller molecules, e.g. amylase hydrolysing starch to maltose or pepsin breaking proteins into polypeptides.
bio12a2-dig-7
Explain how three structural features of the small intestine make it well suited to absorbing nutrients. (3 marks)

It is very long and folded, with villi and microvilli, giving a very large surface area for absorption; the epithelium of each villus is only one cell thick, so the diffusion distance into the blood is short; each villus has a dense capillary network (and a lacteal for lipids) that carries absorbed nutrients away, keeping a steep concentration gradient.
bio12a2-dig-8
In coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten damages and flattens the villi of the small intestine. Predict and explain the effect on a person with untreated coeliac disease. (3 marks)

Flattened villi greatly reduce the surface area of the small intestine; so the rate of absorption of nutrients such as glucose, amino acids, iron and vitamins decreases; the person may show malnutrition, weight loss, fatigue or anaemia even though they eat enough (undigested or unabsorbed material may also cause diarrhoea).
bio12a2-dig-9
Which statement about salivary amylase is correct?
It digests proteins into amino acids before food reaches the stomach.
It is secreted by the stomach and converts starch directly into glucose.
It begins starch digestion in the mouth, breaking starch into smaller sugars such as maltose.
It is a lipase that breaks triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol.

Salivary amylase is secreted by the salivary glands and hydrolyses starch into smaller sugars, mainly maltose, while food is in the mouth. It does not produce glucose from starch; that final step is done by maltase in the small intestine.
bio12a2-dig-10
The pancreas secretes sodium hydrogencarbonate into the duodenum. What is the main purpose of this secretion?
To neutralise acidic chyme so that pancreatic enzymes can work at their optimum pH.
To emulsify fats so that lipase can act on a larger surface area.
To kill bacteria by producing hydrochloric acid.
To convert pepsinogen into pepsin.

Chyme leaving the stomach is acidic, and the hydrogencarbonate raises the pH of the duodenum to about 7–8, which suits pancreatic amylase, lipase and trypsin. Emulsification is done by bile, and hydrochloric acid is made in the stomach rather than the pancreas.
bio12a2-dig-11
What is the main protective function of the thick layer of mucus secreted by the stomach lining?
It digests proteins into amino acids.
It protects the stomach wall from being damaged by hydrochloric acid and pepsin.
It absorbs vitamins and minerals into the blood.
It emulsifies fats so that lipase can act on them.

The alkaline mucus forms a barrier between the stomach wall and its acidic, enzyme-rich contents, so the wall is not digested. Mucus does not digest or absorb food, and emulsifying fats is a function of bile.
bio12a2-dig-12
Which is a function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
It emulsifies fats so that lipase can act on them.
It denatures food proteins, kills many ingested microorganisms and converts pepsinogen to pepsin.
It neutralises bile that flows back from the duodenum.
It hydrolyses starch into maltose.

Hydrochloric acid denatures food proteins, kills many microbes in ingested food and activates pepsinogen, creating the low pH that pepsin needs. Bile emulsifies fats rather than being neutralised by acid, and starch is hydrolysed by amylase, not by acid.
bio12a2-dig-13
Fatty acids and monoglycerides absorbed by a villus cell leave the small intestine mainly by which route?
Lacteals, which drain into the lymphatic system before joining the blood.
The hepatic portal vein, directly to the liver.
Blood plasma as free fatty acids dissolved in the blood only.
The bile ducts, back to the gallbladder.

Inside the villus cell the fatty acids and monoglycerides are re-formed into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons, which are too large to enter blood capillaries and so enter a lacteal. The hepatic portal vein carries water-soluble products such as glucose and amino acids, not most lipids.
bio12a2-dig-14
Which statement correctly describes the role of the hepatic portal vein in digestion?
It carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the small intestine.
It carries bile from the liver to the duodenum.
It carries nutrients absorbed by the small intestine, such as glucose and amino acids, to the liver.
It carries lipids from the lacteals directly to the heart.

Blood from the capillaries of the villi drains into the hepatic portal vein, which delivers absorbed glucose and amino acids to the liver for processing and storage. Oxygenated blood reaches the intestine from the aorta, bile travels through bile ducts, and lipids enter the lymphatic system via lacteals rather than the portal vein.
bio12a2-dig-15
Maltase breaks maltose into glucose but does not digest starch. Which explanation is correct?
Starch denatures maltase, so the enzyme stops working when starch is present.
The active site of maltase fits maltose, but not the much larger starch molecule.
Maltase only works in the stomach, where starch is not present.
Starch contains no glucose units, so maltase cannot release any glucose from it.

Enzymes are specific: the active site has a shape complementary to its substrate, so maltase binds maltose but not starch. Starch is a polymer of glucose, so the claim that it has no glucose units is wrong, and denaturation by the substrate is not the cause.
bio12a2-dig-16
Which row correctly pairs a digestive enzyme with its substrate and the products of its action?
Lipase: triglycerides → amino acids.
Amylase: starch → amino acids.
Pepsin: proteins → glucose.
Lipase: triglycerides → fatty acids and glycerol.

Lipase hydrolyses triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol. Amylase acts on starch to form smaller sugars, pepsin acts on proteins to form polypeptides, and no enzyme in this list makes amino acids from triglycerides or glucose from proteins.
bio12a2-dig-17
Herbivores such as cows typically have a much longer intestinal tract than carnivores of similar body size. The most likely reason is that
plant material is harder to digest, so a longer gut gives more time for digestion and absorption.
meat contains less protein than plant material, so carnivores need a smaller surface area for absorption.
herbivores produce more pepsin, which is only active in a long gut.
herbivores do not need to absorb water in the large intestine.

Plant cell walls contain cellulose, which most animals cannot digest, so herbivores need a longer gut to digest and absorb the nutrients that are available. Meat is richer in protein than plant material, and the length of the gut is not set by pepsin or by water absorption.
bio12a2-dig-18
Which pair of teeth is correctly matched with its function?
Molars cut food; incisors grind food.
Canines grind food; molars tear food.
Incisors cut food; molars grind food.
Premolars cut food; incisors crush food.

Incisors have a sharp, chisel-shaped edge for cutting, while the broad, flat surfaces of molars grind food into smaller pieces. Canines tear food, and molars are not adapted for cutting. This is mechanical digestion, which increases the surface area available to enzymes.
bio12a2-dig-19
Which statement correctly describes the role of the pyloric sphincter?
It prevents stomach contents from passing back into the oesophagus.
It controls the movement of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.
It secretes hydrochloric acid into the stomach.
It stores bile before it enters the small intestine.

The pyloric sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the base of the stomach that regulates the release of chyme into the duodenum. The lower oesophageal sphincter prevents reflux into the oesophagus, and bile is stored in the gallbladder.
bio12a2-dig-20
A student heats an amylase solution to 90°C for 10 minutes, then cools it to 37°C and mixes it with starch. The starch will most likely
be digested faster than before heating, because heat permanently activates the enzyme.
be digested at the same rate as before, because enzymes are not affected by heat.
be digested slowly at first, but its activity will recover once the enzyme is cooled to 37°C.
not be digested, because the enzyme's active site has been permanently changed by heat.

Temperatures well above the optimum for human enzymes break the weak bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site is permanently altered. Cooling does not restore the shape, so the enzyme cannot digest starch.
bio12a2-dig-21
Excess glucose absorbed from the small intestine is stored in the liver and muscle cells as which polysaccharide?
Glycogen.
Cellulose.
Starch.
Maltose.

Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose that humans store in the liver and muscles, and it is broken down to release glucose when blood sugar falls. Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, cellulose is structural in plant cell walls, and maltose is a disaccharide rather than a storage polymer.
bio12a2-dig-22
What is the main end product of the complete chemical digestion of proteins?
Glucose.
Maltose.
Fatty acids and glycerol.
Amino acids.

Pepsin, trypsin and peptidases hydrolyse proteins into amino acids, which are absorbed by the villi of the small intestine. Glucose and maltose come from carbohydrates, and fatty acids and glycerol come from lipids.
bio12a2-dig-23
Define the term peristalsis. (1 mark)
Rhythmic, wave-like contractions of the smooth muscle in the wall of the alimentary canal that push food along the gut. [1]
bio12a2-dig-24

A person has a blockage in the pancreatic duct that stops pancreatic juice reaching the duodenum. Explain why this person may have difficulty digesting lipids and proteins even though they eat a normal diet. (2 marks)

Pancreatic lipase, trypsin and other pancreatic enzymes cannot reach the duodenum, so lipids and proteins are not hydrolysed into smaller molecules that can be absorbed [1]; undigested fats and proteins pass into the large intestine, causing malabsorption and possibly fatty faeces [1].
bio12a2-dig-25
Explain how the muscular wall of the stomach assists digestion. (2 marks)

Contraction of the stomach's smooth muscle in several directions churns the food and mixes it with gastric juice [1]; this breaks the food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area available for enzymes such as pepsin to act on [1].
bio12a2-dig-26
A student adds amylase to a starch solution at 37°C and tests a sample with iodine solution every minute. Describe the expected colour changes and explain what they show. (3 marks)

Early samples turn blue-black, showing that starch is still present [1]; later samples stay brown-orange, the colour of iodine alone, showing that no starch remains [1]; amylase has hydrolysed the starch into smaller sugars such as maltose, which do not give a blue-black colour with iodine [1].
bio12a2-dig-27
Describe the sequence of events that moves a food bolus from the mouth into the stomach, naming the structures involved. (3 marks)

The tongue pushes the bolus back into the pharynx and the swallowing reflex begins [1]; the epiglottis closes over the trachea so the bolus enters the oesophagus [1]; peristalsis moves the bolus down the oesophagus and the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let it into the stomach [1].
bio12a2-dig-28
Trace the chemical digestion of a protein from the stomach to the small intestine, naming the enzyme(s) and the product(s) at each stage. (4 marks)

Stomach: hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen to pepsin [1]; pepsin hydrolyses proteins into polypeptides [1]; small intestine: trypsin from the pancreas hydrolyses polypeptides into smaller peptides [1]; peptidases on the microvilli hydrolyse these into amino acids, which are absorbed [1].
bio12a2-dig-29

A student finds that amylase converts 6.0 g of starch into maltose in 4.0 minutes at 37°C. Calculate the average rate of starch digestion in g min⁻¹, and state one change that would increase the rate without changing the temperature. (2 marks)
Rate = 6.0 g ÷ 4.0 min = 1.5 g min⁻¹ [1]; increase the concentration of amylase in the mixture [1].
bio12a2-dig-30
Explain why the pancreas secretes trypsin as the inactive precursor trypsinogen rather than as active trypsin. (2 marks)

Active trypsin would digest the pancreas's own tissue, causing self-digestion [1]; trypsinogen is converted to active trypsin only in the duodenum, by the enzyme enterokinase, so proteins are digested in the correct place [1].
vce-bio12-dg-c1
Bile contains no digestive enzymes, yet it speeds up fat digestion because it:
Breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol, which are then absorbed in the ileum
Neutralises lipase so that it can work in the alkaline small intestine
Absorbs fats from the gut directly into the blood through the villi
Emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to act on
Emulsification is a physical change. Lipase then hydrolyses the fats chemically.
vce-bio12-endocrine-and-excretory-system: bio12a2-endex-1
Hormones produced by endocrine glands reach their target cells by
travelling along neurons as electrical impulses.
being carried in the bloodstream and binding to specific receptors on or in target cells.
moving through ducts directly into the target organ.
diffusing across the synapse between gland and target.
Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood. Only cells with the matching receptor respond. Ducts are a feature of exocrine glands.
bio12a2-endex-2
The functional unit of the kidney, where urine is formed, is the
ureter.
renal artery.
nephron.
bladder.
Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, each of which filters blood and modifies the filtrate into urine. The ureter only carries urine to the bladder.
bio12a2-endex-3
In a healthy person, which substance would normally be absent from the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule?
Glucose
Urea
Water
Plasma proteins
Filtration at the glomerulus is based on size. Water, glucose, urea and ions pass into the capsule, but large plasma proteins (and blood cells) are too large to pass through the filtration barrier.
bio12a2-endex-4
In a healthy person, glucose that is filtered at the glomerulus is
completely reabsorbed into the blood, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule.
secreted back into the filtrate in the collecting duct.
converted into urea by nephron cells.
excreted in small amounts in the urine at all times.

All filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule. Glucose appears in urine only when blood glucose is so high that the carriers are saturated, as in untreated diabetes mellitus.
bio12a2-endex-5
The pancreas is described as both an endocrine and an exocrine gland because it
produces bile and stores glycogen.
secretes hormones into the blood and digestive enzymes through a duct.
filters blood and produces urine.
secretes hormones that only act on the pancreas itself.

The islets of Langerhans secrete insulin and glucagon into the blood (endocrine), while other pancreatic cells release digestive enzymes into the duodenum through the pancreatic duct (exocrine). Bile and glycogen storage are liver functions.
bio12a2-endex-6
Outline the three main processes involved in forming urine in the nephron. (3 marks)

Filtration: blood pressure forces water and small solutes (glucose, salts, urea) out of the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule; reabsorption: useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, many ions and much of the water move from the tubule back into the blood; secretion: extra wastes or ions such as H⁺, K⁺ and some drugs are actively moved from the blood into the tubule.
bio12a2-endex-7
Hormones circulate throughout the whole body, yet each one affects only certain cells. Explain why. (2 marks)

A hormone can only act on cells that have receptors complementary in shape to that hormone; only these target cells bind the hormone and start a response, while other cells lack the receptor and are not affected.
bio12a2-endex-8
The anterior pituitary gland is sometimes called the master gland. Explain this description, and explain why the hypothalamus is also important in endocrine control. (3 marks)

The anterior pituitary secretes tropic hormones such as TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH; these stimulate other endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads) to release their own hormones, so it controls many glands; however, the pituitary is itself controlled by releasing hormones from the hypothalamus (e.g. TRH), which links the nervous system to the endocrine system.
bio12a2-endex-9
Which cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin?
alpha cells
acinar cells
beta cells
delta cells
Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin into the blood. Alpha cells secrete glucagon, while acinar cells are exocrine cells that release digestive enzymes through the pancreatic duct.
bio12a2-endex-10
A diet lacking iodine would most directly reduce the production of which hormone?
thyroxine
insulin
adrenaline
antidiuretic hormone

Thyroxine is made by the thyroid gland from iodine and tyrosine. Insulin and antidiuretic hormone are peptides, and adrenaline is derived from tyrosine without iodine, so none of these depends on iodine.
bio12a2-endex-11
Which sequence correctly describes the negative feedback control of blood glucose after a meal?
High blood glucose stimulates glucagon release; glucagon lowers blood glucose, which then stimulates more glucagon release.
High blood glucose stimulates insulin release; insulin raises blood glucose, which then reduces insulin release.
High blood glucose stimulates adrenaline release; adrenaline lowers blood glucose, which then stimulates more adrenaline release.
High blood glucose stimulates insulin release; insulin lowers blood glucose, which then reduces insulin release.

Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and storage, and the falling glucose removes the stimulus for further insulin release.
