Glucagon and adrenaline raise blood glucose, so they are not released in response to high glucose, and an insulin-driven rise in glucose would reinforce the problem rather than correct it.
bio12a2-endex-12
A person has lost a large volume of water through sweating. Which response is expected?
ADH secretion decreases, so the collecting ducts become less permeable and more dilute urine is produced.
ADH secretion increases, so the collecting ducts become more permeable to water and more concentrated urine is produced.
ADH secretion increases, so the collecting ducts become more permeable to water and less concentrated urine is produced.
ADH secretion decreases, so more water is reabsorbed and urine volume increases.

Dehydration raises the solute concentration of the blood, which increases ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so less water is lost and the urine is concentrated. The other options reverse either the direction of the ADH change or its effect on urine.
bio12a2-endex-13
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), produced in the hypothalamus, acts mainly on which part of the nephron?
Collecting duct
Bowman's capsule
Glomerulus
Ureter

ADH makes the cells of the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed. Bowman's capsule and the glomerulus are sites of filtration, and the ureter only transports urine to the bladder.
bio12a2-endex-14
The loop of Henle is part of the nephron. What is its main function?
To filter blood under high pressure at the glomerulus.
To produce urea from ammonia in the nephron.
To reabsorb all the remaining glucose before the collecting duct.
To create a concentration gradient in the medulla so that water can be reabsorbed in the collecting duct.

The ascending limb of the loop of Henle actively pumps out salts, so the medulla becomes concentrated and water can leave the collecting duct by osmosis when ADH is present. Filtration occurs at the glomerulus, urea is made in the liver, and glucose is reabsorbed mainly in the proximal tubule.
bio12a2-endex-15
Urea, the main nitrogenous waste in humans, is formed in the liver from which substance?
glucose
ammonia produced when excess amino acids are broken down
cholesterol
glycogen
Excess amino acids are deaminated, producing toxic ammonia, which the liver converts into urea. Glucose, glycogen and cholesterol contain no nitrogen, so they cannot be a source of nitrogenous waste.
bio12a2-endex-16
In haemodialysis, what is the main purpose of the dialysis fluid?
To hold a lower concentration of waste substances than the blood, so wastes diffuse out of the blood.
To add urea to the blood so that the kidneys can filter it.
To replace red blood cells that are lost during treatment.
To pump blood through the kidney to increase filtration pressure.

Haemodialysis relies on diffusion across a semi-permeable membrane down a concentration gradient, so wastes such as urea move from the blood into the fluid. The other options describe adding wastes, replacing cells, or pumping blood, none of which removes wastes by diffusion.
bio12a2-endex-17
Which statement best describes the cause of type 1 diabetes mellitus?
The pancreas produces too much glucagon, so liver glycogen is broken down continuously.
Cells cannot respond to insulin because glucagon blocks their receptors.
The proximal tubule of the kidney is blocked, so glucose cannot be reabsorbed.
The beta cells of the islets are destroyed, usually by the immune system, so little or no insulin is made.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune destruction of beta cells, so the body makes little or no insulin and must be treated with injections. Type 2 diabetes is mainly a problem of cells responding poorly to insulin, and glucose spills into urine because blood glucose is too high rather than because a tubule is blocked.
bio12a2-endex-18
A sudden fright causes the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline. Which change is a direct effect of adrenaline?
Decreased heart rate and constriction of the bronchioles.
Increased heart rate and dilation of the bronchioles.
Increased blood flow to the digestive system.
Decreased breakdown of glycogen in the liver.

Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight by increasing heart rate, dilating the bronchioles and stimulating glycogen breakdown to release glucose. It also redirects blood towards skeletal muscle, so blood flow to the digestive system falls rather than rises.
bio12a2-endex-19
Aldosterone, which increases sodium reabsorption in the kidney, is secreted by the
adrenal medulla.
posterior pituitary.
adrenal cortex.
thyroid gland.

Aldosterone is a steroid hormone made by the outer part of the adrenal gland, the adrenal cortex. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline, the posterior pituitary releases ADH, and the thyroid makes thyroxine.
bio12a2-endex-20
Which of these is an example of excretion rather than egestion?
Removal of undigested fibre in the faeces.
Secretion of digestive enzymes into the duodenum.
Absorption of glucose across the wall of a villus.
Release of carbon dioxide from the lungs.

Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes produced by cells, such as carbon dioxide. Undigested fibre is egestion because it was never made by or absorbed into body cells, while enzyme secretion and glucose absorption are part of digestion.
bio12a2-endex-21
Where in the nephron is the greatest proportion of the filtered water reabsorbed?
Proximal convoluted tubule, where about two-thirds of the filtered water is reabsorbed.
Bowman's capsule, where most of the filtered water returns to the blood.
Ureter, where urine is concentrated before it reaches the bladder.
Urethra, where most of the remaining water is reabsorbed.

The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered water, along with nearly all the glucose and amino acids. Bowman's capsule is the site of filtration, and the ureter and urethra carry urine without reabsorbing water.
bio12a2-endex-22
Which statement correctly describes steroid hormones such as aldosterone?
They are made of amino acids and are stored in vesicles until released.
They are water-soluble and bind only to receptors on the outer cell membrane.
They are lipid-soluble, cross the cell membrane and bind receptors inside the target cell.
They travel only through nerves to reach their target cells.

Steroid hormones are derived from cholesterol, which makes them lipid-soluble, so they diffuse through the cell membrane and bind intracellular receptors. Water-soluble hormones such as insulin cannot cross the membrane and instead bind to receptors on the cell surface.
bio12a2-endex-23
The anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary gland differ in where their hormones come from. Describe this difference. (2 marks)

The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, which are made in the hypothalamus [1]; the anterior pituitary makes and secretes its own tropic hormones, whose release is controlled by releasing hormones from the hypothalamus [1].
bio12a2-endex-24
When blood thyroxine concentration falls, the hypothalamus and pituitary respond. Describe the sequence of events that restores thyroxine to normal levels. (3 marks)

Falling thyroxine removes inhibition of the hypothalamus, which releases TRH [1]; TRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete TSH [1]; TSH stimulates the thyroid to secrete more thyroxine, which returns to normal and then inhibits TRH and TSH release [1].
bio12a2-endex-25
Explain why insulin must be injected rather than swallowed as a tablet by a person with type 1 diabetes. (2 marks)
Insulin is a protein, so it would be digested by enzymes in the stomach and small intestine and lose its function [1]; injection delivers intact insulin directly into the blood [1].
bio12a2-endex-26
Name two organs, other than the kidneys, that excrete wastes, and state one waste each removes. (2 marks)
Lungs remove carbon dioxide (and water vapour) [1]; skin removes water, salts and urea in sweat [1].
bio12a2-endex-27
Explain why urea accumulates in the blood of a person whose kidneys have failed. (2 marks)
Urea is normally filtered at the glomerulus and removed from the body in urine [1]; when kidney function fails, urea is not filtered out or excreted, so it builds up in the blood [1].
bio12a2-endex-28
Name the process by which the liver converts excess glucose into glycogen for storage. (1 mark)
Glycogenesis [1]
bio12a2-endex-29
Explain why a person who drinks a large volume of water produces a large volume of dilute urine. (3 marks)

Drinking a large volume lowers the solute concentration of the blood [1]; less ADH is released from the posterior pituitary [1]; the collecting ducts become less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed and dilute urine is produced [1].
bio12a2-endex-30
Describe how a fall in blood glucose is detected and corrected, naming the cells and hormone involved. (4 marks)

Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans respond to the fall by secreting glucagon into the blood [1]; glucagon binds to receptors on liver cells and stimulates the breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis) [1]; glucose is released into the blood, raising blood glucose towards normal [1]; the rising glucose reduces glucagon secretion, which is negative feedback [1].
bio12a2-endex-31
Outline how the structure of the proximal convoluted tubule cells suits their function in reabsorption. (2 marks)
Microvilli on the cell surface increase surface area for reabsorption of glucose, amino acids and ions [1]; many mitochondria supply the ATP needed for active transport [1].
vce-bio12-en-c1
A hormone travels in the blood to every cell, but it affects only some. This is because:
The hormone is destroyed before it reaches most cells
Only target cells have receptors complementary to that hormone
Only cells near the gland receive it
Other cells are too small
Specific receptors (on the membrane or inside the cell) determine which cells respond.
vce-bio12-stimulus-response-model-and-ne: bio12a2-srm-1
Which sequence correctly shows the stimulus-response model?
Stimulus → modulator → receptor → effector → response
Receptor → stimulus → effector → modulator → response
Stimulus → receptor → modulator → effector → response
Stimulus → effector → receptor → modulator → response
A change (stimulus) is detected by a receptor, which sends a message to a modulator (control centre). The modulator signals an effector, which produces the response.
bio12a2-srm-2
Negative feedback is best described as a mechanism in which
the response increases the size of the original change.
the response counteracts the original change, returning the variable towards its set point.
the body stops responding to a stimulus after repeated exposure.
receptors are switched off so the variable can change freely.
In negative feedback the response reverses the change that triggered it, keeping the variable within a narrow range. A response that amplifies the change is positive feedback.
bio12a2-srm-3

When blood pressure rises, stretch receptors in the walls of the aorta send impulses to the medulla oblongata, which then sends impulses to the heart that slow the heart rate. In this pathway, the medulla oblongata acts as the
modulator.
receptor.
effector.
stimulus.
The medulla receives information from the receptors and coordinates a response, so it is the modulator (control centre). The heart is the effector and the rise in blood pressure is the stimulus.
bio12a2-srm-4
Which of the following is an example of positive feedback?
Sweating when body temperature rises
Release of insulin when blood glucose rises
Release of ADH when blood becomes more concentrated
Release of oxytocin during childbirth, which causes stronger contractions that trigger more oxytocin release

During labour, contractions push the baby against the cervix, stimulating more oxytocin release and even stronger contractions. The change is amplified until the baby is born. The other three responses reverse the change, so they are negative feedback.
bio12a2-srm-5
A student's core body temperature was recorded every hour for 24 hours. It varied between 36.4 °C and 37.2 °C. The best conclusion from these data is that
the student's thermoregulation was failing.
homeostasis keeps a variable within a narrow tolerance range rather than at one fixed value.
body temperature is controlled by positive feedback.
the student was ill, because temperature should stay at exactly 37.0 °C.
Homeostatic variables fluctuate around a set point. Small changes are detected and corrected, so the variable stays within a narrow range. A range of less than 1 °C over a day is normal.
bio12a2-srm-6
Distinguish between negative feedback and positive feedback. (2 marks)

In negative feedback, the response reduces or reverses the original stimulus, returning the variable towards its set point and maintaining homeostasis; in positive feedback, the response increases or amplifies the original stimulus, moving the variable further from its starting value until an end point is reached (e.g. childbirth, blood clotting).
bio12a2-srm-7
A person touches a hot pan and immediately pulls their hand away. Using the stimulus-response model, identify the stimulus, receptor, modulator, effector and response. (3 marks)

Stimulus: high temperature of the pan on the skin; receptor: thermoreceptors/pain receptors in the skin of the hand; modulator: the spinal cord (a reflex arc through interneurons); effector: skeletal muscles of the arm (e.g. biceps); response: muscle contraction that moves the hand away from the pan. (3 marks for all five correct, 2 for four, 1 for two or three.)
bio12a2-srm-8
Explain why keeping body temperature and pH within narrow ranges is important for the functioning of cells. (2 marks)

Cell metabolism depends on enzymes, which have an optimum temperature and pH; large changes alter the shape of the active site or denature the enzyme (or slow reactions a lot if too cold), so metabolic reactions could not continue at the rates cells need.
bio12a2-srm-9
The value around which a homeostatic variable is normally maintained is called the
stimulus.
set point.
effector.
modulator.

The set point is the reference value that the variable is kept close to. A stimulus is the change that is detected, and the modulator is the control centre that processes information; neither is the reference value.
bio12a2-srm-10
Which of the following best defines a receptor in the stimulus-response model?
a structure that detects a change in the internal or external environment and sends information to the modulator.
a structure that carries out the response, such as a muscle or gland.
the change in the environment that starts the pathway.
the control centre that compares the information with the set point and decides on a response.

A receptor detects the stimulus and passes information on to the modulator. The effector is the structure that produces the response, the stimulus is the change itself, and the modulator is the control centre.
bio12a2-srm-11
During sweating on a hot day, the sweat glands in the skin act as the
stimulus.
receptor.
modulator.
effector.

Sweat glands carry out the response by producing sweat that cools the body, so they are the effector. The rise in body temperature is the stimulus and the thermoreceptors are the receptors, so neither describes the glands.
bio12a2-srm-12
After a meal, blood glucose rises and insulin is released, causing body cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it. Which statement about this pathway is correct?
It is positive feedback, because insulin raises blood glucose further.
It is negative feedback, because insulin increases the original rise in blood glucose.
It is negative feedback, because the response lowers blood glucose back towards the set point.
It is not feedback, because the response does not involve the nervous system.

Insulin acts to reverse the rise in blood glucose, which is the defining feature of negative feedback. Feedback loops can involve hormones as well as nerve impulses, so the hormonal route does not make it 'not feedback'.
bio12a2-srm-13
Which statement about blood clotting is correct?
It is negative feedback, because the clot reverses the cut in the blood vessel.
It is positive feedback, because each clotting factor activates more clotting factors, amplifying the response until a clot forms.
It is negative feedback, because platelets stop clotting once bleeding starts.
It is not a feedback process, because it does not involve a receptor.

In clotting, each step activates further steps, so the response is amplified until a clot seals the wound, which is the defining feature of positive feedback. Describing clotting as negative feedback is a common mistake, because the clot seals the wound rather than reversing the cut.
bio12a2-srm-14
Normal arterial blood pH is 7.35–7.45. Which value lies outside this normal range?
A pH of 7.31 is below the lower limit of 7.35, so it is outside the normal range. The value 7.36 is only just above the lower limit, so it is still within the range.
bio12a2-srm-15
When the blood becomes more concentrated, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change and more ADH is released. What is the effect of ADH on the kidney, and on the blood?
The collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so the blood becomes more dilute.
The collecting ducts reabsorb less water, so the blood becomes more dilute.
The collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so the blood becomes more concentrated.
The collecting ducts reabsorb more salt, so the blood becomes more concentrated.

ADH increases the water reabsorbed by the collecting ducts, which dilutes the blood and reverses the original rise in concentration. Reabsorbing less water would make the blood more concentrated, so that option has the wrong direction.
bio12a2-srm-16
Why do most homeostatic control systems use negative feedback rather than positive feedback?
Negative feedback makes the variable change faster, which is needed in emergencies.
Negative feedback keeps the variable close to its set point, so conditions stay within the limits cells need.
Negative feedback removes the need for receptors and effectors.
Negative feedback allows the stimulus to be maintained indefinitely.

Negative feedback reverses changes, so variables such as temperature and pH stay within the narrow ranges that enzymes and cells need. Positive feedback drives a change further and would move a variable away from its set point.
bio12a2-srm-17
A person has not eaten for several hours and their blood glucose begins to fall. In the stimulus-response model, the stimulus is the
release of glucagon from the pancreas.
release of glucose from the liver.
uptake of glucose by body cells.
fall in blood glucose concentration.
The stimulus is the change in the internal environment that is detected, here the fall in blood glucose. Glucagon release and glucose release from the liver are later steps in the response.
bio12a2-srm-18
Which of the following is a response rather than a stimulus?
Shivering, the rapid contraction of skeletal muscles that generates heat.
A fall in environmental temperature.
A rise in blood pressure detected by stretch receptors.
An increase in blood carbon dioxide concentration.
Shivering is an action carried out by an effector, so it is a response. The other three options are changes in the body or environment that receptors detect, which makes them stimuli.
bio12a2-srm-19
A homeostatic response reduces a deviation from the set point, but the variable overshoots the set point before settling back. How should this pattern be classified?
Positive feedback, because the variable moved past the set point.
Negative feedback, because the response still acts to reduce the deviation from the set point.
Positive feedback, because the response needed more than one correction.
Not feedback, because the variable did not stay at the set point.
The response still opposes the change, so it is negative feedback. Overshoot happens because the response takes time to act, and it does not mean the response is amplifying the original change.
bio12a2-srm-20
What is the main purpose of a positive feedback loop in the body?
To keep a variable within a narrow range around its set point.
To switch off the stimulus once it has been detected.
To rapidly drive a process to completion, such as childbirth or blood clotting.
To stop receptors from responding to repeated stimuli.
Positive feedback amplifies a change until an end point is reached, which suits processes that must finish quickly. Keeping a variable near its set point is the role of negative feedback.
bio12a2-srm-21
A person is exposed to cold air and their core body temperature begins to fall. Which part of the pathway is the effector?
Thermoreceptors in the skin.
The hypothalamus, which compares the temperature with the set point.
The fall in core body temperature.
The skeletal muscles, which contract to shiver and produce heat.

Skeletal muscles carry out the response by contracting and producing heat, so they are the effector. The thermoreceptors are the receptors, the hypothalamus is the modulator, and the fall in temperature is the stimulus.
bio12a2-srm-22
Define the term stimulus in the stimulus-response model. (1 mark)
A change in the internal or external environment that is detected by a receptor. [1]
bio12a2-srm-23
State the role of the modulator in the stimulus-response model. (1 mark)
The modulator (control centre) receives information from the receptor and coordinates the response by signalling the effector. [1]
bio12a2-srm-24
Define the term tolerance range as it applies to homeostasis. (1 mark)
The narrow band of values, either side of the set point, within which a homeostatic variable is kept. [1]
bio12a2-srm-25
Explain why sweating is an example of negative feedback. (2 marks)

The stimulus is a rise in body temperature, which is detected and triggers sweating. [1] Evaporation of sweat cools the body, reversing the original rise and returning temperature towards the set point. [1]
bio12a2-srm-26
Identify the stimulus and describe the response that helps restore blood pH during vigorous exercise. (2 marks)

Stimulus: a rise in blood carbon dioxide concentration (fall in pH), detected by chemoreceptors. [1] Response: increased rate and depth of breathing, produced by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, expels carbon dioxide and returns blood pH towards its set point. [1]
bio12a2-srm-27
Explain why it is important that the modulator compares information from receptors with the set point before signalling an effector. (2 marks)
The modulator determines whether the variable has deviated from the set point. [1] This allows an appropriately sized and directed response to be sent to the effector to reverse the change. [1]
bio12a2-srm-28
Explain why a negative feedback response that is too slow or too weak may fail to keep a variable within its tolerance range. (2 marks)

The response must reverse the stimulus quickly and strongly enough to counteract it. [1] If it is too slow or too weak, the variable keeps changing and can move outside the tolerance range, which may damage cells or disrupt function. [1]
bio12a2-srm-29
Describe a negative feedback pathway that increases water reabsorption when the blood becomes more concentrated, identifying the receptor, modulator and effector. (3 marks)

Receptor: osmoreceptors that detect the increased solute concentration of the blood. [1] Modulator: the hypothalamus, which signals the posterior pituitary to release ADH into the blood. [1] Effector: the kidney collecting ducts, which reabsorb more water, diluting the blood and reversing the change. [1]
vce-bio12-sr-c1
Which is an example of positive feedback rather than negative feedback?
Sweating when body temperature rises, which lowers body temperature back to normal
Oxytocin increasing uterine contractions during childbirth, which cause more oxytocin release
Insulin release when blood glucose rises, which lowers blood glucose back to normal
ADH release when the blood becomes concentrated, which increases water reabsorption
Negative feedback reverses a change, keeping conditions stable. Positive feedback amplifies a change until an endpoint (birth) is reached.
vce-bio12-thermoregulation: bio12a2-thermo-1
The thermoregulatory control centre in humans is located in the
medulla oblongata.
cerebellum.
hypothalamus.
thyroid gland.
The hypothalamus receives information from central and peripheral thermoreceptors and coordinates responses. The thyroid gland is an effector gland that it controls indirectly through the pituitary.
bio12a2-thermo-2
On a cold morning, which response would reduce heat loss from the body?
Vasodilation of arterioles supplying the skin
Increased sweating
Decreased secretion of thyroxine
Vasoconstriction of arterioles supplying the skin

Vasoconstriction lowers blood flow near the skin surface, so less heat is lost by radiation and conduction. Vasodilation and sweating increase heat loss, and less thyroxine would lower heat production.
bio12a2-thermo-3
During shivering, the effectors that generate heat are
skeletal muscles, which contract rapidly and involuntarily.
sweat glands, which release warm fluid onto the skin.
smooth muscles in the stomach wall.
thermoreceptors in the skin.
Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles. The extra cellular respiration releases heat. Thermoreceptors are receptors, not effectors.
bio12a2-thermo-4
Runners in a humid tropical marathon in Darwin are more likely to overheat than runners in a dry race at the same air temperature. The best explanation is that in humid air
sweat glands stop producing sweat.
less sweat evaporates, so less heat is removed from the skin.
the hypothalamus cannot detect the rise in body temperature.
vasodilation cannot occur.
Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates, because evaporation takes heat energy from the skin. When the air is already humid, evaporation is slow, so sweat drips off without much cooling.
bio12a2-thermo-5
A central bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps) lies in the sun on a rock in the early morning, then moves into a burrow at midday. This is best described as
physiological thermoregulation by an endotherm.
structural thermoregulation by an ectotherm.
behavioural thermoregulation by an ectotherm.
shivering thermogenesis.
Bearded dragons are ectotherms; they get most body heat from the environment. Moving between sun and shade is a behaviour that adjusts how much heat they gain.
bio12a2-thermo-6
Describe how the hypothalamus increases heat production through the thyroid gland when the body is cold. (2 marks)

The hypothalamus releases TRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH; TSH stimulates the thyroid to secrete thyroxine, which increases the metabolic (cellular respiration) rate of body cells, releasing more heat.
bio12a2-thermo-7
Explain why a person's skin often looks flushed (red) during hard exercise. (2 marks)

Exercise raises core temperature, which is detected and leads to vasodilation of arterioles supplying the skin; more warm blood flows close to the skin surface, making it look red and increasing heat loss by radiation.
bio12a2-thermo-8

A bushwalker caught in a snowstorm near Mount Kosciuszko begins to cool. Use the stimulus-response model to explain how the body tries to return core temperature to normal. Include two different effector responses. (3 marks)

Stimulus: fall in skin and core temperature, detected by thermoreceptors in the skin and in the hypothalamus; the hypothalamus acts as modulator and sends nerve impulses to effectors; e.g. skeletal muscles shiver to produce heat, and smooth muscle in skin arterioles contracts (vasoconstriction) to reduce heat loss (also accept piloerection or a behavioural response such as putting on clothing or seeking shelter); this is negative feedback because the responses counteract the fall in temperature.
bio12a2-thermo-9
Which statement correctly describes peripheral thermoreceptors?
They are located in the skin and detect changes in external temperature.
They are located in the hypothalamus and detect changes in the temperature of the blood.
They are effectors that contract to produce heat when the body is cold.
They are endocrine glands that secrete thyroxine in response to cold.

Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin respond to temperature at the body surface and send impulses to the hypothalamus. The option describing receptors in the hypothalamus describes central thermoreceptors, and the other two options describe effectors, not receptors.
bio12a2-thermo-10
A runner's core temperature rises above the set point during a race. Which sequence correctly describes how the body responds?
Sweat glands secrete sweat, the hypothalamus detects the rise, thermoreceptors respond, and evaporation cools the skin.
Thermoreceptors detect the rise, the hypothalamus receives the impulses, sweat glands secrete sweat, and evaporation removes heat from the skin.
The hypothalamus secretes sweat, thermoreceptors send impulses to the sweat glands, and evaporation removes heat from the skin.
The thyroid gland releases thyroxine, the hypothalamus sends impulses to skeletal muscles, and shivering increases heat production.

Thermoreceptors are the receptors, the hypothalamus is the control centre, and the sweat glands are the effectors, so the correct order runs from receptor to control centre to effector. The option in which the hypothalamus secretes sweat confuses the control centre with an effector, and the last option describes a heat-producing response that would not cool the runner.
bio12a2-thermo-11
The large, thin ears of the desert fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) help the animal survive hot conditions mainly because they
trap a layer of warm air against the head, reducing heat gain from the Sun.
absorb solar radiation, which warms the blood flowing through them.
have a large surface area with many blood vessels close to the skin, so heat is lost by radiation and convection.
reduce heat loss by stopping blood flow to the ears.

Heat leaves the body across the surface of the ears, so a large, thin ear with blood vessels close to the skin increases heat loss in hot conditions. Trapping warm air describes insulating fur rather than thin ears, and absorbing sunlight would add heat.
bio12a2-thermo-12
Huddling together in a tight group during a blizzard is an example of which type of response to a cold stimulus?
A physiological response that is controlled by the hypothalamus.
A physiological response that increases heat production.
An endocrine response mediated by thyroxine.
A behavioural response that reduces heat loss.

Huddling is an action the animal performs, so it is behavioural, and it reduces the exposed surface area through which heat is lost. Vasoconstriction, shivering and thyroxine secretion are physiological responses that occur inside the body, so the other options describe the wrong type of response.
bio12a2-thermo-13
Which statement about ectotherms is correct?
They rely mainly on heat from the external environment and on behaviour to regulate their body temperature.
They maintain a constant core temperature by metabolic heat production alone.
Their body temperature is always higher than that of endotherms of the same size.
They cannot change their behaviour to alter how much heat they gain.

Ectotherms gain most of their body heat from the environment and use behaviours such as basking or sheltering to adjust it. Metabolic heat production alone describes endotherms, and ectotherms' body temperatures generally follow their surroundings, so the other options are incorrect.
bio12a2-thermo-14
Why does a mouse lose heat from its body faster, per gram of body mass, than an elephant in the same cold environment?
A mouse has a lower metabolic rate per gram of body mass, so it produces less heat.
A mouse has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so more heat is lost through its surface for each gram of body tissue.
An elephant has more sweat glands per gram of body mass, so it loses more heat by evaporation.
A mouse has a lower core temperature than an elephant, so heat flows out faster.

Heat is produced throughout the body's volume but lost through its surface, and small animals have a larger surface area relative to volume. The option about a lower metabolic rate is wrong because small endotherms have a higher metabolic rate per gram than large ones.
bio12a2-thermo-15
Why can a person in water at 20 °C lose body heat faster than a person standing in air at 20 °C?
Water is denser than air, so it pushes heat out of the skin by pressure.
Water removes heat from the skin by evaporation more quickly than air does.
Water conducts heat away from the skin much more rapidly than air does.
Water stops the hypothalamus from detecting the change in body temperature.

Water has a much higher thermal conductivity than air, so heat moves from the skin into the surrounding water far more quickly by conduction. A submerged person cannot lose heat by evaporation, so the option about evaporation is wrong.
bio12a2-thermo-16
During an infection, pyrogens act on the hypothalamus and raise the set point to 39 °C. Which response occurs as the core temperature rises towards the new set point?
Sweat glands increase their secretion to cool the blood.
Arterioles supplying the skin dilate, increasing heat loss by radiation.
Thermoreceptors stop sending impulses to the hypothalamus.
Vasoconstriction and shivering increase heat production and reduce heat loss.

Relative to the raised set point, the body now detects its temperature as too low, so it conserves heat and produces more of it until the core temperature reaches the new set point. Sweating and vasodilation are responses to a temperature above the set point, so the first two options are wrong.
bio12a2-thermo-17
A hiker loses a large volume of water through sweating and does not drink enough. Why does dehydration reduce the body's ability to cool itself?
The hypothalamus can no longer detect a rise in core temperature.
Less water is available to be secreted as sweat, so less sweat evaporates and less heat is removed.
Sweat becomes hotter than the skin, so it cannot evaporate.
Vasodilation of the arterioles is blocked, so blood cannot flow near the skin.

Sweat is formed mostly from water in the blood plasma, so a lower water volume means less sweat is available to evaporate and less heat is removed. A dehydrated person's hypothalamus still detects temperature changes, so the first option is wrong.
bio12a2-thermo-18
Which statement correctly describes negative feedback in the control of body temperature?
The response to a change in temperature increases that change, moving the temperature further from the set point.
The response occurs only after the stimulus has stopped.
The responses counteract the change, moving the core temperature back towards the set point.
The responses have no effect on the stimulus that started them.

In negative feedback, the output of the response opposes the original change, which keeps the core temperature close to the set point. The first option describes positive feedback, which does not normally control body temperature.
bio12a2-thermo-19
The normal core body temperature of a healthy adult human is approximately
Core temperature is regulated at around 37 °C in healthy adults. A temperature of 39 °C is a fever in many people, and 42 °C is dangerously high, while 35 °C is below normal.
bio12a2-thermo-20
Dense fur reduces heat loss from a mammal's body mainly because
it increases the rate of sweat evaporation from the skin.
trapped air is a poor conductor, so heat loss by conduction and convection is reduced.
it increases blood flow to the skin surface.
its hairs produce heat directly through cellular respiration.

Still air trapped among the fur is a poor conductor, so it slows heat moving away from the skin by conduction and reduces convection. Fur does not cause evaporation or increase blood flow, and the hair itself does not generate heat.
bio12a2-thermo-21
A lizard is sluggish on a cold morning. Explain why, in terms of body temperature and enzyme activity. (2 marks)

As the lizard's body temperature falls, enzyme-controlled reactions, including cellular respiration, slow down [1]; less energy is released and nerve impulses and muscle contraction slow, so the lizard moves sluggishly [1].
bio12a2-thermo-22
Heat stroke can occur when core temperature rises to around 40 °C. Explain why this is dangerous for body cells. (2 marks)

High temperature denatures enzymes and other proteins, so their shape and function are lost [1]; metabolic reactions, including cellular respiration, cannot proceed normally, damaging cells and organs [1].
bio12a2-thermo-23
Explain how a layer of subcutaneous fat (blubber) reduces heat loss from a marine mammal in cold water. (2 marks)

Fat has a low thermal conductivity, so heat conducts slowly from the warm core through the fat towards the surrounding water [1]; fat tissue has relatively few blood vessels, so less blood flows to the outer layer and less heat is carried to the skin surface [1].
bio12a2-thermo-24
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube-shaped body with sides of 2 cm. Show your working. (2 marks)
Surface area = 6 × 2² = 24 cm² [1]; volume = 2³ = 8 cm³, so the ratio is 24 : 8 = 3 : 1 (3 cm⁻¹) [1].
bio12a2-thermo-25
Dogs have few sweat glands. Explain how panting helps a dog lose heat. (2 marks)
Water evaporates from the moist surfaces of the tongue and respiratory tract [1]; the evaporation removes heat energy from the blood and body, cooling the dog [1].
bio12a2-thermo-26
Describe three adaptations that help desert animals reduce heat gain from their environment. (3 marks)
Light-coloured fur or skin reflects solar radiation [1]; nocturnal activity avoids the hottest part of the day [1]; burrowing into cooler soil or shade reduces heat gained from the environment [1].
vce-bio12-th-c1
A person walks into a very cold room. Which response would NOT occur?
Vasodilation of arterioles supplying the skin
Shivering of skeletal muscles to produce heat
Hairs standing on end to trap a layer of air
An increase in metabolic rate to release heat
In the cold, skin arterioles constrict (vasoconstriction) to reduce heat loss. Vasodilation happens when the body is too hot.
vce-bio12-blood-glucose-regulation: bio12a2-bgr-1
Insulin is secreted by
alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
hepatocytes in the liver.
the adrenal medulla.
Beta cells in the pancreatic islets secrete insulin. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline.
bio12a2-bgr-2
When blood glucose concentration falls, glucagon acts mainly on the liver to
stimulate glycogenesis, converting glucose into glycogen.
increase glucose uptake by muscle cells.
stimulate glycogenolysis, breaking glycogen down into glucose that enters the blood.
stop the pancreas releasing insulin.
Glucagon makes liver cells break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood, raising the blood glucose level. Glycogenesis is promoted by insulin.
bio12a2-bgr-3

After a meal, a person's blood glucose rose from 4.8 mmol L⁻¹ to 8.0 mmol L⁻¹ within 30 minutes, then returned to 5 mmol L⁻¹ after two hours. Which change would be expected in the first 30 minutes after the meal?
Insulin secretion increases
Glucagon secretion increases
Glycogen stores in the liver decrease
Glucose uptake by muscle cells decreases

Rising blood glucose is detected by beta cells, which secrete more insulin. Insulin increases glucose uptake into cells and glycogen storage, which explains the return to normal. Glucagon secretion would decrease.
bio12a2-bgr-4
Which of the following is NOT an effect of insulin?
Increasing glucose uptake by skeletal muscle and fat cells
Promoting the conversion of glucose to glycogen in the liver
Lowering blood glucose concentration
Stimulating the breakdown of glycogen into glucose
Breaking down glycogen raises blood glucose and is stimulated by glucagon (and adrenaline). Insulin has the opposite effect, promoting glucose uptake and storage.
bio12a2-bgr-5
Insulin cannot be taken as a tablet because it is a protein (peptide) hormone. The main reason a tablet would be ineffective is that insulin would
be broken down by proteases in the stomach and small intestine before it reached the blood.
diffuse straight through the plasma membrane of gut cells.
be converted into glucose in the stomach.
bind to receptors in the stomach and lower stomach pH.
Proteases such as pepsin and trypsin would digest the insulin into amino acids, so active hormone would not reach the blood. Insulin is hydrophilic and is too large to diffuse through membranes.
bio12a2-bgr-6
A student skips breakfast and their blood glucose level begins to fall. Explain how negative feedback returns the level to normal. (3 marks)

The fall in blood glucose is detected by alpha cells (and beta cells) in the islets of Langerhans; alpha cells secrete more glucagon and beta cells secrete less insulin; glucagon causes liver cells to break glycogen down into glucose (glycogenolysis), which is released into the blood, so blood glucose rises back towards the set point and the stimulus is removed.
bio12a2-bgr-7
Explain the role of the liver in regulating blood glucose concentration. (2 marks)

When blood glucose is high, insulin causes liver cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen (glycogenesis); when blood glucose is low, glucagon causes liver cells to break glycogen down and release glucose into the blood (glycogenolysis), so the liver acts as a glucose store that buffers changes.
bio12a2-bgr-8
During a frightening event, adrenaline is released and blood glucose rises. Explain how this rise is an advantage to the person. (2 marks)

Adrenaline stimulates the breakdown of glycogen in the liver (and muscles), releasing glucose; the extra glucose supplies muscle and brain cells with more fuel for cellular respiration, giving more ATP for a fight-or-flight response.
bio12a2-bgr-9
Which statement best describes the set point for blood glucose concentration in a healthy person?
A narrow range, around 4–6 mmol L⁻¹ when fasting, that the body works to keep blood glucose within
A single fixed value of 5 mmol L⁻¹ that never changes, even after eating
The renal threshold, the concentration above which glucose first appears in urine
The concentration at which the pancreas stops secreting insulin

The set point is a narrow target range that negative feedback works to maintain, not a single unchanging value. Blood glucose rises after a meal and falls during fasting, while the renal threshold and the point where insulin secretion stops are different quantities.
bio12a2-bgr-10
Insulin and glucagon are both peptide hormones, yet they have opposite effects on blood glucose. What explains their opposite effects?
Both hormones bind to the same receptor, but glucagon binds to it more strongly
Each hormone binds to its own specific receptor on target cells, and the cell's response depends on which hormone binds
Glucagon passes through the plasma membrane, whereas insulin cannot cross it
Insulin and glucagon are secreted by the same cell type, so their effects cancel out

Each hormone acts only on target cells carrying its specific receptor, so the hormone that binds determines the response. Both hormones are peptides that cannot cross the plasma membrane, and they are secreted by different islet cells (beta and alpha cells), so the other options are wrong.
bio12a2-bgr-11
In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the beta cells of the pancreatic islets. What is the most likely effect on blood glucose after a meal?
Blood glucose falls below the set point because glucagon is no longer secreted
Blood glucose stays unchanged because insulin is only needed during fasting
Blood glucose rises higher and stays elevated for longer, because cells take up and store less glucose
Blood glucose returns to normal quickly because the liver makes its own insulin

Without beta cells, little or no insulin is secreted, so cells take up less glucose and the liver stores less glycogen, and blood glucose stays high after a meal. Insulin is needed after meals to lower blood glucose, and the liver does not make insulin.
bio12a2-bgr-12
Type 2 diabetes is often linked to insulin resistance. Which description best matches insulin resistance?
The pancreas stops producing insulin altogether
Insulin is secreted by the liver rather than the pancreas
Glucagon is secreted in excess by the alpha cells of the pancreas
Target cells respond less strongly than normal to a given concentration of insulin

In insulin resistance the pancreas usually still secretes insulin, but target cells such as muscle and fat cells respond poorly to it. Complete loss of insulin production describes type 1 diabetes, and excess glucagon would raise blood glucose rather than describe resistance.
bio12a2-bgr-13
The brain uses a large amount of energy but stores very little of it. Why does a fall in blood glucose quickly affect brain function?
The brain relies almost entirely on glucose from the blood for cellular respiration and has very little stored energy
The brain stores large amounts of glycogen that it cannot access in an emergency
Insulin builds up in brain cells and blocks cellular respiration when glucose is low
The brain makes its own glucose from amino acids, so it does not depend on blood glucose

Brain cells depend on a continuous supply of blood glucose because they store only small amounts of glycogen. Insulin does not accumulate in brain cells, and the brain does not make glucose from amino acids.
bio12a2-bgr-14
Glucose is too polar to pass directly through the lipid bilayer of a cell membrane. How does glucose enter skeletal muscle cells, and what effect does insulin have on this?
Active transport that uses ATP; insulin switches off the transport pumps
Facilitated diffusion through glucose transporter proteins; insulin increases the number of transporters in the membrane
Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer; insulin makes the membrane more permeable to lipids
Osmosis through aquaporins; insulin opens more aquaporins

Glucose moves down its concentration gradient through transporter proteins, which is facilitated diffusion, and insulin increases the number of these transporters in the membrane. Osmosis describes water movement, and simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer does not suit a polar molecule like glucose.
bio12a2-bgr-15
A person's blood glucose concentration is 4.2 mmol L⁻¹ before a 45-minute run and 3.1 mmol L⁻¹ after it. Which hormonal change is most consistent with this fall?
Insulin secretion increases to lower blood glucose further
Glucagon secretion decreases because blood glucose is falling
Glucagon secretion increases and insulin secretion decreases, both of which help raise blood glucose
Neither hormone changes, because exercise does not affect blood glucose
A falling blood glucose is detected by alpha cells, which secrete more glucagon, while beta cells reduce insulin secretion. The other options reverse these responses or ignore the fall altogether.
bio12a2-bgr-16
A blood glucose concentration of 16 mmol L⁻¹ measured after a meal is best described as which condition?
hyperglycaemia
hypoglycaemia
normoglycaemia
glycolysis

Hyperglycaemia is blood glucose above the normal range, which 16 mmol L⁻¹ clearly is. Hypoglycaemia is below normal, normoglycaemia is within the normal range, and glycolysis is a metabolic pathway rather than a condition.
bio12a2-bgr-17
Insulin promotes the conversion of excess glucose into fat for storage in adipose tissue. What is this process called?
lipolysis
lipogenesis
glycogenolysis
proteolysis
Lipogenesis is the synthesis of fat for storage, whereas lipolysis breaks stored fat down. Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen into glucose, and proteolysis breaks proteins into amino acids.
bio12a2-bgr-18
Why do hormones, rather than nerve impulses alone, play a major role in regulating blood glucose?
Hormones travel along nerve axons and reach target cells faster than nerve impulses
Hormones act only on the cell that secreted them, so their responses are very localised
Hormones are carried in the blood to target cells throughout the body, giving slower but longer-lasting responses
Hormones are electrical signals that pass instantly across synapses

Hormones are transported in the blood and can reach many target cells, producing slower but more sustained responses than nerve impulses. The other options describe nerve signals or misstate how hormones act.
bio12a2-bgr-19
Blood glucose falls from 9.0 mmol L⁻¹ to 4.5 mmol L⁻¹. What is the percentage decrease?

The decrease is 9.0 − 4.5 = 4.5 mmol L⁻¹, and 4.5 ÷ 9.0 × 100 = 50%. Dividing the change by the new value gives 100%, dividing the original value by the new value gives 200%, and 25% would require a change of only 2.25 mmol L⁻¹.
bio12a2-bgr-20
Insulin is a peptide hormone that cannot cross the plasma membrane. Where does insulin bind to produce its effect on a target cell?
Inside the nucleus, where it switches genes on directly
In the cytoplasm, where it binds to the enzymes of glycolysis
In the bloodstream, where it binds directly to glucose molecules
A specific receptor protein on the outer surface of the target cell membrane

Because insulin cannot enter the cell, it binds to a receptor protein on the outer surface of the plasma membrane and triggers a response inside the cell. Insulin does not bind glucose, and it does not enter the nucleus or cytoplasm.
bio12a2-bgr-21
Glucose absorbed from a meal in the small intestine is carried to the liver by which blood vessel?
The hepatic vein
The aorta
The hepatic portal vein
The renal artery

Blood from the small intestine drains into the hepatic portal vein, which delivers absorbed glucose to the liver before it reaches the rest of the body. The hepatic vein carries blood away from the liver, the aorta carries blood away from the heart, and the renal artery supplies the kidneys.
bio12a2-bgr-22
Define the terms glycogenesis and glycogenolysis. (2 marks)
Glycogenesis is the conversion of glucose into glycogen for storage [1]; glycogenolysis is the breakdown of glycogen into glucose [1].
bio12a2-bgr-23
A person with type 2 diabetes is advised to take up regular exercise. Explain how exercise can help lower blood glucose. (2 marks)
Contracting muscle cells take up glucose from the blood, lowering blood glucose [1]; this improves the response of body cells to insulin and reduces the amount of insulin needed [1].
bio12a2-bgr-24
A person's blood glucose concentration is 5.5 mmol L⁻¹ before a meal and rises by 40% after the meal. Calculate the blood glucose concentration after the meal. Show your working. (2 marks)
Increase = 0.40 × 5.5 = 2.2 mmol L⁻¹ [1]; new concentration = 5.5 + 2.2 = 7.7 mmol L⁻¹ [1].
bio12a2-bgr-25
Explain why a person with untreated type 1 diabetes may lose weight and pass large volumes of urine. (3 marks)

Without insulin, body cells cannot take up glucose, so they break down stored fats and proteins for energy [1]; blood glucose rises above the renal threshold, so glucose is excreted in the urine [1]; the glucose draws water into the urine by osmosis, increasing urine output [1].
bio12a2-bgr-26
Compare the roles of insulin and glucagon in regulating blood glucose concentration, including the conditions that trigger each hormone. (4 marks)

Insulin is secreted by beta cells when blood glucose is high [1]; glucagon is secreted by alpha cells when blood glucose is low [1]; insulin promotes glucose uptake by cells and the conversion of glucose into glycogen [1]; glucagon promotes the breakdown of liver glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood [1].
bio12a2-bgr-27
Explain why the pancreas is described as both an endocrine and an exocrine gland. (2 marks)

The islets of Langerhans secrete hormones directly into the blood, which is an endocrine function [1]; acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes into ducts that carry them to the small intestine, which is an exocrine function [1].
bio12a2-bgr-28
State one reason why blood glucose concentration must be kept within a narrow range. (1 mark)
Cells, especially brain cells, need a constant supply of glucose for cellular respiration [1].
bio12a2-bgr-29
Explain why an overdose of insulin can be dangerous, even though insulin normally lowers blood glucose as intended. (3 marks)

Blood glucose can fall well below the set point [1]; the brain depends on glucose for cellular respiration, so it is deprived of fuel, causing confusion and, in severe cases, unconsciousness [1]; the body's glucagon and adrenaline responses may not restore blood glucose quickly enough to prevent this [1].
bio12a2-bgr-30
Explain why glucose is stored as glycogen in liver and muscle cells rather than as free glucose in the cytoplasm. (2 marks)

Glycogen is a large, insoluble molecule, so storing glucose as glycogen does not raise the solute concentration of the cytoplasm and does not draw water into the cell by osmosis [1]; glycogen can be quickly broken down into glucose when the cell needs it [1].
vce-bio12-bg-c1
How does type 2 diabetes differ from type 1 diabetes?
In type 2, the immune system destroys beta cells; in type 1, body cells respond poorly to insulin
In type 1, diet is the only cause; in type 2, a lack of exercise is the only cause
In type 2, body cells respond poorly to insulin; in type 1, the immune system destroys beta cells
In type 2, beta cells make too much glucagon; in type 1, alpha cells make no insulin
Type 1 is autoimmune, so insulin must be injected. Type 2 involves insulin resistance and is often managed by diet, exercise and medication at first.
vce-bio12-water-balance: bio12a2-wb-1
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is produced in the hypothalamus and released into the blood from the
anterior pituitary gland.
posterior pituitary gland.
adrenal cortex.
kidney cortex.

ADH is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus, then travels down their axons and is stored in and released from the posterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones, such as TSH.
bio12a2-wb-2
ADH helps the body retain water by
increasing the rate of filtration at the glomerulus.
decreasing the permeability of the collecting ducts to water.
increasing the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water, so more water is reabsorbed.
actively pumping urea back into the blood.

ADH causes more aquaporins to be inserted into the membranes of distal tubule and collecting duct cells. More water moves by osmosis back into the blood, producing a small volume of concentrated urine.
bio12a2-wb-3
The receptors that detect a rise in the solute concentration (osmolarity) of the blood are
osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus.
baroreceptors in the aorta.
chemoreceptors in the stomach.
thermoreceptors in the skin.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood solute concentration and adjust ADH release and thirst. Baroreceptors detect pressure, not concentration.
bio12a2-wb-4
A person drinks 1.5 L of water in a short time. Which set of changes would be expected over the next hour?
ADH secretion increases; a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
ADH secretion decreases; a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
ADH secretion increases; a large volume of dilute urine is produced
ADH secretion decreases; a large volume of dilute urine is produced

Drinking lots of water dilutes the blood. Osmoreceptors detect this and ADH release falls. Collecting ducts become less permeable to water, so more water stays in the filtrate and a large volume of dilute urine results.
bio12a2-wb-5
Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH. A person who has drunk a lot of alcohol would be expected to
produce less urine and retain excess water.
produce more urine and become dehydrated.
produce urine that contains glucose.
have a decreased rate of glomerular filtration only.
With less ADH, less water is reabsorbed from the collecting ducts. More dilute urine is produced and the body loses water, which contributes to dehydration.
bio12a2-wb-6
On a hot day a worker sweats heavily and drinks very little. Explain how the body reduces further water loss. (3 marks)

Water loss in sweat raises the solute concentration of the blood, which is detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus; the hypothalamus causes more ADH to be released from the posterior pituitary (and thirst is stimulated); ADH increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.
bio12a2-wb-7

The spinifex hopping mouse (Notomys alexis) lives in the arid interior of Australia and produces some of the most concentrated urine of any mammal. Suggest one feature of its kidneys and explain how it helps the mouse conserve water. (2 marks)

Very long loops of Henle (relative to kidney size); these build a very high solute concentration in the medulla, so a large amount of water moves by osmosis out of the collecting ducts and is reabsorbed, leaving a very small volume of highly concentrated urine. (Also accept high ADH levels or highly permeable collecting ducts with matching explanation.)
bio12a2-wb-8
Explain why urine is usually darker in colour on a hot day when a person has not drunk much water. (2 marks)

Water lost by sweating raises blood solute concentration, so more ADH is released and more water is reabsorbed from the collecting ducts; the same amount of urea and pigment is dissolved in a smaller volume of water, so the urine is more concentrated and darker.
bio12a2-wb-9
Ultrafiltration of the blood takes place in the
collecting duct.
loop of Henle.
glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
distal convoluted tubule.

Blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries forces water and small solutes out into Bowman's capsule. The loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct mainly reabsorb and secrete substances rather than filter the blood.
bio12a2-wb-10
Which sequence correctly shows the path of filtrate through the nephron?
Bowman's capsule → loop of Henle → proximal convoluted tubule → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct
Bowman's capsule → proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct
Bowman's capsule → distal convoluted tubule → proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → collecting duct
Bowman's capsule → proximal convoluted tubule → distal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → collecting duct

Filtrate passes from Bowman's capsule to the proximal tubule, then down and up the loop of Henle, through the distal tubule and finally into the collecting duct. The loop of Henle always lies between the proximal and distal tubules.
bio12a2-wb-11
The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water but actively pumps sodium and chloride ions out of the filtrate. What is the main result?
Water is reabsorbed into the blood, concentrating the filtrate as it rises.
Glucose is pumped into the filtrate, making the medulla more dilute.
Urea is secreted into the collecting duct in large amounts.
The filtrate becomes more dilute, and the surrounding medulla becomes more concentrated.

Removing ions while keeping water in the tubule makes the filtrate more dilute as it rises, and the ions build up in the surrounding medulla. This gradient later allows water to be drawn out of the collecting duct by osmosis.
bio12a2-wb-12
Which solution has the highest osmolarity?
0.4 mol L⁻¹ sodium chloride solution
0.6 mol L⁻¹ glucose solution
0.5 mol L⁻¹ urea solution
0.3 mol L⁻¹ glucose solution

Sodium chloride dissociates into two ions, so 0.4 mol L⁻¹ gives about 0.8 osmol L⁻¹, more than 0.6 osmol L⁻¹ from glucose or 0.5 osmol L⁻¹ from urea. Ignoring dissociation makes the sodium chloride solution look like only 0.4 osmol L⁻¹, which is lower than the glucose solution.
bio12a2-wb-13
After eating a very salty meal, which sequence describes the negative feedback loop that brings blood osmolarity back to normal?
Blood osmolarity falls, ADH release rises, and more water is reabsorbed, so osmolarity falls further.
Blood osmolarity rises, ADH release rises, more water is reabsorbed, and osmolarity falls back towards normal.
Blood osmolarity rises, ADH release falls, less water is reabsorbed, and osmolarity rises further.
Blood osmolarity rises, ADH release rises, less water is reabsorbed, and osmolarity rises further.

Negative feedback reverses the change: higher osmolarity raises ADH, which increases water reabsorption and dilutes the blood back towards its set point. The other options either push the change further (positive feedback) or have ADH moving in the wrong direction.
bio12a2-wb-14
A freshwater fish has blood that is more concentrated than the surrounding water. Which statement describes how it maintains water balance?
It drinks large volumes of water and excretes a small volume of concentrated urine.
It drinks seawater and excretes the excess salt in concentrated urine.
It takes in very little water by mouth and excretes a large volume of dilute urine.
It loses water by osmosis through its gills and must drink to replace it.

Water enters the fish by osmosis across its gills and body surface, so it drinks very little and produces large volumes of dilute urine while actively taking up salts. A marine fish has the opposite problem, losing water by osmosis and drinking seawater.
bio12a2-wb-15
A person with diabetes insipidus produces very large volumes of dilute urine. What is the most likely cause?
Too little ADH is produced, or the collecting ducts do not respond to ADH.
Too much ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.
Too little insulin is produced by the pancreas.
The glomerulus filters the blood at a much lower pressure.

Without ADH, or without a response to it, the collecting ducts stay impermeable to water, so little water is reabsorbed. Excess ADH would produce a small volume of concentrated urine, and insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus rather than insipidus.
bio12a2-wb-16
The kidneys filter about 180 L of plasma each day but excrete about 1.5 L of urine. Approximately what percentage of the filtrate is excreted as urine?
1.5 ÷ 180 × 100 ≈ 0.83%, so more than 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed. Misplacing a decimal point gives 8.3%, which would wrongly suggest ten times as much filtrate is excreted.
bio12a2-wb-17
The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many microvilli. What is the main advantage of this feature?
They allow the tubule to filter blood at a higher pressure.
They produce ADH, which increases water reabsorption.
They increase the surface area for reabsorption of substances from the filtrate.
They make the tubule wall impermeable to water and solutes.

The microvilli form a brush border that greatly increases surface area, so more glucose, ions and water can be reabsorbed into the blood. Filtration occurs in the glomerulus, and ADH is made in the hypothalamus rather than the tubule.
bio12a2-wb-18
Which substance is normally present in blood plasma but absent from normal urine?
plasma proteins
urea
creatinine
excess sodium ions
Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the glomerular filter, so they stay in the blood. Urea, creatinine and excess sodium ions are wastes or regulated substances that are excreted in urine.
bio12a2-wb-19
When ADH levels are high, the maximum osmolarity of human urine is roughly how many times that of blood plasma?
about the same
about 40 times
about 100 times
about 4 times

Human urine can reach about 1200 mOsm L⁻¹, while plasma is about 300 mOsm L⁻¹, so urine is roughly four times more concentrated. Answers of 40 or 100 times assume the kidney can concentrate urine far beyond this.
bio12a2-wb-20
Sweat is hypotonic compared with blood plasma. Why does heavy sweating tend to increase blood osmolarity?
Sweat contains more solute than plasma, so the blood loses solute.
Sweat loses more water than solute, leaving the blood more concentrated.
Sweat contains large amounts of urea, which raises blood osmolarity.
Sweating increases the glomerular filtration rate, so less water is reabsorbed.

Sweat has a lower solute concentration than plasma, so the body loses proportionally more water than solute and the blood becomes more concentrated. The first option ignores the word hypotonic, and urea is not a major component of sweat.
bio12a2-wb-21
Name the region of the nephron where about 65% of the filtered water and solutes are reabsorbed. (1 mark)
Proximal convoluted tubule [1].
bio12a2-wb-22
Describe the role of blood pressure in ultrafiltration in the glomerulus. (2 marks)

Blood pressure forces water and small solutes (such as glucose, urea and ions) out of the glomerular capillaries and into Bowman's capsule [1]; blood cells and large molecules are too big to pass through the filtration membrane, so they remain in the blood [1].
bio12a2-wb-23
Describe how the descending limb of the loop of Henle is adapted to help produce a concentrated medulla. (2 marks)
The descending limb is permeable to water [1]; water moves out of the filtrate by osmosis into the more concentrated medulla, so the filtrate becomes more concentrated as it descends [1].
bio12a2-wb-24
Explain how a dialysis machine removes urea from a patient's blood, referring to the membrane and the concentration gradient. (3 marks)

Blood flows past a semi-permeable (dialysis) membrane [1]; urea diffuses across the membrane from the blood, where its concentration is higher, into the dialysis fluid, where it is lower [1]; small waste molecules pass through the membrane while blood cells and large proteins are retained in the blood [1].
bio12a2-wb-25
Name two routes, other than urine, by which water leaves the body. (2 marks)
Sweat from the skin [1]; water vapour in exhaled air [1] (water lost in faeces is also accepted).
bio12a2-wb-26
Define osmolarity. (1 mark)
The total concentration of dissolved solute particles in a solution, measured in osmol L⁻¹ [1].
bio12a2-wb-27
Describe the role of thirst in restoring water balance after a person loses a large volume of water. (2 marks)
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise in blood osmolarity and stimulate the sensation of thirst [1]; the person drinks water, which dilutes the blood back towards normal [1].
vce-bio12-wb-c1
After a long run on a hot day without drinking, a person's body will most likely:
Release less ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb more water and urine becomes dilute
Stop the kidneys filtering blood, so no urine is produced until the person drinks
Release more ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb more water and urine becomes concentrated
Release more insulin, which makes the kidneys retain more water and salt
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect concentrated blood; the posterior pituitary releases ADH, increasing water reabsorption.
vce-bio12-malfunctions-of-homeostasis: bio12a2-mal-1
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is caused by
the immune system destroying the beta cells of the pancreas, so little or no insulin is produced.
body cells becoming less responsive to insulin.
the posterior pituitary failing to release ADH.
the liver producing too much glucagon.
Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which beta cells are destroyed, so insulin must be supplied by injection or pump. Reduced cell response to insulin describes type 2.
bio12a2-mal-2
Which statement best describes type 2 diabetes mellitus in its early stages?
The pancreas cannot produce any insulin.
It is always caused by a single inherited allele.
Insulin is produced, but target cells respond poorly to it (insulin resistance).
Blood glucose is abnormally low.
In type 2 diabetes, insulin is often still produced, sometimes in large amounts, but cells such as muscle and fat cells respond poorly. It is linked to genetic and lifestyle factors, not one allele.
bio12a2-mal-3

Two adults fasted overnight and then had their blood glucose and blood insulin measured. Person P: glucose 9.5 mmol L⁻¹, insulin higher than normal. Person Q: glucose 12 mmol L⁻¹, insulin almost undetectable. The most likely conclusion is that
P has type 1 diabetes and Q has type 2 diabetes.
both P and Q have type 1 diabetes.
P is healthy and Q has diabetes insipidus.
P has type 2 diabetes and Q has type 1 diabetes.

P has high glucose despite high insulin, which points to insulin resistance (type 2). Q produces almost no insulin, which fits beta cell destruction (type 1). A healthy fasting level is about 4–6 mmol L⁻¹.
bio12a2-mal-4
In Graves' disease, the thyroid gland secretes too much thyroxine. Which symptom would be expected?
Weight gain and feeling cold all the time
Weight loss, a fast heart rate and feeling hot
Very low blood glucose after meals
Producing large volumes of dilute urine because ADH is absent

Thyroxine raises metabolic rate. Too much speeds up cellular respiration and heat production, causing weight loss, heat intolerance and a fast heart rate. Weight gain and feeling cold fit hypothyroidism.
bio12a2-mal-5
Glucose is often found in the urine of a person with untreated diabetes mellitus because
the glomerulus becomes permeable to glucose only in diabetes.
insulin is normally needed for glucose to be filtered.
the amount of glucose in the filtrate is greater than the nephron's carriers can reabsorb.
glucose is actively secreted into the collecting duct.
Glucose is always filtered. Normally the proximal tubule reabsorbs all of it, but when blood glucose is very high the transport proteins become saturated and the excess stays in the urine.
bio12a2-mal-6
Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus in terms of their cause and how each is commonly managed. (3 marks)

Type 1 is an autoimmune disease in which beta cells are destroyed, so little or no insulin is made; type 2 involves insulin resistance (cells respond poorly to insulin), sometimes with reduced insulin output later, and is linked to genetics, obesity and inactivity; type 1 is managed with insulin injections or a pump, while type 2 is often first managed with diet, exercise and weight loss, then oral medication and sometimes insulin.
bio12a2-mal-7
In central diabetes insipidus, the posterior pituitary releases little or no ADH. Predict the volume and concentration of urine produced and explain one other symptom the person may show. (3 marks)

Without ADH, the distal tubules and collecting ducts stay poorly permeable to water, so little water is reabsorbed; the person produces a very large volume of dilute urine; as a result they lose water and become dehydrated, and blood solute concentration rises, which is detected by osmoreceptors, so they feel extreme thirst and drink large amounts.
bio12a2-mal-8
A diet lacking iodine means the thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine. Such people often develop a goitre (an enlarged thyroid). Use negative feedback to explain why. (3 marks)

Thyroxine normally inhibits the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary (negative feedback); with low thyroxine, this inhibition is removed, so TSH levels stay high; continuous TSH stimulation makes thyroid cells grow and divide, so the gland enlarges, yet it still cannot make thyroxine without iodine.
bio12a2-mal-9
A person with type 1 diabetes injects too much insulin. Which homeostatic response would help restore blood glucose?
Beta cells release more insulin, which lowers blood glucose further.
Alpha cells release glucagon, which stimulates the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose.
The posterior pituitary releases more ADH so that glucose is excreted in the urine.
The thyroid releases less thyroxine, which raises blood glucose immediately.

Falling blood glucose is detected by the alpha cells of the pancreas, which secrete glucagon to trigger glycogen breakdown in the liver. Releasing more insulin would push glucose even lower, and ADH controls water balance rather than blood glucose.
bio12a2-mal-10
Regular aerobic exercise helps people with type 2 diabetes lower their blood glucose. Which explanation is most accurate?
Exercise stimulates the pancreas to secrete more glucagon, which lowers blood glucose.
Exercise causes the liver to convert glucose into fat, permanently removing insulin resistance.
Working muscles take up glucose from the blood, even when the response to insulin is weak.
Exercise increases the release of ADH, which removes glucose from the blood in the urine.

Contracting muscles take up glucose through a pathway that does not depend on a strong insulin response, so blood glucose falls. Glucagon raises blood glucose, and ADH controls water balance rather than glucose.
bio12a2-mal-11
Why is iodine essential for the production of thyroxine?
Iodine is a component of the thyroxine molecule, so thyroxine cannot be made without it.
Iodine activates the liver enzyme that breaks down glycogen.
Iodine is needed to make insulin, which thyroid cells use to divide.
Iodine is required for ADH to bind to receptors in the collecting ducts.
Thyroxine contains four iodine atoms, so a dietary lack of iodine stops thyroxine production. The other options link iodine to hormones or processes that it does not control.
bio12a2-mal-12
A person passes large volumes of dilute urine. Which test result would point to diabetes insipidus rather than diabetes mellitus?
Urine contains glucose, and blood glucose is high.
Urine is concentrated and contains glucose.
Blood glucose is high, and urine contains ketones.
Urine contains no glucose, and blood glucose is normal.

Diabetes insipidus results from too little ADH and does not involve glucose, so urine contains no glucose and blood glucose is normal. Diabetes mellitus causes glucose to spill into the urine, where it draws water with it.
bio12a2-mal-13
Why does untreated type 1 diabetes sometimes lead to ketoacidosis?
Excess insulin causes the liver to release large amounts of ketones into the blood.
Without insulin, cells cannot use glucose effectively, so fats are broken down for energy and acidic ketones build up.
The kidneys reabsorb too much glucose, which makes the blood acidic.
ADH secretion increases, concentrating ketones in the blood.

Without insulin, body cells cannot take in glucose, so the body breaks down fat for energy, producing acidic ketones that lower blood pH. The other options describe excess insulin, kidney reabsorption or water balance, none of which causes this.
bio12a2-mal-14
During a fever caused by an infection, what happens in the hypothalamus?
It stops detecting body temperature, so sweating stops.
It increases heat loss by dilating skin arterioles to cool the body.
Its temperature set point is raised, so the body conserves and produces heat until it reaches the new set point.
It secretes TSH, which increases metabolic rate in all cells until the fever breaks.

Pyrogens released during infection reset the hypothalamic set point to a higher temperature. The body then shivers and constricts skin blood vessels to conserve and produce heat, and cooling responses only begin once the temperature is above the new set point.
bio12a2-mal-15
During haemodialysis, how does urea move across the dialysis membrane?
From the blood into the dialysis fluid, by diffusion down a concentration gradient.
From the dialysis fluid into the blood, because the fluid contains more urea.
Only by active transport using ATP, so that it is removed from the blood faster.
Not at all, because the membrane is impermeable to all waste products.

The dialysis fluid has little or no urea, so urea diffuses out of the blood through the semi-permeable membrane. Movement in the other direction would need more urea in the fluid than in the blood, and the membrane allows small waste molecules through.
bio12a2-mal-16
A person's blood glucose falls from 16.0 mmol L⁻¹ to 8.0 mmol L⁻¹ after treatment. What is the percentage decrease?

(16.0 − 8.0) ÷ 16.0 × 100 = 50%. Dividing by the new value (8.0) gives 100%, dividing the starting value by the new value gives 200%, and 8% comes from reading the difference of 8 mmol L⁻¹ as a percentage.
bio12a2-mal-17
Why does diabetes mellitus with very high blood glucose cause increased urine volume (polyuria)?
Glucose left in the filtrate lowers its water potential, so less water is reabsorbed by osmosis.
Excess insulin makes the nephrons produce more filtrate.
High blood glucose stimulates ADH secretion, which increases water loss.
Glucose is actively secreted into the collecting duct, which increases urine volume.

Unabsorbed glucose makes the filtrate solute-rich, so water stays in the tubule and is excreted (osmotic diuresis). ADH would reduce urine volume rather than increase it, and insulin does not control filtrate production.
bio12a2-mal-18
Which substance would be expected to build up in the blood of a person with kidney failure?
Oxygen
Glycogen
Urea
Pepsin
The kidneys normally excrete urea, so it accumulates when they fail. The other substances are not waste products the kidneys remove in this way, and pepsin is a digestive enzyme made in the stomach.
bio12a2-mal-19
Explain how an insulin pump helps a person with type 1 diabetes manage blood glucose more closely than daily injections. (3 marks)

The pump delivers a small, continuous (basal) dose of insulin over 24 hours, similar to the steady insulin release of a healthy pancreas between meals [1]; it can also deliver extra bolus doses at mealtimes, so insulin is available as glucose enters the blood after eating [1]; the dose can be adjusted for activity and food, so blood glucose stays closer to the normal range and hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia is less likely [1].
bio12a2-mal-20
Describe the normal response to a rise in blood glucose after a high-carbohydrate meal, and explain why this response does not occur in type 1 diabetes. (3 marks)

Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans detect the rise and secrete insulin into the blood [1]; insulin causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen, so blood glucose falls back towards normal [1]; in type 1 diabetes the beta cells have been destroyed by the immune system, so no insulin is released and glucose stays high in the blood [1].
bio12a2-mal-21
Explain why a person with kidney failure needs regular dialysis, referring to the effects on blood wastes and on water and ion balance. (4 marks)

The failed kidneys cannot excrete urea and other nitrogenous wastes, so these build up in the blood [1]; excess water and ions such as potassium also accumulate, which can cause swelling, high blood pressure and heart problems [1]; in haemodialysis, blood flows past a semi-permeable membrane and wastes diffuse into the dialysis fluid down their concentration gradient [1]; the dialysis fluid has suitable ion concentrations so useful ions are not lost, and excess water can be removed by applying pressure to the blood side [1].
bio12a2-mal-22
Central diabetes insipidus can be treated with desmopressin, a synthetic form of ADH. Explain how this treatment reduces the volume of urine produced. (2 marks)

Desmopressin binds to receptors on the cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing their permeability to water [1]; more water is reabsorbed by osmosis, so less urine is produced and it is more concentrated [1].
bio12a2-mal-23

A person working outdoors in extreme heat has stopped sweating and has a body temperature of 41 °C. Explain why this is dangerous, referring to the effect of the high temperature and to the failed homeostatic responses. (4 marks)
