Sweating and the evaporation of sweat are the main cooling responses, so with sweating stopped much less heat is lost from the body [1]; heat is still produced by metabolism and gained from the environment, so body temperature keeps rising [1]; at this temperature enzymes and proteins begin to denature, disrupting metabolic reactions and damaging cells, especially in the brain [1]; the negative feedback responses have failed to return the body to its set point, so the condition becomes life-threatening without rapid cooling [1].
bio12a2-mal-24

During an infection the hypothalamic set point rises to 39 °C. A person whose body temperature is 37 °C now has cold skin and shivers. After recovery the set point returns to 37 °C, and their body temperature is 38.5 °C, so they begin sweating. Explain both responses using negative feedback. (3 marks)

At 37 °C with a set point of 39 °C, the body detects its temperature as too low, so it shivers and constricts skin blood vessels to produce and conserve heat [1]; with the set point back at 37 °C and body temperature at 38.5 °C, the temperature is detected as too high, so the body sweats and dilates skin arterioles to lose heat [1]; in both cases the responses oppose the change and stop once body temperature returns to the set point [1].
bio12a2-mal-25
Explain how insulin resistance can lead to beta cell exhaustion in type 2 diabetes, and why blood glucose becomes harder to control over time. (3 marks)

Target cells respond poorly to insulin, so blood glucose stays high and the beta cells are stimulated to secrete more insulin [1]; over years the beta cells are overworked and can be damaged, so their insulin output falls [1]; with less insulin and continuing resistance, glucose uptake and storage decline, so blood glucose rises further and is harder to control [1].
bio12a2-mal-26
Explain why a person with hypoglycaemia (very low blood glucose) may feel shaky and confused, referring to the energy needs of the brain. (3 marks)

The brain relies almost entirely on glucose as its energy source for cellular respiration [1]; low blood glucose reduces the glucose supplied to brain cells, so less ATP is produced and neurons cannot function normally, causing confusion [1]; the body responds by releasing adrenaline and glucagon, and the adrenaline causes shakiness [1].
vce-bio12-mh-c1
In Graves' disease, antibodies bind to and activate TSH receptors on the thyroid. Why does negative feedback fail to lower the high thyroxine levels?
The antibodies stimulate the thyroid regardless of TSH, so reducing TSH has no effect
The pituitary stops making TSH completely, raising thyroxine
Thyroxine has no effect on the hypothalamus
The thyroid stops responding to everything
High thyroxine does reduce TSH, but the antibodies keep stimulating the gland, so the feedback loop cannot correct the level.
vce-bio12-genomes-genes-and-alleles: bio12a2-gen-1
An organism's genome is best defined as
the set of alleles it has for one trait.
the complete set of genetic material (DNA) present in its cells.
all the proteins expressed by one cell.
the genes found on its sex chromosomes.
The genome is all the DNA of an organism, including genes and non-coding regions (and mitochondrial DNA in eukaryotes). The full set of proteins is the proteome.
bio12a2-gen-2
An allele is
a section of DNA that never codes for a protein.
the position of a gene on a chromosome.
one of the alternative forms of a gene, found at the same locus.
a pair of identical chromosomes.
Different alleles of a gene have slightly different base sequences but sit at the same locus on homologous chromosomes. The position itself is the locus.
bio12a2-gen-3
Which statement about the human nuclear genome is correct?
It contains about 3 billion base pairs, and less than 2% codes for proteins.
It contains about 3 million base pairs, all of which code for proteins.
It contains about 200 000 protein-coding genes.
Every human has an identical genome sequence.

The human haploid nuclear genome has about 3 billion base pairs and around 20 000 protein-coding genes. These make up only a small fraction (about 1–2%) of the DNA. Apart from identical twins, individuals differ in sequence.
bio12a2-gen-4
In vinegar flies, the gene for wing shape has an allele for normal wings and an allele for vestigial wings. A fly has one copy of each allele. This fly is
homozygous, and must have vestigial wings.
haploid for the wing shape gene.
homozygous dominant for wing shape.
heterozygous for the wing shape gene.
Having two different alleles at a locus means the fly is heterozygous. Its phenotype depends on which allele is dominant (here normal wings is dominant), but it is heterozygous either way.
bio12a2-gen-5
Two people have different alleles of the gene that codes for an enzyme. The difference between these alleles is most likely
the number of chromosomes in each cell.
a difference in the sequence of nucleotide bases in the gene.
the type of sugar in the DNA backbone.
the locus of the gene on the chromosome.
Alleles differ in their base sequences. These differences may change the amino acid sequence of the protein produced. Alleles of the same gene share the same locus.
bio12a2-gen-6
Distinguish between the terms genome, gene and allele. (3 marks)

Genome: the complete set of DNA (genetic material) of an organism; gene: a section of DNA at a particular locus that carries the code for a functional product such as a protein; allele: one of the different forms (variants) of a gene, with a slightly different base sequence, found at the same locus.
bio12a2-gen-7
Describe two differences between the organisation of the genome in a prokaryote, such as Escherichia coli, and in a eukaryote, such as a human. (2 marks)

Prokaryotes usually have a single circular chromosome found free in the cytosol (nucleoid region), while eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus; prokaryotes often also carry small circular plasmids, whereas eukaryotes have DNA in mitochondria (and chloroplasts) and much more non-coding DNA wound around histone proteins.
bio12a2-gen-8
Explain how two different alleles of the same gene can result in different phenotypes. (2 marks)

The alleles have different base sequences, so they may code for a different amino acid sequence; this changes the shape and function of the protein (or stops it being made or working), which changes the observable characteristic.
bio12a2-gen-9
A typical human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human egg cell contain?
Gametes are haploid, carrying one chromosome from each homologous pair, so 46 ÷ 2 = 23. The 92 comes from doubling the chromosome number, and 46 is the body cell number, not the gamete number.
bio12a2-gen-10
Which statement describes a pair of homologous chromosomes?
A pair of chromosomes with the same genes at the same loci, one inherited from each parent.
Two identical copies of one chromosome, produced by DNA replication.
The X and Y chromosomes of a male, which are homologous along their full length.
Two chromosomes that carry only non-coding DNA.

Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes in the same order, though they may carry different alleles. Identical copies made by replication are sister chromatids, and the X and Y are only partly homologous.
bio12a2-gen-11
Which statement correctly distinguishes genotype from phenotype?
Genotype is the observable characteristic; phenotype is the set of alleles carried.
Genotype and phenotype are two names for the same thing.
Genotype is the set of alleles an organism carries; phenotype is the observable characteristic that results.
Phenotype is the DNA sequence; genotype is the protein it makes.

Genotype is the allele combination an organism carries, while phenotype is the observable trait that results, which can also be affected by the environment. The option that reverses the two terms is the most common mistake.
bio12a2-gen-12
In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant to the allele for white flowers (p). Which genotype produces white flowers?
PP
Pp
pp
PP or Pp
White flowers need two copies of the recessive allele, pp. Pp has one dominant P allele, so the plant is purple, and PP is also purple.
bio12a2-gen-13
What is the main source of new alleles in a population?
Meiosis, which halves the chromosome number.
Mutation, which changes the base sequence of a gene.
The addition of a new locus to a chromosome.
The removal of all non-coding DNA from a cell.
Mutation changes base sequences, creating new variants of a gene at the same locus. Meiosis reshuffles existing alleles into new combinations but does not create new ones.
bio12a2-gen-14
A gene exists as three alleles in a population. Which statement is correct?
Each diploid individual can carry at most two of these alleles, but the population as a whole can carry all three.
Each individual must carry all three alleles.
Each individual has three copies of the gene in every body cell.
Only one of the three alleles can exist in the population at a time.

A diploid individual has two homologous chromosomes, so it can carry at most two alleles at that locus, while the population gene pool can contain more. Carrying all three would need three homologous chromosomes.
bio12a2-gen-15
A single base change in the coding sequence of a gene creates a new allele. Which outcome is possible?
The new allele always produces a non-functional protein.
The gene moves to a different locus on the chromosome.
The chromosome number of the cell increases by one.
The protein is unchanged, because more than one codon can code for the same amino acid.

The genetic code is degenerate, so some base changes leave the amino acid unchanged. A single base change does not move a gene or change the chromosome number, and not every change to a protein makes it non-functional.
bio12a2-gen-16
How many pairs of autosomes (non-sex chromosomes) does a typical human body cell contain?
A human cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes, one of which is the sex chromosome pair, leaving 22 pairs of autosomes. The 44 is the number of autosome chromosomes, not pairs.
bio12a2-gen-17
Two genetically identical plants grow to different heights because one receives less water. This shows that
the phenotype depends only on the genotype.
the genotype changed during growth.
the alleles are not located on chromosomes.
the phenotype can be influenced by the environment as well as the genotype.
Phenotype results from genotype and environment together, so identical genotypes can produce different phenotypes under different conditions. The genotype itself did not change.
bio12a2-gen-18
The genome of Escherichia coli is about 4.6 × 10⁶ base pairs, and the human genome is about 3 × 10⁹ base pairs. Approximately how many times larger is the human genome?
about 6.5 times
about 650 times
about 65 times
about 6 500 times
3 × 10⁹ ÷ 4.6 × 10⁶ ≈ 6.5 × 10², which is about 650 times. The 65 and 6 500 distractors come from errors in powers of ten.
bio12a2-gen-19
Which list correctly orders these from smallest to largest?
nucleotide, gene, chromosome, genome
gene, nucleotide, chromosome, genome
nucleotide, chromosome, gene, genome
genome, chromosome, gene, nucleotide
A nucleotide is a single unit, a gene is many nucleotides, a chromosome carries many genes, and the genome is the full set of chromosomes. Placing the genome before the chromosome reverses the order.
bio12a2-gen-20
Which statement about a eukaryotic chromosome is correct?
It is a single long molecule of DNA associated with histone proteins.
It is made of RNA and protein, with no DNA.
It always carries exactly one gene.
It is always found in pairs, even in haploid gametes.
Each eukaryotic chromosome is one linear DNA molecule wound around histones and carries many genes. Chromosomes in a haploid gamete are unpaired, so the last option is a tempting but wrong idea.
bio12a2-gen-21
Name the molecule that carries the genetic information in a human cell. (1 mark)
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) [1]
bio12a2-gen-22
Define the term single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP). (2 marks)
A variation in the DNA sequence in which a single base (nucleotide) differs at a specific position [1], and the variant is common enough to be found in a substantial proportion of a population [1].
bio12a2-gen-23
The haploid human genome contains about 3 × 10⁹ base pairs. Calculate the number of base pairs in the diploid genome of one human body cell, and express your answer in scientific notation. (2 marks)
Diploid genome = 2 × haploid genome [1]; 2 × 3 × 10⁹ = 6 × 10⁹ base pairs [1].
bio12a2-gen-24
Outline one way that knowing the complete DNA sequence of a species can help scientists. (2 marks)
Comparing sequences can identify genes or alleles linked to a trait or disease [1]; this can support diagnostic tests, treatments or the study of evolutionary relationships [1].
bio12a2-gen-25
Explain why a dominant allele is not necessarily more common in a population than a recessive allele. (2 marks)

Dominance describes how an allele's effect shows in a heterozygote, not how often the allele occurs [1]; allele frequency depends on factors such as mutation, selection and chance in a population [1].
bio12a2-gen-26

In a sample of 10 pea plants, 4 are homozygous for allele A (AA), 3 are heterozygous (Aa) and 3 are homozygous for allele a (aa). Calculate the frequency of allele A in this sample. Show your working. (3 marks)
Copies of allele A = 4 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 11 [1]; total alleles = 10 × 2 = 20 [1]; frequency of A = 11 ÷ 20 = 0.55 (55%) [1].
bio12a2-gen-27
Define the term homozygous. (1 mark)
Having two identical alleles of a gene at a locus (for example AA or aa) [1].
bio12a2-gen-28
Explain why a skin cell and a liver cell from the same person have the same genome, even though they have different structures and functions. (2 marks)

Both cells developed by mitosis from the same fertilised egg, so each carries an identical copy of the DNA [1]; the cells express different sets of genes, producing different proteins that give each cell its structure and function [1].
bio12a2-gen-29
Define the term haploid. (1 mark)
Having a single set of chromosomes, so one allele of each gene in a cell [1].
vce-bio12-gg-c1
Two alleles of the same gene:
Occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes but differ in nucleotide sequence
Occupy different loci on the same chromosome and have identical nucleotide sequences
Always produce identical proteins, because they are copies of the same gene
Are two complete copies of the genome, one inherited from each parent
Alleles are alternative versions of a gene, at the same position on a homologous pair.
vce-bio12-chromosomes-and-karyotypes: bio12a2-chr-1
A typical human somatic cell contains
23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes and one sex chromosome.
46 chromosomes: 23 pairs of autosomes.
46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.
92 chromosomes after DNA replication.
Human somatic cells are diploid (2n = 46), with 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. After replication there are still 46 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids.
bio12a2-chr-2
When a karyotype is prepared, chromosomes are arranged into homologous pairs according to their
size, centromere position and banding pattern.
number of alleles and dominance.
colour after staining with iodine.
rate of transcription.
Karyotypes pair and order chromosomes by length, centromere position and the pattern of light and dark bands from staining (e.g. G-banding). Dominance and alleles cannot be seen in a karyotype.
bio12a2-chr-3
A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21 and one X and one Y chromosome. This person is
a female with Turner syndrome.
a male with Down syndrome.
a female with Down syndrome.
a male with Klinefelter syndrome.
Three copies of chromosome 21 is trisomy 21 (Down syndrome). The XY sex chromosomes indicate a male. Klinefelter syndrome is XXY, and Turner syndrome is a single X (45,X).
bio12a2-chr-4
Which statement about a pair of homologous chromosomes is correct?
They are identical copies made during DNA replication.
They carry different genes at different loci.
They are only present in gametes.
They carry the same genes at the same loci, but may have different alleles, with one inherited from each parent.

Homologous chromosomes have the same genes in the same order, but one comes from the mother and one from the father, so alleles may differ. Identical copies joined at a centromere are sister chromatids.
bio12a2-chr-5
A karyotype would NOT be useful for detecting
trisomy 18.
a missing sex chromosome.
a single base substitution in the gene linked to cystic fibrosis.
a large section of chromosome 5 that has been deleted.
Karyotypes show chromosome number and large structural changes. A change of one nucleotide in a gene is far too small to see and needs DNA analysis instead.
bio12a2-chr-6
Explain why cells used to prepare a karyotype are usually stopped at metaphase of mitosis. (2 marks)

At metaphase the chromosomes are fully condensed (supercoiled), so they are at their shortest and thickest and easiest to see and count; each chromosome is made of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, so their size, shape, centromere position and banding pattern can be compared to pair them.
bio12a2-chr-7

A somatic cell of a domestic dog contains 78 chromosomes. State the diploid number, the haploid number, and the number of autosomes in a dog sperm cell. Explain your answer for the sperm cell. (3 marks)

Diploid number 2n = 78; haploid number n = 39; a sperm cell has 38 autosomes, because a gamete contains one chromosome from each of the 39 pairs, and one of these is a sex chromosome (X or Y), leaving 38 autosomes.
bio12a2-chr-8
A karyotype of a female shows 45 chromosomes with only one X chromosome (Turner syndrome, 45,X). Explain how this could arise during gamete formation in one of her parents. (3 marks)

Nondisjunction occurred during meiosis in one parent; the sex chromosomes (homologues in meiosis I, or sister chromatids in meiosis II) failed to separate, producing a gamete with no sex chromosome; this gamete was fertilised by a normal gamete carrying one X, giving a zygote with 45 chromosomes and a single X.
bio12a2-chr-9
During anaphase of mitosis, the chromosomes moving towards opposite poles of the cell are
sister chromatids, each now an individual chromosome.
homologous chromosomes, one from each parent.
chromosomes still paired as bivalents.
replicated chromosomes, each with four chromatids.

In anaphase the centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles, each becoming an individual chromosome. Homologous chromosomes separate only in meiosis I, and bivalents do not form in mitosis.
bio12a2-chr-10
The centromere of a chromosome is best described as
the tip of the chromosome, which protects the DNA from degradation.
the region where two sister chromatids are joined and where spindle fibres attach.
a gene that codes for a protein in the spindle apparatus.
the site where homologous chromosomes exchange segments in prophase I.

The centromere is the constricted region that holds sister chromatids together and is the attachment point for spindle fibres. The tip is a telomere, and crossing over happens along the arms between non-sister chromatids, not at the centromere.
bio12a2-chr-11
A chromosome is best described as
a single molecule of RNA wound around ribosomes.
two DNA molecules joined at the telomere, with no protein present.
a long DNA molecule wound around histone proteins and condensed for division.
a protein chain that carries the genes of an organism.

Chromosomes are long DNA molecules packaged around histone proteins, and they condense into visible structures for division. Chromosomes are not made of RNA, and genes sit on DNA rather than on a protein chain.
bio12a2-chr-12
A segment of a chromosome breaks off and is lost, and it does not reattach anywhere. This structural change is called
a deletion.
a duplication.
an inversion.
a translocation.

A deletion loses the segment and the genes on it, so that chromosome carries less genetic material. A duplication adds an extra copy, an inversion reverses the segment in place, and a translocation moves it to a different chromosome.
bio12a2-chr-13
A segment of a chromosome is cut out, turned end-to-end and rejoined at the same site. This structural change is called
a deletion.
an inversion.
a translocation.
a duplication.

In an inversion the segment stays on the same chromosome but is reversed, so the same genes are present in reverse order. A deletion removes material, a duplication adds a copy, and a translocation moves a segment to another chromosome.
bio12a2-chr-14
A fruit fly has a diploid number of 8. How many pairs of homologous chromosomes does each somatic cell contain?
A diploid number of 8 means four homologous pairs, because each pair has two chromosomes. 8 counts individual chromosomes rather than pairs, 2 is too few, and 16 is double the diploid number.
bio12a2-chr-15
In humans, the gene that normally triggers development of testes (SRY) is located on the
Y chromosome.
X chromosome.
chromosome 21.
chromosome 1.

The SRY gene on the Y chromosome directs development of male gonads, so the presence of a Y chromosome normally leads to male development. The X chromosome does not carry SRY, and autosomes such as chromosomes 1 and 21 are not involved in sex determination.
bio12a2-chr-16
Crossing over between non-sister chromatids during prophase I of meiosis results in
gametes with one more chromosome than normal.
chromosomes with new combinations of alleles, while the chromosome number stays the same.
chromosomes that have lost their centromere.
a doubling of the chromosome number in each gamete.

Crossing over swaps segments between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations without changing the chromosome number. Changes in number come from nondisjunction, and a doubling of the number would be polyploidy.
bio12a2-chr-17
A karyotype is best described as
a chart showing which alleles a person inherits from each parent.
a map of the positions of genes along a single chromosome.
a photographed, ordered display of the chromosomes from one cell, arranged in homologous pairs.
a list of the base sequence of an entire genome.

A karyotype is an ordered image of the chromosomes from a single stained cell, usually at metaphase. A gene map shows loci along a chromosome and a genome sequence lists the bases, so neither is a karyotype.
bio12a2-chr-18
Which cell type is most commonly used to prepare a karyotype of a living person?
mature red blood cells.
neurons.
mature sperm cells.
white blood cells stimulated to divide in culture.

White blood cells can be stimulated to divide in culture and then arrested at metaphase. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, and neurons and mature sperm cells are not dividing, so their chromosomes cannot be arranged for a karyotype.
bio12a2-chr-19
A person has 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 18 and all other chromosomes in pairs. This condition is called
trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome.
monosomy 18, with one copy of chromosome 18 missing.
a deletion of chromosome 18.
a translocation of chromosome 18.

Three copies of an autosome is a trisomy, and trisomy 18 is Edwards syndrome. Monosomy means one copy is missing, while deletions and translocations change the segments of a chromosome without adding a whole extra chromosome.
bio12a2-chr-20
Which of the following cells is haploid?
a human zygote.
a human sperm cell.
a human neuron.
a human liver cell.
Sperm cells are gametes and contain one set of 23 chromosomes. A zygote forms when two gametes fuse, so it is diploid, and neurons and liver cells are somatic cells that are also diploid.
bio12a2-chr-21
State the karyotype notation for a female with 47 chromosomes and three X chromosomes. (1 mark)
bio12a2-chr-22
Describe the difference between a karyotype and a pedigree chart. (2 marks)
A karyotype is an image of the chromosomes from one cell, showing their number and structure [1]; a pedigree is a family diagram that traces the inheritance of a trait across generations [1].
bio12a2-chr-23
Explain why the X and Y chromosomes in a human male are not a true homologous pair along their full length. (2 marks)

The X and Y differ in size and carry different genes, so most of their length does not pair [1]; they share only a small pairing region at their tips, where they can pair and cross over in meiosis I [1].
bio12a2-chr-24
Describe two processes in meiosis I that produce genetic variation among gametes. For each process, explain how it produces different chromosome combinations. (4 marks)

Crossing over: non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I [1], so the chromatids carry new combinations of alleles [1]; independent assortment: during metaphase I each homologous pair lines up and orients at random [1], so each gamete receives a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes [1].
bio12a2-chr-25

A plant species has a haploid number of n = 12. State the diploid number and the number of chromosomes in a triploid cell of this species. Explain why a triploid cell is not described as a trisomy. (3 marks)

Diploid number 2n = 24 [1]; a triploid cell has 3n = 36 chromosomes [1]; triploidy adds a complete extra haploid set so every chromosome appears three times, whereas trisomy involves an extra copy of only one chromosome [1].
bio12a2-chr-26
Compare the karyotypes of a male with Klinefelter syndrome and a female with Turner syndrome. Include the total number of chromosomes and the sex chromosome make-up for each. (4 marks)
Klinefelter (male): 47 chromosomes [1], sex chromosomes XXY [1]; Turner (female): 45 chromosomes [1], a single X chromosome with no second sex chromosome (45,X) [1].
bio12a2-chr-27
Explain why trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is compatible with survival to birth, whereas autosomal monosomies are almost always lethal in humans. (3 marks)

Monosomy removes one copy of every gene on the chromosome, halving the expression of those genes and usually disrupting development so the embryo does not survive [1]; trisomy 21 adds one copy of one of the smallest autosomes, which has relatively few genes, so the extra dose is tolerated and the embryo can develop to birth [1]; the extra dose still causes Down syndrome features, such as intellectual disability [1].
bio12a2-chr-28
Name the stain most commonly used to produce the light and dark bands in G-banded karyotypes. (1 mark)
Giemsa stain [1]
bio12a2-chr-29
A karyotype is written as 46,XX,t(9;22). Interpret this notation by stating the sex of the person, the total number of chromosomes, and the type of chromosome change. (3 marks)
Female (XX) [1]; 46 chromosomes, so there is no change in the total number [1]; a translocation in which segments are exchanged between chromosomes 9 and 22 [1].
vce-bio12-ck-c1
A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21. The most likely cause is:
Non-disjunction during meiosis, giving a gamete with an extra chromosome 21
A point mutation on chromosome 21 that copied the whole chromosome
Crossing over between chromosomes 21 and 22 during prophase I
An error-free mitosis in the zygote that copied chromosome 21 twice
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) usually arises when chromosome 21 fails to separate in meiosis I or II.
vce-bio12-meiosis-and-variation: bio12a2-mei-1
Crossing over occurs during
prophase I, between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
metaphase II, between sister chromatids.
anaphase I, when homologous chromosomes are pulled apart.
prophase of mitosis, between non-homologous chromosomes.
In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up and non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata. This makes new combinations of alleles on each chromatid.
bio12a2-mei-2
Independent assortment during meiosis is the result of
DNA replication during interphase.
crossing over at chiasmata.
separation of sister chromatids in anaphase II.
the random orientation of homologous pairs at the cell equator during metaphase I.

Each homologous pair lines up at metaphase I independently of the others. Which parental chromosome goes to each pole is random, so many combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes are possible.
bio12a2-mei-3
A species of plant has a diploid number of 8 (2n = 8). Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different combinations of chromosomes can its gametes have due to independent assortment?
The number of combinations is 2ⁿ, where n is the haploid number. Here n = 4, so 2⁴ = 16. A common error is to use 2n instead and calculate 2⁸ = 256, or to just double 8.
bio12a2-mei-4
At the end of meiosis, one diploid cell has produced
two genetically identical diploid cells.
four genetically different haploid cells.
four genetically identical haploid cells.
two genetically different diploid cells.

Meiosis has two divisions, giving four cells, each with half the chromosome number. Crossing over and independent assortment make each one genetically different. Two identical diploid cells is the result of mitosis.
bio12a2-mei-5
If homologous chromosomes fail to separate (nondisjunction) during meiosis I, and meiosis II then proceeds normally, the gametes produced will be
all normal.
half normal and half abnormal.
all abnormal: two with an extra chromosome and two missing a chromosome.
all triploid.

If a homologous pair moves to the same pole in meiosis I, one cell gets both and the other gets neither. Both cells then divide normally, so all four gametes are abnormal (two n + 1 and two n − 1). Nondisjunction in meiosis II gives two normal and two abnormal gametes.
bio12a2-mei-6
Compare mitosis and meiosis by giving three differences. (3 marks)

Mitosis involves one division and produces two daughter cells, while meiosis involves two divisions and produces four; mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same (diploid to diploid), while meiosis halves it (diploid to haploid); mitosis produces genetically identical cells for growth and repair, while meiosis produces genetically different gametes because of crossing over and independent assortment (homologues pair up only in meiosis).
bio12a2-mei-7
Explain how crossing over increases genetic variation in gametes. (2 marks)

During prophase I, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange equivalent segments of DNA at chiasmata; this creates chromatids with new combinations of maternal and paternal alleles (recombinants), so each gamete gets a unique combination of alleles.
bio12a2-mei-8
Two brothers who are not identical twins have the same parents but differ genetically. Explain three processes that account for this. (3 marks)

Crossing over in prophase I swaps segments between non-sister chromatids, making new allele combinations on each chromosome; independent assortment of homologous pairs at metaphase I produces many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in each gamete; random fertilisation means any one of the father's genetically different sperm can fuse with any one of the mother's genetically different eggs.
bio12a2-mei-9
During prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up. What is this pair of homologous chromosomes, with four chromatids in total, called?
A bivalent, also called a tetrad.
A dyad, made of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
A single chromosome with two centromeres.
A pair of sister chromatids that separate at anaphase I.

Synapsis brings a homologous pair together, and because each chromosome has already replicated, the pair contains four chromatids. A dyad is a single replicated chromosome with only two chromatids, as seen in meiosis II.
bio12a2-mei-10
A horse has 64 chromosomes in each body cell. How many chromosomes does each egg cell contain?

An egg is a haploid gamete formed by meiosis, so it has half the diploid number: 64 ÷ 2 = 32. The answer 128 is the number of chromatids after DNA replication, and 16 wrongly halves the number twice, as if meiosis had two halving steps.
bio12a2-mei-11
Which process is the original source of new alleles in a population?
Crossing over, which exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids.
Independent assortment, which sorts homologous pairs randomly at metaphase I.
Mutation, which changes the base sequence of DNA.
Random fertilisation, which combines gametes from two parents.
Mutations change the DNA sequence and are the only source of entirely new alleles. The other three processes shuffle alleles that already exist into new combinations.
bio12a2-mei-12
During which stage of meiosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
Anaphase I.
Metaphase II.
Telophase I.
Anaphase II.

In anaphase II the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles, as in mitosis. In anaphase I it is homologous chromosomes that separate, while sister chromatids remain joined.
bio12a2-mei-13
Which statement best describes a pair of homologous chromosomes?
One chromosome from each parent, carrying genes for the same characteristics at the same loci.
Two identical copies of one chromosome, joined at the centromere after DNA replication.
The X and Y chromosomes, which determine sex in humans.
Two chromosomes of the same size, always found in the same parent.

Homologues are a matching pair, one inherited from each parent, carrying the same genes in the same order, although the alleles may differ. Two identical copies joined at the centromere are sister chromatids, and X and Y are only partly homologous.
bio12a2-mei-14
Sister chromatids are first formed when
homologous chromosomes separate at anaphase I.
DNA replicates during interphase, before meiosis begins.
crossing over occurs during prophase I.
two gametes fuse at fertilisation.

During S phase of interphase, each chromosome replicates into two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Crossing over and the separation of homologues happen later in meiosis, and fertilisation occurs after meiosis is complete.
bio12a2-mei-15
In humans, in which tissues does meiosis take place?
Skin and liver.
Bone marrow.
The lining of the intestine.
The testes and ovaries.
Meiosis produces gametes, which are sperm in the testes and eggs in the ovaries. Skin, liver, intestinal and bone marrow cells divide by mitosis to grow, repair and replace cells.
bio12a2-mei-16
An individual has genotype AaBb, with the two genes on different pairs of homologous chromosomes. What percentage of its gametes are expected to be AB?

Each pair assorts independently, so the chance of an A allele is 1/2 and of a B allele is 1/2, giving 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, or 25%. The answer 50% accounts for only one gene, and 12.5% comes from multiplying three halves as if a third gene were involved.
bio12a2-mei-17
A cell from an organism with 2n = 6 is at metaphase I of meiosis. How many bivalents are present, and how many chromatids are there in total?
6 bivalents, 24 chromatids
3 bivalents, 12 chromatids
6 bivalents, 12 chromatids
3 bivalents, 6 chromatids

Six chromosomes form three homologous pairs, so there are three bivalents, each with four chromatids, giving 12 in total. Six bivalents would count each chromosome as a pair, and 24 chromatids wrongly gives four chromatids for every chromosome.
bio12a2-mei-18
A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21 and two copies of every other chromosome. This is an example of
monosomy 21, caused by the loss of a chromosome.
polyploidy, caused by an extra complete set of chromosomes.
trisomy 21, usually caused by nondisjunction during meiosis.
a translocation between chromosomes 21 and 22.

Having three copies of one chromosome is trisomy, usually caused when homologues or sister chromatids fail to separate (nondisjunction). Polyploidy adds whole sets of chromosomes, and monosomy has only one copy of a chromosome.
bio12a2-mei-19
At the end of meiosis I, each daughter cell is
diploid, with each chromosome made of one chromatid.
haploid, with each chromosome made of one chromatid.
diploid, with each chromosome made of two chromatids.
haploid, with each chromosome still made of two chromatids.

Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, halving the chromosome number, but sister chromatids stay joined until anaphase II. Cells with one chromatid per chromosome describe the state after meiosis II, and diploid cells would result from mitosis.
bio12a2-mei-20
Why is meiosis necessary for sexual reproduction?
It doubles the chromosome number so that the zygote has more DNA.
It halves the chromosome number, so that fertilisation restores the diploid number.
It produces identical cells for growth and repair.
It makes the zygote haploid so that it can divide by mitosis.

Gametes must be haploid so that fusing two of them produces a diploid zygote with the normal chromosome number. Mitosis, not meiosis, makes identical cells for growth and repair, and the zygote is diploid, not haploid.
bio12a2-mei-21
Explain why meiosis I is described as a reduction division. (2 marks)
Homologous chromosomes are separated and move into different daughter cells [1]; each daughter cell therefore has half the chromosome number of the parent cell, so it is haploid [1].
bio12a2-mei-22
Compare crossing over and independent assortment as sources of genetic variation. (3 marks)

Crossing over occurs in prophase I and exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids, creating chromosomes with mixed alleles [1]; independent assortment occurs at metaphase I when each homologous pair is oriented at random, so each gamete receives a random mix of whole maternal and paternal chromosomes [1]; both occur in the same meiosis, so together they make each gamete genetically different from the others [1].
bio12a2-mei-23
Explain why sister chromatids are usually genetically identical, but homologous chromosomes may carry different alleles. (2 marks)

Sister chromatids are two copies of the same chromosome, made by DNA replication during S phase [1]; homologous chromosomes come from different parents, so they may carry different alleles of the same genes [1].
bio12a2-mei-24

A human germ cell has 46 chromosomes and has just completed DNA replication. State the number of chromosomes and chromatids in this cell, and the number of chromosomes in each gamete it produces. (3 marks)
46 chromosomes in the replicated cell [1]; 92 chromatids, since each chromosome has two chromatids [1]; 23 chromosomes in each gamete, because gametes are haploid [1].
bio12a2-mei-25
Describe how a mutation differs from crossing over as a source of genetic variation. (3 marks)

A mutation is a change in the base sequence of DNA, so it creates new alleles [1]; crossing over only rearranges existing alleles into new combinations on chromosomes [1]; mutations are rare and random, whereas crossing over occurs regularly during prophase I of meiosis [1].
bio12a2-mei-26
Describe the role of the centromere and spindle fibres in separating sister chromatids in anaphase II. (2 marks)

The centromere of each chromosome divides, so the two sister chromatids become separate chromosomes [1]; spindle fibres attached to the centromeres pull each chromosome to opposite poles of the cell [1].
bio12a2-mei-27
Describe the events of meiosis I that separate homologous chromosomes, from prophase I to anaphase I. (3 marks)

In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents, and crossing over may occur [1]; at metaphase I, bivalents line up at the equator with the two homologues of each pair facing opposite poles [1]; at anaphase I, homologous chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles while sister chromatids remain joined at their centromeres [1].
bio12a2-mei-28
A student claims that mitosis also produces genetic variation because crossing over and independent assortment occur in it. Identify the error and explain your answer. (2 marks)

Crossing over and independent assortment occur only in meiosis, not in mitosis [1]; in mitosis homologous chromosomes do not pair and the daughter cells are genetically identical, so no new variation is produced [1].
bio12a2-mei-29

A species has a diploid number of 12 (2n = 12). Ignoring crossing over, calculate the number of genetically different gametes possible from independent assortment, and the number of genetically different zygotes possible from random fertilisation of two gametes. (3 marks)
n = 6, so independent assortment gives 2⁶ = 64 different gametes [1]; 64 different sperm types can each combine with 64 different egg types [1]; 64 × 64 = 4096 possible zygotes [1].
vce-bio12-me-c1
Ignoring crossing over, independent assortment alone can produce how many chromosome combinations in human gametes (n = 23)?
About 4 (2²)
About 8.4 million (2²³)
Each of the 23 homologous pairs can line up two ways at metaphase I: 2²³ ≈ 8.4 × 10⁶. Crossing over adds even more variation.
vce-bio12-genotype-phenotype-and-environ: bio12a2-gpe-1
An organism's phenotype is best described as
the alleles it carries for a particular gene.
its observable characteristics, resulting from the interaction of its genotype with the environment.
the complete set of its DNA.
the characteristics it will pass on to its offspring.
Phenotype covers observable traits, including biochemical ones such as blood type. It depends on genotype and environment together. The alleles an organism carries are its genotype.
bio12a2-gpe-2

Two cuttings taken from the same hydrangea plant were planted in different gardens. One produced blue flowers in acidic soil and the other produced pink flowers in alkaline soil. The best explanation is that
the cuttings had different genotypes.
a mutation occurred in one cutting.
flower colour in hydrangeas is controlled by the environment only.
the same genotype produced different phenotypes because of differences in the environment.

The cuttings are clones with the same genotype. Soil pH affects how much aluminium the plant can take up, which changes flower pigment colour. Genes still matter, since the plant must have the genes for the pigment.
bio12a2-gpe-3

Siamese cats have dark fur on their ears, paws and tail but pale fur on the body. The enzyme that makes the dark pigment is inactive above about 33 °C. If a patch of fur on a Siamese cat's back is shaved and the skin is kept cold with an ice pack while the fur grows back, the new fur will most likely be
dark, because the enzyme is active at the lower temperature.
pale, because the cat's genotype for the body is different.
pale, because shaving removes the pigment genes.
white, because cold damages the hair follicles.

The cat has the same genotype in all skin cells. The temperature-sensitive enzyme works only in cooler regions, so cooling the skin lets dark pigment form. This shows the environment influencing phenotype.
bio12a2-gpe-4
Which human characteristic is most likely to be polygenic and show continuous variation?
ABO blood group
The ability to roll the tongue
Height
Cystic fibrosis

Height is controlled by many genes and is also affected by nutrition. It produces a continuous range of values, not distinct categories. ABO blood group and cystic fibrosis are each controlled by one gene and fall into distinct classes.
bio12a2-gpe-5
In a study of a trait in twins, concordance (both twins having the trait) was 45% for identical twins and 20% for non-identical twins. The best conclusion is that the trait is
determined entirely by genes.
determined entirely by the environment.
influenced by both genetic and environmental factors.
caused by a chromosomal abnormality.

Identical twins share all their DNA. Their higher concordance shows a genetic influence, but if genes alone decided the trait concordance would be close to 100%. A value of 45% shows the environment also matters.
bio12a2-gpe-6
Distinguish between continuous and discontinuous variation, using one example of each. (2 marks)

Continuous variation shows a range of values with no distinct categories, usually because the trait is polygenic and affected by environment, e.g. height or skin colour; discontinuous variation falls into a few distinct categories, usually controlled by one or a few genes, e.g. ABO blood group or attached versus free earlobes.
bio12a2-gpe-7

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by inheriting two recessive alleles that result in a non-functional enzyme that normally breaks down the amino acid phenylalanine. Untreated, phenylalanine builds up and damages the brain. Babies diagnosed at birth and fed a low-phenylalanine diet develop normally. Explain what this shows about the relationship between genotype, environment and phenotype. (3 marks)

The genotype (homozygous recessive) cannot be changed, so the enzyme is still non-functional; the environment (a diet low in phenylalanine) stops phenylalanine building up to harmful levels; so the phenotype depends on the interaction of genotype and environment, and the same genotype can produce a different phenotype under different conditions.
bio12a2-gpe-8

Identical twins have the same DNA sequence, yet differences in gene expression between them often increase as they age. Explain how epigenetic factors such as DNA methylation could cause this. (2 marks)

Methyl groups can be added to DNA (or histones can be modified), which can switch genes off or reduce their expression without changing the base sequence; the twins experience different environments (diet, smoking, stress), which cause different methylation patterns, so different genes are expressed and their phenotypes diverge.
bio12a2-gpe-9
Which term describes the range of phenotypes that one genotype can produce across different environments?
norm of reaction
codominance
linkage
mutation rate

The norm of reaction is the range of phenotypes a genotype can produce depending on the environment. Codominance and linkage describe patterns of inheritance, and mutation rate describes how often changes occur in DNA.
bio12a2-gpe-10
Which of the following describes a genotype rather than a phenotype?
Curly hair
Blue eyes
A height of 172 cm
Two copies of the allele for free earlobes
Curly hair, blue eyes and a height of 172 cm are observable characteristics, so they are phenotypes. Two copies of an allele describe the genetic makeup of an individual.
bio12a2-gpe-11
Which of these is an environmental influence on a human phenotype, rather than a genetic one?
Inheriting two alleles for sickle-cell haemoglobin
Eye colour set by melanin genes inherited from parents
Weight gain after a long period of high-energy eating
Blood group inherited from both parents
Diet is an environmental factor, and eating more kilojoules than are used can increase body mass without any change in alleles. The other options are all determined by inherited alleles.
bio12a2-gpe-12
Which characteristic is least affected by environmental conditions?
Adult body mass
ABO blood group
Tanning after sun exposure
Muscle size after resistance training
ABO blood group is set by the alleles inherited, and diet or exercise does not change it. Body mass, tanning and muscle size all respond to food, sunlight and training.
bio12a2-gpe-13
A trait in a population shows continuous variation. Which statement is most likely to be correct?
The trait is usually controlled by many genes and influenced by the environment.
The trait is controlled by a single gene with two alleles.
Individuals fall into a small number of distinct classes.
The trait cannot be measured on a numerical scale.

Continuous variation arises when many genes and environmental factors together produce a range of values. A single gene with two alleles usually gives distinct categories rather than a continuous range, and continuous traits can be measured on a scale.
bio12a2-gpe-14

Snowshoe hares grow brown coats in summer and white coats in winter. In an experiment, hares kept at a winter temperature but exposed to a summer day length kept their brown coats. Which conclusion is best supported?
Temperature is the only environmental factor that can change coat colour.
Coat colour is fixed by genotype and cannot change with the environment.
The hares must have mutated to grow brown coats in summer.
Day length is an environmental factor that changes coat colour, so one genotype can produce different phenotypes at different times of year.

Only day length was set to summer conditions, and the brown coat was kept despite winter temperatures, so day length acts as an environmental cue. The coat changes with the season each year, which rules out a mutation as the explanation.
bio12a2-gpe-15
A dairy cow genotype has a narrow norm of reaction for milk yield, with yields of 6 000 L to 6 500 L across all farms. Which interpretation is best?
The trait is controlled by many genes with large effects, so it shows discrete categories.
The environment has no effect on milk yield at all.
The genotype gives a similar phenotype across these farms, so the environment has only a small effect on milk yield.
The genotype has mutated on each farm.

A narrow norm of reaction means the phenotype changes little between environments. The environment still has some effect because the range is not zero, and milk yield here is a continuous measure, not discrete categories.
bio12a2-gpe-16
A student wants to test whether a fertiliser affects plant height while keeping genotype constant. Which design is best?
Seedlings from different parent plants, all given fertiliser
Genetically identical seedlings, all grown under the same conditions except for the fertiliser
Seedlings of different species, with and without fertiliser
One seedling given fertiliser, with its height compared with results from a previous year

Genetically identical seedlings keep genotype constant, and changing only the fertiliser isolates its effect on phenotype. The other designs allow genotype or other conditions to vary, so any height difference could have another cause.
bio12a2-gpe-17
Why does a trait controlled by several genes usually show a wider range of phenotypes than a trait controlled by one gene?
Several genes produce many allele combinations, and each gene adds a small effect to the phenotype.
Each gene in the group has a large effect on the phenotype.
The genes are always sex-linked.
The environment is the only source of variation in such traits.
Polygenic traits combine many small effects, which produces many intermediate phenotypes. Sex linkage does not widen the range, and environment is only one source of variation, not the only one.
bio12a2-gpe-18
Which statement about the link between genes and phenotype is most accurate?
A gene always produces the same phenotype, whatever the environment.
The environment has no effect once an individual's genotype is set, except by mutating its genes.
A gene's product affects the phenotype, and the size of that effect can depend on environmental conditions.
The phenotype is set entirely by the alleles present, so the environment has no role.

Genes code for proteins that influence traits, but environmental conditions can modify how strongly that influence is expressed. The other options wrongly claim fixed genetic control or no environmental role.
bio12a2-gpe-19
Which of these can be passed on to offspring?
A tan acquired from a summer at the beach
A scar from a cut to the skin
A weight gain from a high-kilojoule diet
A mutation in a sperm or egg cell
Only changes to the DNA in gametes can be inherited by offspring. A tan, a scar and weight gain are environmentally caused changes in phenotype that do not alter the DNA of gametes.
bio12a2-gpe-20
A person with a normal thyroid genotype develops a goitre (enlarged thyroid) because their diet lacks iodine. Which statement is best supported?
The goitre shows that the person's genotype has mutated.
The goitre is a phenotype produced by an environmental factor acting on a normal genotype.
The goitre must be controlled by a dominant allele.
Diet has no effect on phenotype when the genotype is normal.
Iodine deficiency is an environmental factor that can produce a goitre even when the genotype is normal. A goitre does not show a mutation or a particular allele, and diet does affect phenotype.
bio12a2-gpe-21
Which of the following is an environmental factor that can change a plant's phenotype?
Soil nitrogen availability
Its chromosome number
A dominant allele for flower colour
A mutation in a stem cell
Soil nitrogen is an environmental factor that affects plant growth and leaf colour without changing the DNA. The other options are genetic factors, such as chromosome number, alleles and mutations.
bio12a2-gpe-22

Two genetically identical plants are grown, one in a bright, sunny position and one in shade. The sunny plant is taller with thicker stems. Explain this difference in terms of genotype and environment. (2 marks)
The plants have the same genotype, so genes do not explain the difference [1]; sunlight (the environment) acts on this genotype to produce a different phenotype [1].
bio12a2-gpe-23
Some people carry the same disease-causing genotype for a genetic disorder but show different severity of symptoms. Explain why. (2 marks)
Other genes and environmental factors, such as diet, lifestyle or medical care, interact with the genotype [1]; so the same genotype can produce different phenotypes [1].
bio12a2-gpe-24
Name one environmental factor that can change human skin colour, and state the change it causes. (1 mark)
Sunlight (UV exposure) increases melanin production, so the skin darkens [1].
bio12a2-gpe-25
Explain why the phenotype of an organism can differ from what its genotype alone would predict. (2 marks)

Environmental factors such as diet, temperature or light act on the genotype during development [1]; the genotype sets a range of possible phenotypes and the environment determines where in that range the organism falls [1].
bio12a2-gpe-26
A student claims that because identical twins have the same DNA, any difference between them must be genetic. Evaluate this claim. (3 marks)

The claim is not valid [1]; environmental differences, such as diet, illness or lifestyle, can produce different phenotypes from the same genotype [1]; epigenetic changes or mutations that arise after the twins develop can also change gene expression [1].
bio12a2-gpe-27
A student states that the environment can change an organism's phenotype but never its genotype. Evaluate this statement. (2 marks)

Partly incorrect: environmental factors change the phenotype without altering the DNA sequence in most cases [1]; but environmental mutagens such as UV radiation or chemicals can cause mutations that do change the genotype [1].
vce-bio12-ge-c1
Identical twins raised apart differ in height by 8 cm. The best explanation is that:
Their genotypes are different, because identical twins develop from two separate eggs
Height is controlled by one gene only, and one twin inherited a different allele
Their genotypes are the same, but environmental factors such as nutrition affected their phenotypes
Mutations always occur in twins, so one twin's height genes were changed
Phenotype = genotype + environment. Height is polygenic and strongly affected by diet and health.
vce-bio12-monohybrid-crosses-and-test-cr: bio12a3-mono-1
In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p). Two heterozygous purple-flowered plants are crossed. What is the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring?
1 purple : 1 white
3 purple : 1 white
1 purple : 2 white
All purple
Pp × Pp gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. PP and Pp are both purple, so the phenotypic ratio is 3 purple : 1 white. A 1 : 1 ratio comes from Pp × pp, not from two heterozygotes.
bio12a3-mono-2
A breeder wants to know whether a black-coated guinea pig (black, B, is dominant to brown, b) is homozygous or heterozygous. Which cross is the most appropriate test cross?
Cross the black guinea pig with a homozygous black guinea pig
Cross the black guinea pig with a heterozygous black guinea pig
Cross the black guinea pig with a brown guinea pig
Cross the black guinea pig with another black guinea pig of unknown genotype

A test cross pairs the individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive individual (bb, brown). Any recessive allele carried by the unknown parent will then show up in the offspring phenotype. Crossing with BB would give all black offspring whatever the unknown genotype is.
bio12a3-mono-3
In a test cross between a tall plant of unknown genotype and a short (tt) plant, 52 tall and 48 short offspring are produced. What is the most likely genotype of the tall parent?
TT
Tt
tt
It cannot be determined from these results
About 1 : 1 tall : short is the result expected from Tt × tt. If the tall parent were TT, all offspring would be Tt and tall. The parent cannot be tt because it shows the dominant phenotype.
bio12a3-mono-4
In snapdragons, flower colour shows incomplete dominance: CᴿCᴿ plants are red, CᵂCᵂ are white and CᴿCᵂ are pink. What proportion of offspring from a cross of two pink plants will be pink?

CᴿCᵂ × CᴿCᵂ gives 1 CᴿCᴿ (red) : 2 CᴿCᵂ (pink) : 1 CᵂCᵂ (white), so half (50%) are pink. With incomplete dominance the heterozygote has its own intermediate phenotype, so the 3 : 1 pattern does not apply.
bio12a3-mono-5

Human ABO blood group is controlled by three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant and both are dominant to i. A person with blood group A (IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi) and a person with blood group B have a child with blood group O. Which statement is correct?
Both parents must be heterozygous
Only the group A parent must be heterozygous
The child must have inherited a mutation
The group B parent must be IᴮIᴮ
A group O child is ii, so it received an i allele from each parent. The parents must therefore be Iᴬi and Iᴮi. An IᴮIᴮ parent could not pass on i, and no mutation is needed to explain the result.
bio12a3-mono-6

In Labrador retrievers, a dominant allele B produces black coat and the recessive allele b produces brown coat (ignore other genes). A heterozygous black dog is mated with a brown dog. (a) Write the genotypes of the parents and the gametes each can produce. (b) Using a Punnett square or other working, state the expected genotypic and phenotypic ratios of the puppies. (3 marks)
(a) Parents Bb (black) and bb (brown); Bb produces B and b gametes, bb produces only b gametes; (b) offspring genotypes 1 Bb : 1 bb; phenotypes 1 black : 1 brown (50% each).
bio12a3-mono-7

A student crosses two heterozygous plants and predicts 75 offspring with round seeds and 25 with wrinkled seeds out of 100. She actually obtains 70 round and 30 wrinkled. Explain why the observed results differ from the expected ratio, and suggest how the reliability of the result could be improved. (2 marks)

Fertilisation is random, so each offspring has an independent 3/4 probability of being round and real counts deviate by chance from the predicted ratio; a larger sample (more offspring) or repeating the cross would make the results more reliable and closer to 3 : 1.
bio12a3-mono-8
Define the terms genotype, phenotype and homozygous, and use a single-gene example to show how two organisms with the same phenotype can have different genotypes. (3 marks)

Genotype is the combination of alleles an organism has for a gene (e.g. Tt); phenotype is the observable characteristic produced by the genotype interacting with the environment (e.g. tall); homozygous means having two identical alleles for a gene (TT or tt); for example a TT plant and a Tt plant are both tall because T is dominant, so the same phenotype can come from different genotypes.
bio12a3-mono-9
Which term describes the alternative forms of a single gene, such as T and t, that occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes?
Alleles
Genotypes
Phenotypes
Gametes

Alleles are the alternative forms of a gene at the same locus on homologous chromosomes. Genotype is the allele combination an individual carries, phenotype is its observable trait, and gametes are sex cells, so none of these names the alternative forms.
bio12a3-mono-10
In sheep, horns (H) are dominant to polled, meaning no horns (h). A heterozygous horned ram is mated with a polled ewe. What proportion of their lambs is expected to be polled?
Hh × hh gives 1 Hh : 1 hh, so half the lambs are hh and polled. A 25% result applies to a cross between two heterozygotes, and 100% would require both parents to be polled.
bio12a3-mono-11
In tomatoes, red fruit (R) is dominant to yellow fruit (r). A cross is made between two heterozygous plants (Rr × Rr). How many different genotypes are possible among the offspring?

The four squares of the Punnett square give RR, Rr, Rr and rr, which is three different genotypes. Four is the number of squares rather than genotypes, and 9 is the number of genotypes produced by a dihybrid cross.
bio12a3-mono-12

In radishes, long roots (L) are dominant to round roots (l). A long-rooted radish of unknown genotype is test-crossed with a round-rooted radish (ll). All 20 offspring have long roots. What is the most likely genotype of the unknown plant?
Ll
ll
It cannot be determined
LL
An LL parent gives only Ll offspring, all long-rooted. An Ll parent would give about half round-rooted offspring, so 20 long-rooted offspring would be extremely unlikely.
bio12a3-mono-13
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f); the dominant allele (F) is normal. Two unaffected carriers (Ff) have a child. What is the probability that the child has cystic fibrosis?
Ff × Ff gives 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff, so 1 in 4 children is ff and affected. The 50% figure applies to a carrier crossed with an affected parent, and 75% is the chance that a child is unaffected.
bio12a3-mono-14
A heterozygous plant with genotype Aa forms gametes by meiosis. Which statement about these gametes is correct?
It produces one type of gamete, A, only
It produces two types, A and a, in a 1 : 1 ratio
It produces two types, A and a, in a 1 : 2 ratio
It produces four types of gamete, each carrying both alleles

Segregation places one allele into each gamete, so the A and a gametes form in equal numbers. An AA plant would produce only A gametes, and the 1 : 2 ratio confuses gametes with the genotypes of offspring.
bio12a3-mono-15
Which cross would produce the greatest proportion of offspring with the dominant phenotype?
Aa × aa
Aa × Aa
AA × aa
aa × aa
AA × aa gives only Aa offspring, so all (100%) show the dominant phenotype. Aa × Aa gives 75% dominant, Aa × aa gives 50%, and aa × aa gives none.
bio12a3-mono-16
A plant shows the recessive phenotype for a gene with complete dominance. What can be concluded about its genotype?
It is heterozygous, because recessive alleles are hidden
It has one dominant allele that is not expressed
Its genotype cannot be known from its phenotype
It has two copies of the recessive allele

A recessive phenotype appears only when no dominant allele is present, so the genotype must be homozygous recessive. A heterozygote carries the recessive allele but shows the dominant phenotype, and a single dominant allele would be expressed, so neither can produce the recessive trait.
bio12a3-mono-17

Achondroplasia, a form of dwarfism, is caused by a dominant allele (A); the recessive allele (a) gives normal stature. A person with achondroplasia who is heterozygous (Aa) has children with a person of normal stature (aa). What is the probability that each child has achondroplasia?

Aa × aa gives 1 Aa : 1 aa, so half the children inherit the dominant allele and have achondroplasia. A 25% chance applies to two carriers of a recessive disorder, and 100% would require every child to inherit the dominant allele, which this cross cannot give.
bio12a3-mono-18
According to Mendel's law of segregation, what happens to the two alleles of a gene during the formation of gametes?
They separate, so each gamete receives one allele
They are copied, so each gamete receives both alleles
They fuse together before meiosis begins
They are always inherited from the same parent

During meiosis the two alleles separate into different gametes, so each gamete carries one allele. A gamete carrying both alleles would not be a normal haploid gamete, and the other options do not describe gamete formation.
bio12a3-mono-19
Two black guinea pigs (black, B, is dominant to brown, b) are mated and produce a brown offspring. What can be concluded about the parents?
Both parents must be homozygous dominant (BB)
Both parents must be heterozygous (Bb)
One parent must be brown
The brown offspring must have a new mutation

A brown offspring (bb) must receive a b allele from each parent, so both black parents carry b and must be Bb. Homozygous dominant parents would produce only black offspring, and no mutation is needed to explain the result.
bio12a3-mono-20
Which statement about a heterozygous individual for a single gene with complete dominance is correct?
It always shows the recessive phenotype
It is homozygous for the dominant allele
It produces only one type of gamete
It has two different alleles for the gene

A heterozygote carries two different alleles at the locus, one dominant and one recessive, and under complete dominance it shows the dominant phenotype. It is not homozygous, and it produces two types of gamete.
bio12a3-mono-21
In a Punnett square for Dd × Dd, how many of the four squares contain the genotype DD?

The four squares are DD, Dd, Dd and dd, so only one contains DD. Two squares contain Dd, which is the count of heterozygous squares, and three would match the count of dominant-phenotype squares rather than DD.
bio12a3-mono-22
What is a monohybrid cross?
A cross between two homozygous individuals only
A cross between individuals that differ in two characteristics
A cross in which neither parent has a dominant allele
A cross between individuals that differ in one characteristic controlled by a single gene

A monohybrid cross follows the inheritance of one characteristic controlled by one gene. Crosses involving two characteristics are dihybrid crosses, and a monohybrid cross does not require homozygous parents or any particular dominance pattern.
bio12a3-mono-23
Explain why an individual of unknown genotype is test-crossed with a homozygous recessive individual rather than with another individual showing the dominant phenotype. (2 marks)

The homozygous recessive partner contributes only recessive alleles, so each offspring's phenotype directly reflects the allele passed on by the unknown parent [1]; crossing with another dominant-phenotype individual can hide a recessive allele, because heterozygotes and homozygous dominant individuals look the same [1].
bio12a3-mono-24
State the genotype ratio expected from a Tt × Tt cross. (1 mark)
1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt [1].
bio12a3-mono-25
Two children are born to a pair of heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa). Calculate the probability that both children are aa, and show your working. (2 marks)
Probability that one child is aa = 1/4 [1]; both children aa = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 (6.25%) [1].
bio12a3-mono-26

In mice, a rough coat (R) is dominant to a smooth coat (r). A rough mouse of unknown genotype is test-crossed with a smooth mouse. (a) State the genotype of the smooth mouse and the gametes it can produce. (b) Predict the offspring if the rough mouse is RR, and if it is Rr. (c) Explain why smooth offspring would show that the unknown mouse carries an r allele. (4 marks)

(a) rr; produces only r gametes [1]; (b) RR gives all rough offspring (Rr) [1]; Rr gives about 1 rough : 1 smooth offspring [1]; (c) each smooth offspring must have received r from the unknown parent, since the smooth parent contributes only r [1].
bio12a3-mono-27
Explain why a heterozygous individual can be described as a carrier of a recessive allele. (2 marks)
It has one copy of the recessive allele, which it can pass on to its offspring [1]; it shows the dominant phenotype because the dominant allele masks the recessive one [1].
bio12a3-mono-28

Phenylketonuria is a recessive condition (p), with the normal allele P. Two parents who are both carriers (Pp) have a first child with the condition (pp). (a) Use a Punnett square to state the probability that their next child is a carrier (Pp). (b) State the probability that the next child is unaffected. (c) Explain why the first child's condition does not change these probabilities. (3 marks)
(a) 1/2 (two of four squares are Pp) [1]; (b) 3/4 (PP or Pp are unaffected) [1]; (c) each conception is an independent event, so earlier children do not change the chance for later ones [1].
bio12a3-mono-29

In a monohybrid cross, pure-breeding red-flowered plants (RR) are crossed with pure-breeding white-flowered plants (rr). All F1 offspring are red. (a) Give the genotype of the F1 plants. (b) The F1 plants are self-pollinated. State the expected phenotypic ratio of the F2 generation. (c) Explain what pure-breeding means. (d) Explain why all F1 plants are red. (4 marks)

(a) Rr [1]; (b) 3 red : 1 white [1]; (c) homozygous for the trait, so it breeds true and produces offspring with the same phenotype for that trait when self-pollinated [1]; (d) the R allele is dominant, so the heterozygous Rr plants express red [1].
bio12a3-mono-30

In rabbits, black fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). A black rabbit is mated with a white rabbit and produces a white offspring. Deduce the genotype of the black rabbit and justify your answer. (2 marks)
Bb [1]; the white offspring (bb) must have received a b allele from the black parent, so that parent carries b, and as it shows black it must be heterozygous [1].
vce-bio12-mc-c1
A tall pea plant is crossed with a short plant (tt). The offspring are 48 tall and 52 short. The tall parent's genotype was:
TT
tt
It cannot be determined
Tt
A test cross with the recessive homozygote reveals the unknown genotype: a 1 : 1 ratio means the tall parent was heterozygous. TT would give all tall.
vce-bio12-dihybrid-crosses-and-linked-ge: bio12a3-dihy-1

In peas, yellow seed (Y) is dominant to green (y) and round seed (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r). The genes are on different chromosomes. What is the expected phenotypic ratio from the cross YyRr × YyRr?

Two unlinked genes assort independently, so each heterozygous parent produces YR, Yr, yR and yr gametes in equal proportions. The 16-box Punnett square gives 9 yellow round : 3 yellow wrinkled : 3 green round : 1 green wrinkled. 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 is the ratio from a dihybrid test cross.
bio12a3-dihy-2
Which gametes can be produced by an individual with genotype AaBb, assuming the two genes are unlinked?
AB and ab only
Aa and Bb
AB, Ab, aB and ab in equal proportions
AA, BB, aa and bb

Each gamete gets one allele of each gene. With independent assortment, any A allele can go with any B allele, giving AB, Ab, aB and ab at 25% each. 'AB and ab only' is what you would see with complete linkage and no crossing over.
bio12a3-dihy-3

A fruit fly heterozygous for two genes (genotype GgLl, with G and L inherited from the same parent) is test crossed with a ggll fly. The offspring are: 420 GgLl, 410 ggll, 85 Ggll and 85 ggLl. What best explains these results?
The genes are unlinked and are assorting independently
The genes are linked, and the smaller classes are recombinants produced by crossing over
The genes are linked and no crossing over occurred
One of the alleles is lethal when homozygous

Unlinked genes would give about 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Here the two parental combinations (GL and gl) are much more common than the two recombinant combinations (Gl and gL), which shows the genes are on the same chromosome. The recombinant classes exist, so crossing over between the loci must have happened in some cells.
bio12a3-dihy-4
Using the data in a test cross where 830 offspring show parental phenotypes and 170 show recombinant phenotypes, what is the recombination frequency between the two genes?
Recombination frequency = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring × 100 = 170 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 17%. 83% is the proportion of parental types, not recombinants.
bio12a3-dihy-5
Two genes on the same chromosome are far apart from each other. Compared with two genes located very close together on that chromosome, the far-apart genes will
never be separated during meiosis
show a lower recombination frequency
show a higher recombination frequency, approaching that of unlinked genes
always be inherited together in the same gamete

The further apart two loci are, the more likely a crossover will occur between them in prophase I, so more recombinant gametes are made. Genes very far apart can show close to 50% recombination, which looks like independent assortment. Close genes are the ones rarely separated.
bio12a3-dihy-6

In guinea pigs, black coat (B) is dominant to white (b) and rough coat (R) is dominant to smooth (r). The genes are unlinked. A black, rough guinea pig of genotype BbRr is crossed with a white, smooth guinea pig (bbrr). (a) List the gametes produced by each parent. (b) State the expected phenotypes of the offspring and their ratio. (3 marks)

(a) BbRr produces BR, Br, bR and br gametes in equal proportions; bbrr produces only br gametes; (b) offspring 1 black rough (BbRr) : 1 black smooth (Bbrr) : 1 white rough (bbRr) : 1 white smooth (bbrr), i.e. 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
bio12a3-dihy-7
Explain the difference between independent assortment and linkage, referring to the position of genes on chromosomes and the gametes produced. (3 marks)

Genes on different (non-homologous) chromosomes assort independently because the orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I is random; this gives all allele combinations in gametes in equal proportions; linked genes are on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together, so parental combinations of alleles are more common in gametes and new combinations only arise when crossing over occurs between the loci.
bio12a3-dihy-8

A researcher test crosses a plant heterozygous for two genes and obtains 250 offspring of each of the four possible phenotypes. She concludes the two genes are on different chromosomes. Evaluate this conclusion. (2 marks)

The 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio is consistent with independent assortment, so the genes are probably unlinked; however genes very far apart on the same chromosome can also recombine at close to 50%, so the result alone does not prove they are on different chromosomes.
bio12a3-dihy-9
In a plant, both parents have genotype AaBb and the two genes are unlinked. What is the probability that an offspring has genotype aabb?

The probability of aa from Aa × Aa is 1/4 and the probability of bb from Bb × Bb is also 1/4, so aabb = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. 1/4 is the chance for only one gene, and 3/16 is the chance of a phenotype such as A_bb.
bio12a3-dihy-10
In a cross between AaBb and Aabb, with the genes unlinked, what proportion of offspring are expected to show the dominant phenotype for gene A and the recessive phenotype for gene B (A_bb)?
A_ from Aa × Aa is 3/4 and bb from Bb × bb is 1/2, so A_bb = 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8. The answer 3/4 ignores the probability for gene B, and 1/8 wrongly multiplies 1/4 by 1/2.
bio12a3-dihy-11
How many different genotypes can be produced from a cross of AaBb × AaBb when the two genes are on different chromosomes?

Each gene gives three genotypes (AA, Aa, aa), so 3 × 3 = 9 distinct genotypes. The 16 is the number of boxes in the Punnett square rather than the number of distinct genotypes, and 4 is the number of gamete types from one parent.
bio12a3-dihy-12
Two genes on the same chromosome show 12% recombination. In a test cross producing 500 offspring, how many offspring are expected to show recombinant phenotypes?

Recombination frequency of 12% means 12% of 500 = 60 recombinant offspring across both recombinant classes combined. The answer 12 is the percentage rather than the count, 120 counts the recombinants twice, and 250 is the number expected for unlinked genes (50%).
bio12a3-dihy-13
At which stage of meiosis does crossing over between genes on homologous chromosomes take place?
Metaphase I
Anaphase II
Prophase I
Interphase

Crossing over occurs in prophase I while homologous chromosomes are paired and form chiasmata. Metaphase I is when homologous pairs line up at the equator, and interphase is when DNA replicates before meiosis begins.
bio12a3-dihy-14
An individual has genotype AB/ab and genes A and B are linked, with a recombination frequency of 20%. Which gametes are produced, and in what proportions?
40% AB, 40% ab, 10% Ab and 10% aB
25% each of AB, Ab, aB and ab
80% AB and 20% ab
10% AB, 10% ab, 40% Ab and 40% aB

The 80% parental gametes are split equally into AB and ab, and the 20% recombinant gametes are split equally into Ab and aB. The 25% option assumes unlinked genes, and the last option swaps the parental and recombinant classes.
bio12a3-dihy-15
A plant of genotype AaBb is test crossed with aabb. The genes are unlinked and the cross produces 300 offspring. How many offspring are expected to have genotype Aabb?
Aa from Aa × aa is 1/2 and bb from Bb × bb is 1/2, so Aabb = 1/4 × 300 = 75. The answer 150 uses only one of the two probabilities, and 300 is the total number of offspring.
bio12a3-dihy-16
Two parents, both AaBb, have 800 offspring with the genes unlinked. How many offspring are expected to show both dominant phenotypes (A_B_)?

A_ is 3/4 and B_ is 3/4, so A_B_ = 9/16, and 9/16 × 800 = 450. The answer 200 is 1/4 of the offspring (the expected proportion for one recessive gene only), 400 is half, and 600 is the proportion for one dominant trait only.
bio12a3-dihy-17
Which statement correctly describes crossing over?
It occurs between sister chromatids during mitosis and produces identical daughter cells
It separates homologous chromosomes at anaphase I so that each gamete receives one chromosome of each pair
It exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, producing chromosomes with new combinations of alleles
It is the random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I

During prophase I, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata, so the chromosomes carry new allele combinations. The other options describe mitosis, the separation of homologues, and independent assortment, which are different processes.
bio12a3-dihy-18
Why is a homozygous recessive individual used in a test cross?
It contributes only recessive alleles, so each offspring's phenotype reveals the allele passed on by the unknown parent
It ensures all offspring are heterozygous so the cross is easy to read
It prevents crossing over from occurring in the unknown parent
It makes every offspring show the dominant phenotype

The recessive parent gives only recessive alleles, so each offspring's phenotype directly shows which allele the unknown parent passed on. A test cross does not make offspring heterozygous, does not stop crossing over, and does not produce dominant phenotypes.
bio12a3-dihy-19
Individuals AABb and aaBb are crossed, with the genes unlinked. What proportion of offspring are expected to have genotype AaBb?
All offspring are Aa (AA × aa), and half are Bb from Bb × Bb, so AaBb = 1 × 1/2 = 1/2. The answer 1/4 comes from wrongly halving the Aa probability, and 1 ignores the probability for gene B.
bio12a3-dihy-20
Individuals AaBb and aaBB are crossed, with the genes unlinked. What proportion of offspring are expected to show both dominant phenotypes (A_B_)?
A_ from Aa × aa is 1/2, and every offspring is B_ because the BB parent contributes a dominant allele, so A_B_ = 1/2 × 1 = 1/2. The answer 3/4 wrongly applies a 3 : 1 ratio to gene B.
bio12a3-dihy-21
How many different gamete genotypes can an individual with genotype AaBbCc produce if the three genes are unlinked?
