Each heterozygous gene doubles the number of gamete types, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 (ABC, ABc, AbC, Abc, aBC, aBc, abC and abc). The answer 6 comes from adding rather than multiplying, 4 is the number of gamete types for only two genes, and 16 would come from four heterozygous genes.
bio12a3-dihy-22
Which cross would give a phenotypic ratio of 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 for two unlinked genes?
AaBb × aabb
AaBb × AaBb
AABB × aabb
AaBB × AaBB

A test cross of a heterozygote for two unlinked genes with a homozygous recessive gives four phenotypes in equal proportions. AaBb × AaBb gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, AABB × aabb gives only dominant offspring, and AaBB × AaBB gives a 3 : 1 ratio for gene A only.
bio12a3-dihy-23

In tomatoes, round fruit (R) is dominant to elongated fruit (r), and purple stem (P) is dominant to green stem (p). The genes are on the same chromosome. A plant of genotype RP/rp is test crossed with an rp/rp plant, producing 1000 offspring: 425 round purple, 425 elongated green, 75 round green and 75 elongated purple. (a) Calculate the recombination frequency. (b) State whether the genes are linked, giving a reason. (2 marks)
(a) Recombination frequency = 150 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 15% [1]; (b) the genes are linked because recombinant phenotypes make up only 15% (less than 50%), so the parental phenotypes are far more common [1].
bio12a3-dihy-24
Describe the stage of meiosis in which crossing over occurs, and explain how it produces recombinant gametes. (3 marks)

Crossing over occurs in prophase I [1]; homologous chromosomes pair and non-sister chromatids exchange equal segments at chiasmata [1]; the chromatids then carry new combinations of alleles, so the gametes formed from them are recombinant [1].
bio12a3-dihy-25
Define recombination frequency. (1 mark)
The percentage of offspring (or gametes) that show recombinant phenotypes (or genotypes), calculated as recombinant ÷ total × 100 [1].
bio12a3-dihy-26

In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t) and red flowers (R) are dominant to white flowers (r). The genes are unlinked. A plant of genotype TtRr is crossed with a plant of genotype ttRr. (a) List the gametes produced by each parent. (b) State the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring. (c) Calculate the expected number of tall white-flowered offspring from 320 offspring. (4 marks)

(a) TtRr produces TR, Tr, tR and tr in equal proportions [1]; ttRr produces tR and tr in equal proportions [1]; (b) tall red : tall white : dwarf red : dwarf white = 3 : 1 : 3 : 1 [1]; (c) 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8, so 1/8 × 320 = 40 tall white offspring [1].
bio12a3-dihy-27
Explain how independent assortment and crossing over each contribute to genetic variation in gametes. (2 marks)

Independent assortment: random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I produces different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in gametes [1]; crossing over: exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids in prophase I produces new combinations of alleles on the same chromosome [1].
bio12a3-dihy-28

An individual of genotype AB/ab is test crossed with an ab/ab individual. The genes are linked with a recombination frequency of 30%. (a) State the percentage of the AB/ab parent's gametes that are AB. (b) Calculate the expected number of recombinant offspring from 500 offspring. (c) Calculate the expected number of ab/ab offspring from 500 offspring. (3 marks)
(a) 35% of gametes are AB (70% parental, split equally) [1]; (b) 30% × 500 = 150 recombinant offspring [1]; (c) ab gametes are 35%, so 35% × 500 = 175 ab/ab offspring [1].
bio12a3-dihy-29
Calculate the proportion of offspring from an AaBb × AaBb cross (genes unlinked) that have the genotype aaB_ (aaBB or aaBb). Show your working. (2 marks)
Probability of aa from Aa × Aa = 1/4 [1]; probability of B_ from Bb × Bb = 3/4, so aaB_ = 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16 [1].
bio12a3-dihy-30
List all the gamete genotypes produced by an individual of genotype AABbCc, assuming the genes are unlinked. (1 mark)
ABC, ABc, AbC and Abc, each 25% [1].
vce-bio12-dh-c1
A test cross AaBb × aabb gives mostly AaBb and aabb offspring, with only a few Aabb and aaBb. This suggests that:
The genes are on different chromosomes
Genes A and B are linked, and the few recombinants come from crossing over
There was a mistake, because the ratio must be 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
Both genes are X-linked
Unlinked genes would give 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Linked genes are usually inherited together; crossing over makes a small number of recombinants.
vce-bio12-pedigree-charts-and-modes-of-i: bio12a3-ped-1
In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which mode of inheritance is most strongly supported?
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive

Unaffected parents having an affected child means the trait is recessive (both parents are carriers). Because the affected child is a daughter with an unaffected father, it cannot be X-linked recessive: an affected daughter would need an affected father. So the trait is autosomal recessive.
bio12a3-ped-2
Which feature of a pedigree would rule out X-linked recessive inheritance?
More males than females are affected
An affected male has an unaffected son
An affected female has an unaffected son
The trait skips a generation

An X-linked recessive female (XᵃXᵃ) passes an Xᵃ to every son, and sons have only one X, so all her sons would be affected. An unaffected son of an affected mother rules it out. An affected father never passes his X to his sons, so an unaffected son is expected.
bio12a3-ped-3

Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant. A man who is heterozygous for Huntington's disease has a child with a woman who does not carry the allele. What is the probability that the child will inherit the condition?
Hh × hh gives 1 Hh : 1 hh, so each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele and being affected.
bio12a3-ped-4

Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind has children with a man with normal vision. What is the probability that their first son will be colour blind?

The woman must have received Xᵇ from her colour-blind father, so she is XᴮXᵇ. A son receives his X from his mother, so he has a 1/2 chance of getting Xᵇ and being colour blind. The father's normal X goes only to daughters. 1/4 is the chance that any child (son or daughter) is colour blind.
bio12a3-ped-5

A pedigree shows a trait appearing in every generation. Every affected child has at least one affected parent, and affected fathers pass the trait to all of their daughters but none of their sons. The most likely mode of inheritance is
autosomal recessive
autosomal dominant
X-linked dominant
Y-linked

A trait seen in every generation, with affected children always having an affected parent, suggests dominance. An affected father gives his X to all daughters and his Y to all sons, so an X-linked dominant trait shows up in all his daughters and none of his sons. Y-linked traits pass from fathers to all sons instead.
bio12a3-ped-6

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition. A couple who are both unaffected have a son with cystic fibrosis. (a) State the genotypes of the parents, using F and f. (b) Calculate the probability that their next child will be an unaffected carrier. (c) Their unaffected daughter wants to know the probability that she is a carrier. State this probability and explain it. (4 marks)

(a) Both parents are Ff; (b) Ff × Ff gives 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff, so the probability of a carrier (Ff) child is 1/2; (c) the daughter is unaffected so she cannot be ff; of the remaining unaffected outcomes (1 FF : 2 Ff) two out of three are carriers, so her probability is 2/3.
bio12a3-ped-7
Describe two features you would look for in a pedigree to tell an autosomal dominant trait apart from an autosomal recessive trait. (2 marks)

Autosomal dominant traits usually appear in every generation and every affected person has at least one affected parent, whereas recessive traits can skip generations; two affected parents can have an unaffected child with a dominant trait, but two affected parents with a recessive trait (both homozygous recessive) will only have affected children.
bio12a3-ped-8
Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive. Explain why it is far more common in males than females, and explain why an affected male cannot pass the condition to his sons. (3 marks)

Males have one X chromosome (XY), so a single recessive allele (XʰY) is enough to cause haemophilia; females have two X chromosomes and need two copies of the recessive allele (XʰXʰ), which is much less likely; a father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to his sons, so sons get their X from their mother and cannot inherit the allele from their father.
bio12a3-ped-9
In a standard pedigree chart, what does a shaded square represent?
An affected male
An affected female
An unaffected male
An unaffected female

Squares represent males and circles represent females, and shading shows that the trait is expressed. A shaded square is therefore an affected male, whereas a shaded circle would be an affected female.
bio12a3-ped-10
Two heterozygous parents (Dd) have children. The dominant allele D causes an autosomal dominant condition. What is the probability that a child is unaffected?
Dd × Dd gives 1 DD : 2 Dd : 1 dd, and only dd children are unaffected, so the probability is 1/4. The 3/4 is the probability of being affected, which is easy to confuse with the answer.
bio12a3-ped-11
A woman who is homozygous recessive (aa) for an autosomal recessive condition has a child with a man who is heterozygous (Aa). What is the probability that the child is affected?
Aa × aa gives 1 Aa : 1 aa, so half the children are aa and affected. The 1/4 answer comes from the Aa × Aa cross, which does not apply because the mother is aa.
bio12a3-ped-12
A woman who is heterozygous for an X-linked dominant condition (XᴰXᵈ) has children with an unaffected man (XᵈY). What proportion of their sons will be affected?

Sons inherit their X from their mother, who passes Xᴰ with probability 1/2, so half of sons are affected. The answer 1 wrongly assumes every son receives the dominant allele, and 0 would only apply if the mother had no dominant allele.
bio12a3-ped-13
Which pattern in a pedigree is characteristic of Y-linked inheritance?
Affected fathers pass the trait to all their sons and none of their daughters
Affected fathers pass the trait to half of their sons
Affected mothers pass the trait to all of their children
Affected individuals appear equally in both sexes

The Y chromosome passes only from father to son, so every son of an affected father is affected and no daughter is. The half-of-sons pattern describes an autosomal dominant trait with a heterozygous father, which is a common mix-up.
bio12a3-ped-14
Two affected parents have an unaffected child for an autosomal dominant trait. What must be true of both parents?
Both parents must be DD
Both parents must be Dd
One parent must be DD and the other dd
Both parents must be dd

The unaffected child is dd, so each parent must have given a d allele. Both parents are affected, so each must also carry a D, which means both are Dd. A DD parent could not give a d allele, and a dd parent would be unaffected.
bio12a3-ped-15
In a pedigree, what does a horizontal double line joining two partners indicate?
Identical twins
Adoption
Consanguineous mating, where the parents are related
A pregnancy that ended in miscarriage

A double line between partners shows consanguineous mating, meaning they are related, which increases the chance of a recessive trait. Twins are drawn as lines rising from a shared point, not as a double line between partners.
bio12a3-ped-16
A woman who is a carrier of an X-linked recessive condition (XᴬXᵃ) has children with a man with normal vision (XᴬY). What is the probability that a daughter is affected?

Daughters receive one X from their normal father, so they cannot receive two recessive alleles and cannot be affected. The 1/4 answer applies the autosomal Aa × Aa ratio, which does not apply to sex-linked genes.
bio12a3-ped-17
A boy has an X-linked recessive condition. His mother does not have the condition. What is her genotype?
XᵃXᵃ
XᴬXᴬ
XᴬXᵃ
XᵃY
The affected son must have received Xᵃ from his mother, and an unaffected mother has a dominant Xᴬ, so she is XᴬXᵃ. XᵃXᵃ would be affected, XᴬXᴬ could not pass on Xᵃ, and XᵃY is male.
bio12a3-ped-18
A trait is far more common in males than in females. An affected father never has an affected son, and his daughters are unaffected but carry the allele. Which mode of inheritance fits?
X-linked dominant
Autosomal dominant
Y-linked
X-linked recessive

An affected father passes his X to all daughters, who are unaffected carriers, and his Y to all sons, who are unaffected, which fits the male bias of X-linked recessive inheritance. X-linked dominant would show affected daughters, Y-linked would show affected sons, and autosomal dominant would give affected children of both sexes.
bio12a3-ped-19
Phenylketonuria is autosomal recessive. Both parents are carriers. What is the probability that their first two children are both affected?

Each child has a 1/4 chance of being affected and the births are independent, so the chance that both are affected is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Using 1/4 alone ignores the second child, and 1/8 has no basis in this cross.
bio12a3-ped-20
A man with haemophilia (XʰY) and a woman with no alleles for haemophilia (XᴴXᴴ) have a daughter. What is the probability that she is a carrier?
The daughter receives her father's Xʰ with certainty and her mother's Xᴴ, so she is a carrier. The 1/2 answer treats the daughter like a son, who inherits his X from the mother alone.
bio12a3-ped-21
In a pedigree for an autosomal recessive trait, individual II-3 is unaffected but has an affected child. What can be concluded about II-3's genotype?
Homozygous dominant
Heterozygous
Homozygous recessive
It cannot be determined from the pedigree

The affected child is aa and must receive an a allele from II-3, who is unaffected and so must be Aa. A homozygous dominant parent cannot pass on a, and a homozygous recessive parent would be affected, so the pedigree does determine the genotype.
bio12a3-ped-22
Define the term carrier as used for a recessive condition. (1 mark)
A carrier is a person who is heterozygous for the recessive allele, so is unaffected but can pass the allele to their offspring [1].
bio12a3-ped-23
Explain how an X-linked recessive trait can skip a generation, using a grandfather, his daughter and his grandson in your answer. (3 marks)

The affected grandfather (XᵃY) passes Xᵃ to his daughter, who is an unaffected carrier (XᴬXᵃ) [1]; the dominant Xᴬ masks the recessive allele, so she does not show the trait and the generation is skipped [1]; her son receives Xᵃ with probability 1/2 and is affected, so the trait reappears in the next generation [1].
bio12a3-ped-24

A man with an X-linked dominant condition (XᴰY) marries an unaffected woman (XᵈXᵈ). Calculate the probability that a son and a daughter of this couple are affected, and explain your reasoning. (3 marks)

Sons: probability 0, because sons receive Y from their father and Xᵈ from their unaffected mother [1]; daughters: probability 1, because every daughter receives Xᴰ from her affected father [1]; daughters are affected even though they are heterozygous (XᴰXᵈ), because the allele is dominant [1].
bio12a3-ped-25

In a family pedigree for an autosomal recessive trait, an affected man (I-1) and an unaffected woman (I-2) have an unaffected son (II-1) and an affected daughter (II-2). II-1 has children with an unaffected woman who is a known carrier. (a) State the genotypes of I-2 and II-1, using A and a. (b) State the probability that their first child is affected, and explain your answer. (4 marks)

(a) I-2 is Aa, because she must have given the recessive allele to the affected daughter II-2 [1]; II-1 is Aa, because he received a from his affected father and is unaffected [1]; (b) the probability is 1/4 (25%) [1], because Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa and only aa children are affected [1].
bio12a3-ped-26
Explain why an affected female with an X-linked recessive condition must have an affected father. (2 marks)
She needs two copies of the recessive allele, so she must receive Xᵃ from her father as well as from her mother [1]; a father has only one X chromosome, so he must carry Xᵃ and be affected (XᵃY) [1].
bio12a3-ped-27
Explain why a child of first cousins is at greater risk of an autosomal recessive condition than a child of unrelated parents. (2 marks)
Related parents are more likely to carry the same recessive allele, inherited from a common ancestor [1]; so the child is more likely to inherit two copies of that allele and show the condition [1].
bio12a3-ped-28
An affected man has an unaffected daughter. Explain whether this pedigree rules out X-linked dominant inheritance. (2 marks)
Yes, it rules out X-linked dominant inheritance [1]; an affected father with X-linked dominant inheritance passes the dominant allele to all his daughters, who would all be affected [1].
vce-bio12-pd-c1
Which pedigree observation rules out X-linked recessive inheritance?
More males than females are affected
An affected man has an unaffected son
An affected mother has an unaffected son
Two unaffected parents have an affected son
An affected mother (XᵃXᵃ) must pass Xᵃ to every son, so all her sons would be affected.
vce-bio12-asexual-reproduction: bio12a3-asex-1
Which of the following is an example of vegetative propagation in plants?
A wattle producing seeds after pollination by birds
Strawberry plants producing new plants from runners
A fern releasing spores formed by meiosis
Pollen tubes growing down the style of a flower

Runners (stolons) grow out from the parent strawberry plant and form new, genetically identical plants by mitosis. That is vegetative propagation. Seed production after pollination is sexual reproduction.
bio12a3-asex-2
Yeast cells commonly reproduce by forming a small outgrowth that pinches off from the parent cell. This form of asexual reproduction is called
binary fission
budding
fragmentation
sporogenesis

Budding produces a smaller outgrowth that gets a copy of the nucleus by mitosis and then separates. In binary fission (e.g. bacteria) a cell divides into two cells of roughly equal size. Fragmentation means a body breaks into pieces that each regrow.
bio12a3-asex-3
Some female Komodo dragons in zoos have produced offspring without mating, by parthenogenesis. Which statement about parthenogenesis is correct?
It involves fertilisation of an egg by sperm stored from a previous mating
An unfertilised egg develops into a new individual
It only occurs in bacteria and archaea
It always produces offspring identical to the father

Parthenogenesis is when an unfertilised egg develops into an embryo. It happens in some insects, reptiles, fish and others. No sperm is involved, so stored sperm is not the explanation, and there is no father.
bio12a3-asex-4
A farmer grows a field of genetically identical banana plants propagated from suckers. Which is the greatest risk of this practice?
The plants will take longer to reach maturity than seedlings
A single new disease could infect and kill the whole crop because there is little genetic variation
The plants will produce offspring with many new mutations
The plants will be unable to photosynthesise efficiently

Asexually propagated plants are clones. If one is susceptible to a pathogen, they all are, so the whole population is vulnerable (as seen with Panama disease in bananas). Asexual propagation usually gets plants to maturity faster, not slower.
bio12a3-asex-5
Which statement correctly compares asexual reproduction with sexual reproduction?
Asexual reproduction needs two parents and produces variable offspring
Asexual reproduction allows rapid population growth in a stable environment because every individual can produce offspring
Asexual reproduction involves meiosis and fertilisation
Asexual reproduction produces greater genetic diversity than sexual reproduction

Asexual reproduction needs only one parent, there is no need to find a mate, and every individual can reproduce. Populations can therefore grow quickly, which suits stable conditions. It uses mitosis (or binary fission), not meiosis and fertilisation, and gives little genetic diversity.
bio12a3-asex-6
Describe binary fission in a bacterium and explain why the daughter cells are usually genetically identical. (3 marks)

The circular chromosome is replicated and the two copies attach to the plasma membrane; the cell elongates, separating the copies, and the membrane and cell wall pinch in across the middle to form two daughter cells; each daughter receives an identical copy of the replicated DNA, so they are genetically identical unless a mutation occurred during replication.
bio12a3-asex-7
Give two advantages and two disadvantages of asexual reproduction for a population of organisms. (4 marks)

Advantages: no mate is needed so isolated individuals can reproduce; reproduction is fast and energy-efficient, allowing rapid population growth; (also accept: successful genotypes are passed on unchanged). Disadvantages: offspring have little genetic variation, so the population may not survive a change in the environment or a new disease; harmful mutations can build up in the lineage; offspring may compete closely with the parent for resources.
bio12a3-asex-8
Aphids can reproduce asexually in spring and summer and then switch to sexual reproduction in autumn. Suggest an explanation for why this strategy is advantageous. (2 marks)

In spring and summer food is plentiful and conditions are stable, so asexual reproduction allows rapid population growth to exploit resources; in autumn conditions change and become harsher, so sexual reproduction produces genetically diverse offspring (and overwintering eggs), increasing the chance some will survive the changed conditions.
bio12a3-asex-9
A planarian flatworm is cut into several pieces, and each piece regenerates into a complete worm. Most of the new cells needed for regeneration are produced by which process?
Meiosis of gametes released from the wound
Binary fission of the differentiated cells at the cut surface
Mitosis of stem cells (neoblasts) that replace the missing tissues
Fertilisation between cells from different pieces

Planarians have stem cells called neoblasts that divide by mitosis to replace missing tissues, producing genetically identical cells. Meiosis makes gametes, which do not regenerate body tissue, and fertilisation needs two gametes, so neither is involved. Binary fission is a reproductive process of single-celled organisms, not a way for specialised cells in a worm to divide.
bio12a3-asex-10
Ginger plants are propagated by planting pieces of an underground structure that grows horizontally, has nodes, and produces new shoots and roots. What is this structure?
A taproot
A rhizome
A seed
A fruit

A rhizome is a horizontal underground stem with nodes that produce new shoots and roots, so each piece can grow into a genetically identical plant. A taproot is a root rather than a stem and does not normally produce new plants, while seeds and fruits are products of sexual reproduction.
bio12a3-asex-11
Bread mould (Rhizopus) produces spores inside sporangia at the tips of its aerial hyphae. These spores are produced asexually. Which statement about them is correct?
They are formed by meiosis, so each spore is genetically different from the parent
They are formed by binary fission, so each spore has half the parent's genetic material
They are formed by fertilisation of two hyphae, so they are genetically varied
They are formed by mitosis, so they are genetically identical to the parent

Asexual spores of Rhizopus are produced by mitosis, so they are clones of the parent mycelium. Meiosis and fertilisation are sexual processes that produce variation, and binary fission is a method used by bacteria, not moulds.
bio12a3-asex-12
Which of the following is NOT an example of asexual reproduction?
Sunflower seed formation after cross-pollination by bees
Tuber formation in a potato plant
Binary fission in a bacterium
Root suckers forming from the roots of a poplar tree

Sunflower seeds form when pollen fertilises an ovule, which involves the fusion of gametes from two sources, so this is sexual reproduction. Tubers, binary fission and root suckers each produce new individuals from one parent without the fusion of gametes.
bio12a3-asex-13
Which crop is most commonly propagated by planting sections of stem, rather than from seed?
Wheat
Maize
Sugarcane
Rice

Sugarcane is propagated from stem sections (setts) that each carry buds, and these grow into genetically identical plants. Wheat, maize and rice are normally grown from seed, which comes from sexual reproduction and is genetically varied.
bio12a3-asex-14
A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Starting with one cell, how many cells are present after 2 hours, assuming no cells die?

Two hours is 120 minutes, which gives 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. Each division doubles the cell number, so 2⁶ = 64 cells; answers of 6 or 12 wrongly treat the number of cells as increasing by a fixed amount, and 32 comes from miscounting the divisions as five.
bio12a3-asex-15
A somatic (body cell) mutation occurs in one bud of a tree. The branch grown from that bud carries the mutation, but the rest of the tree does not. Which best explains this?
The mutation was in a cell whose mitotic descendants form only that branch, so the other parts of the tree did not inherit it
Meiosis in the bud produced gametes carrying the mutation, which then spread to other branches
The mutation was caused by pollen from another tree fertilising the bud
The branch has a different number of chromosomes from the rest of the tree

A mutation in a body cell is passed only to the cells that arise from that cell by mitosis, so only that branch shows it. Meiosis produces gametes rather than branches, and pollen cannot change the genes of the other branches, while the chromosome number is normally the same throughout the body.
bio12a3-asex-16
In honeybees, drones (males) develop from unfertilised eggs, while workers (females) develop from fertilised eggs. Which statement about drones is correct?
They are diploid, with the same chromosome number as the queen
They have a father, because they develop from a fertilised egg as workers do
They have two fathers, because they inherit genes from two separate eggs
They are haploid, with half the chromosome number of the females

Drones develop from unfertilised eggs, so they have only one set of chromosomes and no father. Being diploid would require a fertilised egg, which is how workers develop, so the diploid option describes the wrong bee.
bio12a3-asex-17
In somatic cell nuclear transfer, a cell from an adult animal's body is used to create a clone. Before the donor nucleus is inserted into an egg cell, what is removed from the egg?
Its mitochondria
Its cytoplasm
Its own nucleus
Its cell membrane

The egg's own nucleus is removed so that the donor nucleus supplies all the nuclear DNA, while the egg's cytoplasm is kept to support development. The mitochondria and cell membrane are not removed in this process.
bio12a3-asex-18
A grafted apple tree is made by joining a shoot (scion) of one apple cultivar onto the root system (rootstock) of another. Which statement is correct?
The scion grows from cells produced by mitosis, so it is genetically identical to the donor cultivar, while the rootstock keeps its own genotype
The grafted tree is a hybrid, because the scion and rootstock fuse their genetic material through fertilisation
Seeds from the grafted tree's apples will be genetically identical to the scion cultivar
Grafting is a form of sexual reproduction, because the two plants combine their gametes

Grafting is asexual: the scion is a clone of its donor because it grows by mitosis, and the rootstock keeps its own genotype. Seeds inside the apples are produced sexually and vary genetically, and no fertilisation occurs between scion and rootstock.
bio12a3-asex-19
A hydra reproduces asexually by budding. A bud forms as a small outgrowth on the body wall. What is the genetic makeup of the bud compared with the parent hydra?
It is genetically different, because the bud is formed by meiosis
It is genetically identical, because its cells are produced by mitosis from the parent's cells
It has half the genes of the parent and half of a second hydra
It is identical only in its tentacles, because the rest is formed by fertilisation

The bud grows from repeated mitosis of the parent's body cells, so it is a clone of the parent. Meiosis and fertilisation are not involved, so the bud cannot be genetically different or contain genes from a second hydra.
bio12a3-asex-20
Which organism reproduces asexually by fragmentation, where a piece of its body breaks off and grows into a new individual?
Escherichia coli
Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast)
A wheat plant
Spirogyra, a filamentous green alga

Spirogyra filaments break into pieces, and each piece grows into a new filament, so fragmentation is its asexual method. Escherichia coli divides by binary fission, yeast reproduces by budding, and wheat is propagated from seed.
bio12a3-asex-21
A diploid plant has 14 chromosomes in each body cell. It reproduces asexually, and its offspring cells are formed by mitosis from body cells. How many chromosomes does each offspring cell have?

Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell, so each offspring cell keeps 14. Seven is the haploid number produced by meiosis in gametes, and 28 would require the chromosome number to double, as when two gametes fuse.
bio12a3-asex-22
Describe the steps of micropropagation (tissue culture) of an orchid from a small piece of tissue, and explain why the plantlets produced are genetically identical. (3 marks)

A small piece of plant tissue (explant) is removed and placed on sterile nutrient medium containing plant hormones [1]; its cells divide by mitosis to form a mass of undifferentiated cells, which is then induced to form shoots and roots, producing plantlets [1]; the cells are produced by mitosis with no meiosis or fertilisation, so each plantlet has the same genotype as the parent plant [1].
bio12a3-asex-23
Define the term clone as it is used in asexual reproduction. (1 mark)
A group of genetically identical individuals produced asexually from one parent, by mitosis [1].
bio12a3-asex-24
Potatoes are often propagated by planting pieces of tuber, each with at least one eye (bud). Explain why the resulting plants are genetically identical to the parent plant. (3 marks)

Each eye contains a bud from which shoots grow, and the cells of the shoots are produced by mitosis from the parent's own cells [1]; no meiosis or fertilisation is involved, so no new combination of alleles is formed [1]; the new plants have the same genotype as the parent tuber, so they keep its desirable traits [1].
bio12a3-asex-25

Explain why mutation is the only source of new genetic variation in a population of asexually reproducing organisms, and describe how a beneficial mutation can become common in such a population. (4 marks)

Asexual reproduction involves no meiosis or fertilisation, so no new combinations of existing alleles are produced [1]; new alleles can arise only from mutations, which occur during DNA replication [1]; a beneficial mutation in one cell is passed to all of its clone offspring by mitosis [1]; if it improves survival or reproduction, natural selection causes the clone lineage carrying it to increase in frequency in the population [1].
bio12a3-asex-26

Kalanchoe daigremontiana produces small plantlets along the margins of its leaves. Each plantlet falls to the ground and roots. Describe how these plantlets form, and explain why they are genetically identical to the parent plant. (3 marks)

Buds form at the leaf margin, and their cells divide by mitosis to produce a small plant with roots and shoots [1]; the plantlet develops from the parent's own body cells, with no meiosis or fertilisation [1]; so it has the same genotype as the parent and is a clone [1].
bio12a3-asex-27
Liverworts produce small clusters of cells called gemmae in cup-shaped structures on the plant body. Explain why the production of gemmae is an example of asexual reproduction. (2 marks)
Gemmae are formed by mitosis in the parent plant, so no meiosis or fertilisation is involved [1]; each gemma grows into a new plant that is genetically identical to the single parent [1].
bio12a3-asex-28
State one advantage and one disadvantage of using tissue culture, rather than seed, to propagate a rare plant variety with desirable traits. (2 marks)

Advantage: many genetically identical plants can be produced quickly from a small amount of tissue, keeping the desirable traits of the variety [1]; disadvantage: the plants have little genetic variation, so the whole group is at risk from a new disease or environmental change [1].
bio12a3-asex-29
Define the term vegetative propagation. (1 mark)
Asexual reproduction in plants in which a new plant grows from a non-reproductive part of the parent, such as a stem, root or leaf [1].
bio12a3-asex-30
Sponges can reproduce asexually when a fragment breaks away from the parent. Describe how the fragment develops into a new sponge, and state its genetic relationship to the parent. (2 marks)

Cells in the fragment divide by mitosis and reorganise to form the body structures of a complete sponge [1]; the new sponge is genetically identical to the parent because no meiosis or fertilisation occurred [1].
vce-bio12-as-c1
Strawberry plants reproduce both by runners (asexually) and by seeds (sexually). The main advantage of having both is that:
Runners create variation in a good area, while seeds produce clones that spread further
Runners quickly colonise a good area with clones, while seeds produce variation and spread further
Both methods produce identical offspring, so the plant has two ways to make clones
Seeds need no pollination, so both methods avoid the need for another plant
Asexual reproduction is fast and needs no mate; sexual reproduction gives genetic diversity, helping populations survive change.
vce-bio12-sexual-reproduction-and-geneti: bio12a3-sex-1
During which stage of meiosis does crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes occur?
Prophase I
Metaphase I
Anaphase II
Telophase II

Homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) in prophase I, and crossing over swaps segments between non-sister chromatids at chiasmata. Metaphase I is when independent assortment happens, as homologous pairs line up in random orientation.
bio12a3-sex-2
A species has a diploid number of 2n = 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can be produced by independent assortment alone?
The number of combinations is 2ⁿ, where n is the haploid number. Here n = 4, so 2⁴ = 16. Using 2n = 8 as the exponent would give 2⁸ = 256, which is wrong.
bio12a3-sex-3
Which event results in homologous chromosomes separating?
Anaphase of mitosis
Anaphase I of meiosis
Anaphase II of meiosis
Cytokinesis after telophase II
In anaphase I the homologous chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles, which halves the chromosome number. In anaphase II and in mitotic anaphase, it is the sister chromatids that separate.
bio12a3-sex-4
Non-disjunction during meiosis I in a human produces gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers. If one of these gametes with 24 chromosomes is fertilised by a normal gamete, the zygote will have
46 chromosomes
47 chromosomes (a trisomy)
45 chromosomes (a monosomy)
69 chromosomes (triploidy)

A normal human gamete has 23 chromosomes. A gamete with 24 fused with a normal gamete gives 24 + 23 = 47 chromosomes, which is a trisomy (e.g. trisomy 21). A gamete with 22 chromosomes would give a monosomy with 45.
bio12a3-sex-5
Which list contains only sources of genetic variation produced by sexual reproduction?
Crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation
Binary fission, crossing over, budding
Mitosis, random fertilisation, independent assortment
Cytokinesis, crossing over, DNA replication

Crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment (metaphase I) and the random fusion of gametes at fertilisation all add genetic variation in sexual reproduction. Mitosis, binary fission and budding produce genetically identical cells.
bio12a3-sex-6
Explain how crossing over and independent assortment each increase genetic variation in gametes. (4 marks)

Crossing over: during prophase I homologous chromosomes pair and non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata; this produces recombinant chromatids with new combinations of alleles on the same chromosome. Independent assortment: during metaphase I each homologous pair lines up at the equator in a random orientation independent of other pairs; so maternal and paternal chromosomes are distributed to gametes in many different combinations (2ⁿ).
bio12a3-sex-7
Explain why genetic diversity within a population is important for its long-term survival. Use an Australian example in your answer. (3 marks)

Genetic diversity means individuals carry different alleles, so some are more likely to have traits that let them survive a new selection pressure such as disease or climate change; these individuals survive and reproduce so the population persists; for example the Tasmanian devil has very low genetic diversity, which has made it highly vulnerable to devil facial tumour disease, which spreads between devils because their immune systems do not recognise the tumour cells as foreign.
bio12a3-sex-8
Compare meiosis I and meiosis II in terms of what separates and the ploidy of the cells produced. (3 marks)

In meiosis I homologous chromosomes separate, so the two cells produced are haploid (n) although each chromosome still has two chromatids; in meiosis II sister chromatids separate, like mitosis; this produces four haploid cells, each chromosome with a single chromatid, and the ploidy does not change in meiosis II.
bio12a3-sex-9
What are the chromosome numbers of a human sperm cell and a human body (somatic) cell?
23 and 46
46 and 23
23 and 23
46 and 92
A human sperm is haploid with n = 23, and a body cell is diploid with 2n = 46. Reversing the two numbers is a common mix-up, and the option ending in 92 has no basis in the normal human life cycle.
bio12a3-sex-10
A body cell of an organism with 2n = 6 divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell contain?

Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell, so each has 6 chromosomes. The answer 3 confuses mitosis with meiosis, and 12 wrongly assumes the chromosome number doubles.
bio12a3-sex-11
Bacteria reproduce by binary fission. Which statement about the offspring is correct?
They are genetically different from the parent because of crossing over
They have half the number of chromosomes of the parent
They are genetically identical to the parent, apart from any new mutations
They are produced only after fertilisation between two bacteria

Binary fission is asexual: one parent copies its DNA and divides, so the offspring are clones apart from rare mutations. Crossing over and fertilisation are features of sexual reproduction, so they do not apply to binary fission.
bio12a3-sex-12
Two parents each have 2n = 6. Ignoring crossing over, how many different zygotes can be formed when their gametes fuse at random?

Each parent produces 2³ = 8 different gametes, so 8 × 8 = 64 different zygotes are possible. The answer 8 counts only one parent's gametes, and 16 comes from adding the two parents' numbers instead of multiplying them.
bio12a3-sex-13
Which statement correctly compares oogenesis and spermatogenesis?
One primary oocyte forms one functional ovum and polar bodies, while one primary spermatocyte forms four functional sperm
Both processes produce four equal-sized functional gametes from one precursor cell
Oogenesis produces four functional ova, while spermatogenesis produces only one sperm
Polar bodies are a normal product of spermatogenesis, making each sperm smaller

In oogenesis the cytoplasm divides unequally, so one large functional ovum forms and the polar bodies are small and degenerate. Spermatogenesis divides the cytoplasm equally to produce four functional sperm, so the claim that oogenesis yields four ova reverses the fact.
bio12a3-sex-14
Which process is the ultimate source of new alleles in a population?
Crossing over
Mutation
Independent assortment
Random fertilisation
Mutations change the DNA sequence of a gene and so create new alleles. Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation only reshuffle alleles that already exist into new combinations.
bio12a3-sex-15
Cavendish bananas are propagated from suckers, so almost all plants in a plantation are genetically identical. What is the main risk to the crop?
A pathogen that infects one plant can spread to nearly all of them, destroying much of the crop
Crossing over will produce new alleles each season, making the crop unpredictable
Each plant will produce gametes with half the normal chromosome number, reducing fruit yield
Random fertilisation will produce zygotes with too many chromosomes

With almost no genetic variation, few or no plants are likely to carry resistance to a new pathogen, so one disease can spread through the whole plantation. The other options describe meiosis and fertilisation, which do not occur when a crop is propagated from suckers.
bio12a3-sex-16
A gamete with 12 chromosomes fuses with another gamete with 12 chromosomes. What are the chromosome number and ploidy of the zygote?
12, haploid
6, haploid
24, haploid
24, diploid

Fusion of two haploid gametes restores the diploid condition, so the zygote has 12 + 12 = 24 chromosomes and is diploid. The other options either halve the number instead of adding the two sets, or give the wrong ploidy.
bio12a3-sex-17
What is a pair of sister chromatids?
Two identical copies of one chromosome, joined at the centromere, formed by DNA replication
Two homologous chromosomes, one inherited from each parent
The two cells produced at the end of meiosis I
The two sex chromosomes in a human male

DNA replication in interphase copies each chromosome, and the two copies stay joined at the centromere until anaphase. Homologous chromosomes are a different pair, one from each parent, and the two cells formed at the end of meiosis I are daughter cells, not chromatids.
bio12a3-sex-18
What is genetic diversity within a population?
The total number of individuals in the population
The variety of alleles present among the individuals of the population
The number of different species living in the same habitat
The number of chromosomes in each cell of the population members

Genetic diversity is the range of alleles present across the individuals in a population, and a large population alone does not guarantee it. Every member of one species normally has the same chromosome number, so that option cannot describe diversity.
bio12a3-sex-19
A human male has 47 chromosomes with an XXY karyotype (Klinefelter syndrome). What is the most likely cause?
Crossing over between the X and Y chromosomes during mitosis
A mutation in the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote
Non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes during meiosis in one parent, producing a gamete with two sex chromosomes
Failure of DNA replication in the egg before fertilisation

Non-disjunction during meiosis in one parent produces a gamete with two sex chromosomes, which gives 47 chromosomes after fertilisation by a normal gamete. Crossing over does not occur in mitosis, and mitochondrial mutations do not change the number of nuclear chromosomes.
bio12a3-sex-20
A cell from an organism with 2n = 4 undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes does each resulting cell contain?
Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so each of the four haploid cells contains 2 chromosomes. The answer 4 is the diploid number of the parent cell, while 8 wrongly assumes the number doubles.
bio12a3-sex-21
A female mammal has 40 chromosomes in each somatic cell. How many chromosomes does a polar body formed during oogenesis contain?
Oogenesis is a meiotic process, so polar bodies are haploid and contain 20 chromosomes. The answer 40 is the somatic number, while 10 wrongly halves the number twice.
bio12a3-sex-22
Describe what happens at fertilisation and explain why it is needed to maintain the chromosome number of a species. (2 marks)
A haploid sperm nucleus fuses with a haploid ovum nucleus to form a diploid zygote [1]; this restores the diploid chromosome number that meiosis halved, so each generation keeps the same number [1].
bio12a3-sex-23
Explain how non-disjunction in meiosis II differs from non-disjunction in meiosis I in the gametes it produces. (3 marks)

Meiosis II non-disjunction: sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate in anaphase II, so two of the four gametes are normal and two are abnormal, one with an extra chromosome and one missing a chromosome [1]; meiosis I non-disjunction: a homologous pair fails to separate in anaphase I, so all four gametes are abnormal, two with an extra chromosome and two missing one [1]; so meiosis II non-disjunction produces a mix of normal and abnormal gametes, whereas meiosis I non-disjunction makes every gamete abnormal [1].
bio12a3-sex-24
Explain why a mutation in a gamete is more likely to affect future generations than a mutation in a body cell. (2 marks)

Gametes are the cells that fuse to form a zygote, so a mutation in a gamete's DNA can be passed on to the offspring [1]; mutations in body (somatic) cells are not inherited by offspring, so their effects are limited to that individual [1].
bio12a3-sex-25
Compare mitosis and meiosis in a diploid cell with respect to the number of divisions, the number and ploidy of the daughter cells, and the genetic identity of the daughter cells. (4 marks)

Mitosis has one division whereas meiosis has two divisions [1]; mitosis produces two daughter cells and meiosis produces four daughter cells [1]; mitosis daughter cells are diploid and meiosis daughter cells are haploid [1]; mitosis daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell, whereas meiosis daughter cells are genetically different from each other and from the parent [1].
bio12a3-sex-26
Explain how the random union of gametes at fertilisation contributes to genetic variation in offspring. Use the number of possible gamete combinations in your answer. (3 marks)

Any gamete from one parent can fuse with any gamete from the other, so each zygote combines a random gamete from each parent [1]; each gamete carries a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes from independent assortment, so each parent produces 2ⁿ different gametes [1]; the number of possible zygotes is therefore (2ⁿ) × (2ⁿ), a very large number of different combinations [1].
bio12a3-sex-27
State the number of chromatids that each chromosome contains at the start of anaphase I. (1 mark)
Two sister chromatids, joined at the centromere [1].
bio12a3-sex-28
Describe how the sex chromosomes determine the sex of a human offspring. (2 marks)

Females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY) [1]; each ovum carries an X chromosome, and the sex of the offspring depends on whether the sperm that fertilises it carries an X (female) or a Y (male) [1].
vce-bio12-sr2-c1
Which process does NOT increase genetic variation among offspring?
Mitosis
Crossing over
Independent assortment
Random fertilisation
Mitosis produces genetically identical cells. The other three occur in sexual reproduction.
vce-bio12-reproductive-cloning: bio12a3-clone-1
In somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), the nucleus from a somatic cell of the animal to be cloned is inserted into
a sperm cell from a male of the same species
an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed (enucleated)
a fertilised zygote that still contains its own nucleus
a stem cell taken from bone marrow

In SCNT the donor nucleus goes into an enucleated egg cell. The egg is then stimulated (e.g. by an electric pulse) to start dividing. The nucleus has to be removed first so that the clone's nuclear DNA comes only from the donor.
bio12a3-clone-2

Dolly the sheep was produced by SCNT using a nucleus from a Finn Dorset ewe's udder cell, an egg from a Scottish Blackface ewe, and a Scottish Blackface surrogate mother. Dolly's nuclear DNA was identical to that of
the egg donor
the surrogate mother
the Finn Dorset nucleus donor
a combination of all three sheep

The nucleus carries almost all the genes, so Dolly's nuclear DNA matched the Finn Dorset donor, and she looked like a Finn Dorset. Her mitochondrial DNA came from the egg donor's cytoplasm. The surrogate mother only provided the uterus.
bio12a3-clone-3
Embryo splitting involves separating cells from an early embryo to produce several embryos that are implanted into surrogates. The offspring produced are
genetically identical to the surrogate mothers
genetically identical to each other but not identical to either parent
genetically identical to the father only
all genetically different from each other

The embryo started from fertilisation, so it has a new combination of alleles from both parents. The split embryos all come from that one zygote, so they are identical to each other (like identical twins) but not to either parent.
bio12a3-clone-4
Plant tissue culture (micropropagation) is used to produce large numbers of a rare orchid. Which statement is correct?
The plantlets will show high genetic diversity because they form from many different cells
Small pieces of tissue are grown on sterile nutrient media with plant hormones to form genetically identical plantlets
The technique requires pollination and seed formation
The plantlets are haploid because they come from meristem cells

In tissue culture, explants (often meristem tissue) are grown on sterile media with nutrients and plant hormones such as auxins and cytokinins. The resulting plantlets come from mitosis, so they are clones of the parent plant. No pollination is involved, and meristem cells are diploid.
bio12a3-clone-5
Which is the most significant biological concern about using reproductive cloning to conserve an endangered species?
Cloned animals cannot reproduce sexually
Cloning adds no new genetic diversity to a population that already has little
Cloned animals always have shorter lifespans than the donor
Cloning changes the species' chromosome number

Clones copy existing genotypes, so they do not raise the low genetic diversity that endangered populations usually suffer from. Cloned animals can generally reproduce, and not all clones have shortened lifespans.
bio12a3-clone-6
Outline the steps of somatic cell nuclear transfer to produce a cloned cow. (4 marks)

A somatic (body) cell is taken from the cow to be cloned and its nucleus extracted; an egg cell is taken from a donor cow and its nucleus removed (enucleated); the donor nucleus is inserted into (or the somatic cell fused with) the enucleated egg and an electric pulse or chemicals stimulate it to divide; the resulting embryo is grown in culture to an early embryo and implanted into the uterus of a surrogate cow, which gives birth to a calf genetically identical (in nuclear DNA) to the somatic cell donor.
bio12a3-clone-7
A cloned cat was found to have a different coat pattern from the cat that donated the nucleus. Suggest two reasons why a clone may not look exactly like its nuclear donor. (2 marks)

Gene expression is affected by the environment and by random events in development (e.g. X-chromosome inactivation in female cats determines coat patches), so the same genotype can give a different phenotype; the clone also has mitochondrial DNA from the egg donor and develops in a different uterine environment from the donor.
bio12a3-clone-8
Evaluate the use of reproductive cloning in agriculture, giving one benefit and one risk. (2 marks)

Benefit: animals or plants with desirable traits (e.g. high milk yield, disease resistance) can be copied exactly and quickly; risk: herds or crops of clones have low genetic diversity, so a single disease or environmental change could devastate them (also accept low success rates and health problems in cloned animals, or ethical concerns about animal welfare).
bio12a3-clone-9
In somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), the mitochondrial DNA of the cloned embryo comes from which source?
the somatic cell donor, because mitochondria are found in the nucleus
the surrogate mother's uterus
the cytoplasm of the egg donor, which is not removed when the egg nucleus is removed
the sperm donor, because fertilisation takes place

Mitochondria sit in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus, so they stay in the egg when its nucleus is removed. The clone's nuclear DNA matches the body cell donor, but its mitochondrial DNA does not. The surrogate and any sperm donor contribute no genetic material in SCNT.
bio12a3-clone-10
After a donor nucleus is placed in an enucleated egg, the reconstructed cell is given an electric pulse or chemicals. What is the purpose of this step?
to activate the reconstructed egg so that it starts dividing as an embryo
to remove the donor nucleus from the egg
to cause meiosis so that the chromosome number is halved
to fuse the egg with a sperm cell so that it is fertilised

The pulse or chemicals mimic fertilisation and trigger the cell to divide and form an embryo. SCNT uses no sperm, so fertilising the egg would give a mixed-parent embryo, and meiosis would halve the donor's chromosome number.
bio12a3-clone-11
In SCNT, the donor nucleus must be reprogrammed. What does this mean?
the donor DNA is permanently mutated to match the egg's DNA
the donor nucleus is replaced by a sperm nucleus
the donor cell's chromosomes are halved by meiosis before transfer
the egg cytoplasm switches on genes that were silenced during differentiation, so the nucleus can direct development of a whole organism

A nucleus from a specialised cell has most of its genes switched off, and reprogramming switches the needed ones back on. Reprogramming changes which genes are active, not the DNA sequence itself, so the mutation option is wrong.
bio12a3-clone-12
Which statement correctly compares embryo splitting with somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT)?
both produce offspring that are genetically identical to the parent that donated the nucleus
embryo splitting produces offspring that are identical to each other, whereas SCNT produces offspring with the nuclear DNA of the body cell donor
embryo splitting requires an enucleated egg, whereas SCNT does not
both produce offspring that are genetically identical to the surrogate mother

Embryo splitting divides the cells of one early embryo, so the offspring match each other but not either parent. SCNT copies the nuclear DNA of a single adult body cell. The option saying both copy a parent is wrong, because embryo splitting begins with fertilisation.
bio12a3-clone-13
Which plant tissue is most often used as the explant in micropropagation, and why?
meristem tissue, because its cells divide actively and are often free of viruses
mature xylem, because it is fully differentiated and stable
pollen grains, because they are haploid and easy to sterilise
root hairs, because they live for a long time

Meristem cells are actively dividing, undifferentiated cells, and the growing tip is often virus-free. Mature xylem cells are dead and cannot divide to form new plants. Plants grown from haploid pollen would not be clones of the parent.
bio12a3-clone-14
In plant tissue culture, a medium with a high cytokinin to auxin ratio tends to promote which outcome?
root formation
shoot formation
seed formation
leaf abscission

A high cytokinin to auxin ratio favours shoot growth, while a high auxin to cytokinin ratio favours root formation. Root formation is the result of the opposite ratio, which makes it a tempting mistake.
bio12a3-clone-15
Most attempts at SCNT fail or produce abnormal embryos. What is the most likely biological reason?
the donor nucleus is too large to fit inside the egg cell
the surrogate's immune system destroys every embryo on contact
all the donor cell's chromosomes carry faulty alleles from the egg
the donor nucleus is not fully reprogrammed, so development is abnormal or stops early

Many transferred nuclei do not switch on the full set of genes needed for normal development, which is a main reason for the low success rate of SCNT. A nucleus is small enough to fit in the egg, and the enucleated egg supplies no chromosomes that could add faulty alleles.
bio12a3-clone-16
A bull is cloned by SCNT, using a body cell from the bull and an enucleated egg from a different cow. Which statement about the sex of the clone is correct?
the clone's sex is random, as in sexual reproduction
the clone's sex is determined by the surrogate mother
the clone's sex matches the nucleus donor, because the sex chromosomes are in the nucleus
the clone's sex matches the egg donor, because the egg determines sex

Sex chromosomes are part of the nuclear DNA, so the clone is male, like the bull. The egg donor contributes only cytoplasm, and in mammals the sperm, not the egg, carries the sex chromosome that determines sex.
bio12a3-clone-17

Each explant produces 3 new plantlets in each subculture cycle, and every plantlet is subcultured in the next cycle. Starting with 1 explant, how many plantlets are produced after 4 subculture cycles?
The number is multiplied by 3 each cycle, so 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. The answer 27 is the result after only three cycles, and 12 comes from 3 × 4, which ignores that the number multiplies each cycle.
bio12a3-clone-18
Which is a disadvantage of plant tissue culture for producing many plants?
it cannot produce plants with a desirable trait
it requires pollination and seed formation
it cannot produce more than one plant from a single leaf
repeated subculturing can cause mutations, leading to variation among the plantlets

Repeated subculturing can introduce mutations, a problem known as somaclonal variation. Tissue culture needs no pollination or seeds and can produce many plantlets from a small piece of tissue, so the other options are wrong.
bio12a3-clone-19
Which natural process gives the most similar result to plant tissue culture?
pollination by insects, which mixes genes from two plants
vegetative reproduction, such as by runners or tubers, which gives genetically identical plants by mitosis
wind dispersal of seeds from a flower
meiosis in the anthers, which produces haploid pollen

Runners and tubers produce new plants by mitosis from parts of the parent, just as tissue culture does, so the offspring are clones. Pollination, seed dispersal and meiosis all involve sexual reproduction or new gene combinations.
bio12a3-clone-20
A cow's body cell has 60 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does the embryo produced by SCNT contain?
The donor nucleus supplies a full set of 60 chromosomes, and the enucleated egg contributes none. The answer 30 is the gamete number, and 120 wrongly adds two complete sets together.
bio12a3-clone-21
Explain why cells from an early embryo can be separated to produce several complete embryos. (2 marks)
Early embryo cells are undifferentiated and totipotent, so each can develop into any cell type [1]; each separated group of cells can therefore develop into a complete embryo [1].
bio12a3-clone-22
Explain why explants are grown in sterile conditions in plant tissue culture. (2 marks)
Sterile conditions prevent contamination by bacteria or fungi [1]; contaminants would compete with the explant for nutrients or kill the plant tissue [1].
bio12a3-clone-23
Describe how scientists could confirm that a cloned animal is genetically identical in nuclear DNA to its nucleus donor. (3 marks)

Collect DNA samples (e.g. from tissue or blood) from the clone and the donor [1]; compare DNA profiles or markers, such as microsatellites or sequence data, at several loci [1]; matching results at all loci indicate identical nuclear DNA [1].
bio12a3-clone-24
Explain why embryo splitting can produce only a limited number of viable offspring. (2 marks)

Only the cells of an early, undifferentiated embryo can each form a whole organism, and the embryo has a limited number of cells [1]; splitting it into too many pieces leaves each piece with too few cells to develop successfully [1].
bio12a3-clone-25
Compare micropropagation with SCNT in terms of the cells or tissues used, the conditions for growth, and the genetic outcome. (4 marks)

Micropropagation uses small pieces of plant tissue (explants, often meristem), whereas SCNT uses a body cell nucleus placed in an enucleated egg [1]; micropropagation grows explants on sterile nutrient media with hormones, whereas SCNT embryos are stimulated to divide and then implanted into a surrogate uterus [1]; both produce offspring genetically identical to the source of the nuclear DNA [1]; micropropagation involves no egg or sperm, whereas SCNT uses an egg but no sperm [1].
bio12a3-clone-26
Describe two welfare concerns about reproductive cloning of livestock. (2 marks)
Many cloned embryos fail or die before or soon after birth, so many animals suffer [1]; surviving clones may have health problems such as abnormal organ development or shortened lifespan [1].
bio12a3-clone-27

In a cloning trial, 250 SCNT embryos were transferred into surrogate mothers and 12 calves were born alive. Calculate the percentage of transferred embryos that produced a live calf. Show your working. (2 marks)
Working: 12 ÷ 250 × 100 [1]; answer: 4.8% of transferred embryos produced a live calf [1].
bio12a3-clone-28
Explain why a harmful mutation in the nuclear DNA of a donor cell could affect many individuals if that cell is cloned. (2 marks)

Clones are genetically identical in nuclear DNA, so the same mutation is copied into every clone [1]; if the mutation is harmful, all of the clones are affected, so the problem is repeated across the population [1].
vce-bio12-rc-c1
Dolly the sheep was made by putting the nucleus of an udder cell from sheep A into an enucleated egg from sheep B, then implanting the embryo into sheep C. Dolly's nuclear DNA matches:
Sheep B
Sheep A
Sheep C
A mix of sheep A and B
Somatic cell nuclear transfer copies the donor nucleus. Dolly's mitochondrial DNA came from sheep B's egg; sheep C was only the surrogate.
vce-bio12-structural-physiological-and-b: bio12a3-adapt-1
Which of the following is a behavioural adaptation?
The thick fur of a mountain pygmy possum
A bearded dragon basking in the sun in the morning to raise its body temperature
Concentrated urine produced by a hopping mouse
The sunken stomata of a Banksia leaf

A behavioural adaptation is something an organism does. Basking is a behaviour that warms an ectotherm. Thick fur and sunken stomata are structural adaptations, and producing concentrated urine is a physiological one.
bio12a3-adapt-2
A desert mammal has a small surface area to volume ratio relative to a similar species living in a cooler habitat. Which statement about this feature is correct?
It is a behavioural adaptation that increases heat loss
It is a structural adaptation that reduces heat loss
It is a structural adaptation that reduces heat gain from the environment and water loss
It is a physiological adaptation that increases evaporative cooling

Body shape is a structural feature. A smaller SA:V ratio means less surface relative to volume, so less heat is absorbed from a hot environment and less water is lost across the surface. It does not increase heat loss, and it is not a behaviour or an internal process.
bio12a3-adapt-3
Which pair correctly matches a hydrophyte (aquatic plant) adaptation with its function?
Stomata mainly on the upper surface of floating leaves - allows gas exchange with the air
Thick waxy cuticle on submerged leaves - reduces water loss
Extensive deep root system - reaches groundwater
Sunken stomata - traps humid air

Floating leaves like water lily pads have stomata on the upper surface, which is the side in contact with air, so gas exchange can happen there. Thick cuticles, deep roots and sunken stomata are xerophyte features for dry conditions.
bio12a3-adapt-4
Many desert ectotherms enter a dormant state with lowered metabolic rate during hot, dry periods. This is called
hibernation
aestivation
torpor in winter only
migration
Aestivation is dormancy during hot, dry conditions. Australian water-holding frogs, for example, burrow and aestivate underground. Hibernation is long-term dormancy during cold winter conditions.
bio12a3-adapt-5

A student lists the following features of a plant: (1) leaves reduced to spines, (2) CAM photosynthesis with stomata open at night, (3) shallow, widespread roots. Which features are physiological adaptations?
1 only
2 only
1 and 3
2 and 3
CAM photosynthesis is a physiological (biochemical) adaptation: stomata open at night, when it is cooler, to take up CO₂ and reduce water loss. Spines and root systems are structural adaptations.
bio12a3-adapt-6
Explain the difference between structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations, giving one example of each from an Australian animal. (3 marks)

Structural adaptations are physical features of the body, e.g. the large ears of the bilby, which lose heat; physiological adaptations are internal functions or processes, e.g. the spinifex hopping mouse producing highly concentrated urine to conserve water; behavioural adaptations are actions an organism carries out, e.g. kangaroos licking their forearms so evaporation cools the blood in surface vessels.
bio12a3-adapt-7
Describe two structural adaptations of xerophytic plants and explain how each reduces water loss. (4 marks)

A thick waxy cuticle on leaves is waterproof, so less water evaporates through the leaf surface; sunken stomata or stomata in hair-lined pits trap a layer of humid air, which reduces the water vapour concentration gradient and slows transpiration (also accept: reduced leaf surface area/needle-like leaves lower the area for water loss; vertically hanging leaves, as in eucalypts, reduce heat absorbed in the midday sun; rolled leaves enclose stomata).
bio12a3-adapt-8

In an investigation, the ear length of rabbit populations was measured at different latitudes in Australia. Rabbits in the hot, arid north had longer ears on average than rabbits in cooler southern regions. Propose an explanation for this pattern. (2 marks)

Longer ears have a larger surface area with many blood vessels, which increases heat loss to the environment by radiation and convection; in hot climates rabbits with longer ears are more likely to avoid overheating, survive and reproduce, so the trait becomes more common, while in cooler regions shorter ears reduce heat loss.
bio12a3-adapt-9
Which of the following is a physiological adaptation?
A koala sleeping for most of the day in the fork of a eucalypt tree
A camel's body temperature rising by several degrees during the day rather than being held constant
Long, narrow leaves covered in a dense layer of hairs
A desert lizard burrowing underground during the hottest hours

A physiological adaptation is an internal regulated process. A camel letting its body temperature rise during the day, so it does not have to sweat to stay cool, is one. Sleeping and burrowing are behaviours, and leaf hairs are a structural feature.
bio12a3-adapt-10
A bird living in a cold alpine environment has feathers that trap a layer of warm air close to its skin. This feature is best classified as
structural
physiological
behavioural
biochemical

Feathers are a physical feature of the body, so the adaptation is structural. A physiological adaptation is an internal process, such as changing blood flow to the skin, while fluffing the feathers up on purpose would be a behaviour.
bio12a3-adapt-11
A meerkat group posts a sentry that gives a warning call when a hawk approaches, while the rest of the group keeps foraging. Which statement about the sentry is correct?
It is a structural adaptation that makes the meerkats harder to see
It is a physiological adaptation that increases the sentry's alertness
It is a behavioural adaptation that reduces the risk of predation for the group
It is a physiological adaptation that releases a chemical warning

Posting a sentry is something the animals do, so it is a behavioural adaptation, and its function is to warn the group and lower each animal's risk. The structural and physiological options mislabel the category, and the chemical warning option describes a mechanism the sentry does not use.
bio12a3-adapt-12
Two cube-shaped models of an animal have sides of 2 cm and 4 cm. Which statement about surface area to volume ratio is correct?
The 2 cm cube has the smaller ratio, because its surface area is smaller
Both cubes have the same ratio, because both have the same shape
The 2 cm cube has a ratio of 1.5 cm⁻¹ and the 4 cm cube has a ratio of 3 cm⁻¹
The 4 cm cube has the smaller ratio, at 1.5 cm⁻¹, which is half the 3 cm⁻¹ of the 2 cm cube

The 2 cm cube has 24 cm² of surface and 8 cm³ of volume, a ratio of 3 cm⁻¹, while the 4 cm cube has 96 cm² and 64 cm³, a ratio of 1.5 cm⁻¹. A larger body has a smaller ratio, so the common mistake is to compare absolute surface areas instead of the ratio.
bio12a3-adapt-13
Which statement correctly describes the function of the thick, corky bark of a eucalypt trunk?
It stores water that the tree can draw on during drought
It insulates the living cambium beneath, protecting it from heat during bushfires
It absorbs carbon dioxide for photosynthesis
It produces hormones that control the timing of flowering

Thick bark is a structural adaptation that insulates the living tissue beneath it, so a bushfire heats the cambium more slowly. Bark does not store water or absorb carbon dioxide, since photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, and hormone production is a physiological process rather than a function of bark.
bio12a3-adapt-14
Desert mammals lose a large amount of water in exhaled breath. Which structural feature helps reduce this loss?
Convoluted nasal passages that cool exhaled air, so water vapour condenses and is returned to the body
Rapid, shallow panting that increases evaporation from the tongue
Large lungs with a high breathing rate to take in more oxygen
Sweat glands spread over the whole body surface

Convoluted nasal passages cool exhaled air so that water vapour condenses on them and is recovered, which is a structural feature that reduces water loss. Panting, a high breathing rate and sweating all increase water loss, so they are wrong even though they help with cooling.
bio12a3-adapt-15
Mangroves growing in waterlogged, low-oxygen mud produce aerial roots called pneumatophores. What is their main function?
They anchor the tree in soft mud and stop it being uprooted by tides
They excrete excess salt from the plant into the surrounding mud
They project above the mud and take in oxygen for the submerged roots
They absorb water from the mud only at night

Pneumatophores are structural adaptations that project above the mud and take in air, supplying oxygen to the buried root tissues. Anchoring is the role of other root types, and salt removal is a physiological process rather than the function of these roots.
bio12a3-adapt-16
Many desert birds move long distances to areas where rain has recently fallen, because rainfall in these regions is unpredictable. This movement is best classified as
physiological
structural
reproductive
behavioural

Moving to follow unpredictable rain is an action taken by the animal, so it is behavioural. The structural and physiological options describe body features or internal processes, and reproductive describes a different biological function.
bio12a3-adapt-17
A seed-eating bird has a short, thick, cone-shaped beak. Which statement about this feature is correct?
It is a physiological adaptation that increases the bird's production of digestive enzymes
It is a behavioural adaptation that makes the bird choose seeds over insects
It is a structural adaptation that lets the bird crack and husk hard seeds
It is a structural adaptation that stores water for use during dry periods

A short, thick beak is a physical feature, so it is structural, and its shape lets the bird crack and husk hard seeds. The digestive, diet-choice and water-storage options either mislabel the category or describe a function the beak does not have.
bio12a3-adapt-18
Which of the following is a physiological adaptation to cold?
Shivering, which generates heat through rapid muscle contractions
Sheltering in a shaded thicket during the hottest part of the day
Growing a dense, insulating coat of fur
Migrating to a warmer latitude in autumn

Shivering is an internal process that generates heat through muscle contraction, so it is physiological. Sheltering from the heat and migrating are behaviours, and a dense coat is a structural feature.
bio12a3-adapt-19
Seabirds drink seawater and must remove the excess salt. Which feature achieves this?
Thick plumage that keeps seawater away from the skin
Salt glands near the eyes that secrete a concentrated salt solution
Feeding only on prey that contains no salt
A large stomach that stores seawater for later use

Salt glands are a physiological adaptation: they actively excrete concentrated salt, which lets the bird drink seawater safely. Plumage is a structural feature and diet choice is behavioural, and neither removes salt from the body; storing seawater in the stomach would add to the salt load.
bio12a3-adapt-20
A small nocturnal rodent in an arid zone restricts its foraging to the hours after sunset, when the air is cooler. This is best described as
a physiological adaptation that lowers its metabolic rate
a structural adaptation that reduces its surface area
a physiological adaptation that increases its tolerance of heat
a behavioural adaptation that reduces heat stress

Choosing when to forage is an action the animal carries out, so it is behavioural, and it reduces heat stress. The other options name the wrong category, or describe a feature that the timing of foraging does not change.
bio12a3-adapt-21
During drought, many eucalypts close their stomata around midday to reduce water loss. This response is best classified as
structural, because the stomata are a physical feature of the leaf
behavioural, because the plant moves its leaves to shade them
physiological, because it is a regulated internal process
reproductive, because it limits flowering during drought

Closing stomata is a regulated internal response that reduces transpiration, which makes it physiological. Stomata are structures, so calling the response structural confuses the feature with the process it carries out.
bio12a3-adapt-22
A bird living in a dry environment excretes uric acid, a paste-like waste, instead of urea. A student calls this a structural adaptation. Which correction is best?
It is a physiological adaptation, because it is an internal metabolic process that conserves water
It is a behavioural adaptation, because the bird chooses a diet that produces less waste
It is still structural, because the kidneys are body organs
It is not an adaptation, because it does not involve any physical feature

Excreting uric acid is an internal process that saves water, so it is physiological. Calling it structural confuses an organ with the process it carries out, which is the common mistake in this question.
bio12a3-adapt-23
Define a behavioural adaptation and give one example from an Australian animal. (2 marks)
An action or behaviour carried out by an organism [1] that improves its chance of survival or reproduction, e.g. an echidna curling into a ball with its spines facing outwards when threatened [1].
bio12a3-adapt-24
Classify the thick, hard exoskeleton of a crab as a structural or physiological adaptation. (1 mark)
Structural [1].
bio12a3-adapt-25
Explain how a pale, reflective coat helps a desert mammal reduce heat gain from the environment. (3 marks)

Pale colours reflect a greater proportion of incoming solar radiation [1]; less radiant energy is absorbed by the skin [1]; so less heat is gained from the environment, and less evaporative cooling and water loss is needed [1].
bio12a3-adapt-26
Describe two physiological adaptations that help a small mammal in an alpine environment conserve body heat, and explain how each works. (4 marks)

Vasoconstriction: blood vessels in the skin narrow [1], reducing blood flow to the surface so less heat is lost to the air [1]; shivering: rapid, involuntary muscle contractions [1] release heat from the metabolism of the muscles [1].
bio12a3-adapt-27
Explain how sweating cools the human body, using the idea of latent heat. (2 marks)
Water evaporates from the skin surface [1], and the energy needed to change it from liquid to vapour (latent heat) is taken from the skin and blood, cooling the body [1].
bio12a3-adapt-28
Describe two behavioural adaptations that help a small mammal survive a cold winter, and explain how each works. (4 marks)

Huddling with other individuals [1], which reduces the surface area exposed to cold air per animal and so reduces heat loss [1]; sheltering in a nest or burrow lined with insulating material [1], which traps warm air and reduces exposure to wind and cold [1].
bio12a3-adapt-29
Explain why a leaf from a plant in a shaded rainforest understorey is typically larger and thinner than a leaf from a plant in an exposed, dry habitat. (3 marks)

Larger leaves provide more surface area for light capture in low light [1]; thin leaves shorten the diffusion path for CO₂ to reach the chloroplasts [1]; exposed, dry habitats favour smaller, thicker leaves, which reduce the surface area for water loss [1].
bio12a3-adapt-30
Give one example of a physiological adaptation that a marine fish uses to maintain its salt balance. (1 mark)
Chloride cells in the gills actively pump excess salt out of the body [1].
vce-bio12-sa-c1
Which is a physiological adaptation?
A kangaroo licking its forearms to cool down
A cactus having spines instead of leaves
A lizard basking in the morning sun
A desert rodent producing very concentrated urine
Physiological adaptations involve internal body functions. Licking and basking are behavioural; spines are structural.
vce-bio12-adaptations-to-australian-envi: bio12a3-aus-1
Many Australian plants, such as some Banksia species, have serotinous fruits that stay closed until exposed to heat. The main advantage of this adaptation is that
seeds are protected from insect pollinators
seeds are released after fire, when competition is reduced and nutrients from ash are available
seeds can only germinate in very cold conditions
the plant avoids being burnt in a fire

Serotiny holds seeds in woody fruits until fire triggers their release. After a fire the ground is clear, light is plentiful, competition is low and ash adds nutrients, so seedlings have a better chance of establishing. Serotiny does not stop the parent plant from burning.
bio12a3-aus-2
After bushfire, many eucalypts produce new shoots from buds protected beneath thick bark along their trunks. These are called
lignotubers
epicormic buds
proteoid roots
stolons

Epicormic buds sit under the bark on trunks and branches and sprout after fire to regrow the canopy. Lignotubers are woody swellings at or below ground level that can also resprout, but they are not on the trunk.
bio12a3-aus-3
