The spinifex hopping mouse can survive in the Australian desert without drinking water. Which combination of adaptations best explains this?
It sweats heavily and drinks dew
It produces very concentrated urine, obtains metabolic water from food and is nocturnal, staying in humid burrows during the day
It has a large body and thick fur to retain water
It hibernates through summer

The hopping mouse has long loops of Henle and makes extremely concentrated urine. It gets water from seeds and from cellular respiration (metabolic water). By being nocturnal and sheltering in humid burrows it cuts evaporative water loss. Sweating would waste water.
bio12a3-aus-4
Many Australian soils are low in phosphorus. Plants in the family Proteaceae (e.g. Banksia, Hakea) are adapted to these soils by producing
cluster (proteoid) roots that increase surface area and release compounds that free phosphorus from the soil
deep taproots that reach nitrogen in groundwater
pneumatophores that take in oxygen
leaves with very large surface areas

Cluster (proteoid) roots are dense mats of fine rootlets. They have a large surface area and release carboxylates that make bound phosphate soluble, so the plant can take up more phosphorus from poor soils. Pneumatophores are a mangrove adaptation to waterlogged, low-oxygen mud.
bio12a3-aus-5
The thorny devil (Moloch horridus) lives in arid central Australia. Grooves between its scales draw water by capillary action towards its mouth. This adaptation is best classified as
behavioural only
structural
physiological only
an example of aestivation

The grooves between the scales are a physical body feature, which makes this a structural adaptation. (The lizard may also behave in ways that help, such as standing on damp sand, but the grooves themselves are structural.)
bio12a3-aus-6

Red kangaroos live in hot, arid regions of Australia. Describe three adaptations (at least one structural, one physiological and one behavioural) that help red kangaroos survive heat and water shortage. (3 marks)

Structural: a dense network of blood vessels close to the skin of the forearms, which loses heat when licked; physiological: produces concentrated urine and can slow or pause embryo development (embryonic diapause) when conditions are poor; behavioural: rests in shade during the hottest part of the day and is mostly active at dawn, dusk and night, and licks forearms so evaporation cools the blood.
bio12a3-aus-7
Explain how hopping is an energy-efficient form of movement for kangaroos in arid environments where food is sparse. (2 marks)

Elastic tendons in the hind legs (e.g. the Achilles tendon) store energy on landing and release it in the next hop, so above a certain speed the energy cost of hopping barely rises with speed; this lets kangaroos travel long distances between scattered food and water sources with relatively little energy use.
bio12a3-aus-8
Eucalyptus leaves often hang vertically and have a thick waxy cuticle. Explain how these features help eucalypts survive in hot, dry Australian environments. (2 marks)

Vertically hanging leaves present their edge to the midday sun, so less light and heat are absorbed in the hottest part of the day, lowering leaf temperature and transpiration; the thick waxy cuticle is waterproof and reduces evaporation of water from the leaf surface.
bio12a3-aus-9
The platypus hunts for invertebrates on river beds with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed. It locates its prey mainly using
electroreceptors in its bill that detect the weak electric fields produced by prey
echolocation clicks produced by its tongue
a lateral line of sensory organs along its body
smell through its nostrils, which stay open underwater

The platypus bill contains thousands of electroreceptors that detect the weak electrical signals produced by prey muscles. Echolocation is not used by platypuses, and a lateral line belongs to fish; the nostrils close underwater, so smell is not the main sense used there.
bio12a3-aus-10
Grey mangroves (Avicennia marina) grow in salty tidal mud, where salt builds up in their tissues. They get rid of excess salt mainly by
pumping salt into aerial roots (pneumatophores), which release it into the air
keeping their roots completely waterproof so that no salt can enter
secreting salt through salt glands on their leaves, where it crystallises and is shed
opening their stomata only at night so that salt cannot enter

Grey mangroves have salt glands on their leaves that secrete excess salt, which then crystallises on the leaf surface and can be shed. Pneumatophores take in oxygen in waterlogged mud and do not remove salt, and the roots are not waterproof, so some salt is taken up.
bio12a3-aus-11
The water-holding frog (Cyclorana platycephala) survives long dry periods in inland Australia. The water it needs during this time is stored in its
lungs
stomach
gall bladder
urinary bladder
The water-holding frog stores large volumes of water in its urinary bladder, which it draws on during dry periods. The gall bladder stores bile, and the lungs and stomach do not act as water stores.
bio12a3-aus-12
Many annual wildflowers in the arid interior survive dry years as dormant seeds, germinating only after heavy rain. The main advantage of this strategy is that
seeds germinate in the dry season, when temperatures are lower and competition is lower
seedlings germinate only when there is enough water to grow, flower and set seed before the soil dries out
the adult plants store water in their seed coats, which then germinate when needed
seeds are dispersed by wind during drought, when the ground is bare

Germinating after heavy rain gives seedlings enough moisture to complete their short life cycle before drought returns. Germinating in the dry season would usually lead to death, and seed coats do not store water for the adult plant.
bio12a3-aus-13
Cushion plants in the alpine areas of the Australian Alps grow as low, dense mounds close to the ground. Compared with taller plants nearby, the cushion is most likely to be
exposed to higher wind speeds, which increase its rate of photosynthesis
more likely to lose water through its leaves because it is closer to the ground
warmer and less windy, which reduces heat loss and water loss
dispersed further from the parent plant by strong winds

A dense, low cushion creates a warmer, more sheltered microclimate, reducing heat loss and drying out. Higher winds increase water loss and do not improve photosynthesis, and the cushion shape does not help disperse seeds further.
bio12a3-aus-14
Many leaves of Australian rainforest trees have a pointed tip, called a drip tip. The function of this tip is to
trap water on the leaf so it can be absorbed through the surface
increase the leaf's ability to absorb light in the shaded understorey
close the stomata at the tip, reducing transpiration
shed rainwater quickly, so the leaf dries and fungi and algae cannot grow on it

Drip tips channel water off the leaf quickly, so leaves dry faster and epiphylls (fungi and algae) are less likely to grow. Leaves do not absorb water through their upper surface, and the tip does not change light absorption much.
bio12a3-aus-15
The Queensland lungfish (Neoceratodus forsteri) lives in slow, shallow waterholes that can become low in dissolved oxygen. It can survive these conditions because it
gulps air at the surface and takes up oxygen through a single lung
burrows into dry mud and stays dormant until the next wet season
extracts oxygen from air through its gills while out of the water
stores oxygen in its swim bladder for later use

Queensland lungfish have a single lung-like organ and gulp air at the surface when dissolved oxygen falls. Burrowing into mud is a trait of African lungfish, not this species, and gills cannot extract oxygen from air.
bio12a3-aus-16
Bearded dragons are reptiles that live in arid central Australia. Each morning they bask on rocks to warm their bodies before becoming active. Basking is best classified as
a structural adaptation that improves heat absorption
a physiological adaptation that conserves water
a behavioural adaptation for regulating body temperature
a reproductive adaptation that increases mating success
Basking is an action the lizard performs to raise its body temperature, so it is behavioural. Structural adaptations are physical body features, and basking does not conserve water.
bio12a3-aus-17
Echidnas are covered in sharp, pointed spines. These spines are best described as
modified hairs
modified scales, like those of reptiles
modified feathers, like those of birds
modified claws that have grown along the back
Echidna spines are modified hairs made of keratin that protect the animal from predators. Scales and feathers are different structures found in reptiles and birds, and the spines are not claws.
bio12a3-aus-18
Many Australian native legumes, such as wattles (Acacia), grow in nitrogen-poor soils. Their roots form nodules containing bacteria that allow the plant to
dissolve phosphate from rock particles so it can be absorbed
store nitrate in the root cells as a reserve of water
produce nitrogen gas that the plant uses to make chlorophyll
convert nitrogen gas (N₂) from the air into ammonia that the plant can use

Rhizobia bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant uses to make proteins and other compounds. The bacteria do not dissolve phosphate, nitrate in roots is not a water store, and nitrogen gas is not used directly to make chlorophyll.
bio12a3-aus-19
Bogong moths migrate each spring from inland plains to cool caves in the Australian Alps, where they rest through the hot summer. The main advantage of this behaviour is that the moths
can feed on abundant nectar in the caves while they rest
avoid the high temperatures and dry conditions of the lowland plains, saving water and energy
grow faster in the cool conditions, so they reach adult size sooner
avoid predators that are active only in winter

Bogong moths rest in cool caves over summer, which avoids the heat and drought of the lowlands and saves energy and water. The moths are already adults when they migrate, so the caves do not promote growth.
bio12a3-aus-20
A small desert rodent is 5 cm long and a larger rodent of the same body shape is 15 cm long. Compared with the larger rodent, the small rodent has a surface area to volume ratio that is
three times greater
nine times greater
one-third as great
27 times greater

For similar shapes, surface area scales with length squared and volume with length cubed, so the ratio falls as length increases; here it is 15 ÷ 5 = 3 times greater for the small rodent. Squaring the length ratio (nine times) or cubing it (27 times) gives the wrong answer.
bio12a3-aus-21

Koalas feed almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are low in energy and protein and contain toxic compounds. Describe one structural and one behavioural adaptation that help koalas cope with this diet. (2 marks)

Structural: a very long caecum (around 2 m) that houses microbes which ferment cellulose and help break down toxic compounds [1]; behavioural: sleeps for around 18 hours or more each day, which reduces energy use on a low-energy diet [1].
bio12a3-aus-22

Classify each of the following as structural, physiological or behavioural: (i) the nomadic movement of emus to areas that have recently received rain; (ii) the dense, waterproof fur of the platypus. (2 marks)
(i) behavioural: an action the emu performs to find food and water [1]; (ii) structural: a physical feature of the body covering [1].
bio12a3-aus-23

The sugar glider is a nocturnal marsupial of eucalypt forests with a gliding membrane (patagium) stretched between its front and back legs. Explain how gliding helps the sugar glider find food in forests where food resources are patchy. (3 marks)

Gliding lets it cross between widely spaced trees with much less energy than travelling along the ground [1]; this allows it to reach scattered feeding sites, such as flowering eucalypts and trees with sap or insects, more quickly [1]; it avoids ground predators during travel, so more time and energy go into finding food [1].
bio12a3-aus-24

Some Australian skinks that live in cold alpine regions give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. Explain how this reproductive strategy helps the young survive in a cold environment. (2 marks)

The mother can bask and move between sunny and shaded sites to keep herself and her developing embryos warmer than the cold surroundings [1]; the young develop inside the mother, so they are protected from frost and cold, and are born early enough in the season to feed and grow before winter [1].
bio12a3-aus-25
Define the term ectotherm. (1 mark)
An animal whose body temperature depends mainly on external sources of heat, such as the sun, rather than on heat produced by its own metabolism [1].
bio12a3-aus-26

Describe three adaptations of the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus) that help it survive in tropical northern Australian wetlands and coasts, and classify each as structural, physiological or behavioural. (3 marks)

Structural: tough, armoured skin of bony plates (scutes) that reduces water loss and protects against injury [1]; behavioural: basks on riverbanks in the morning to warm up before hunting [1]; behavioural: builds mound nests from vegetation whose decomposition generates heat for the eggs [1].
bio12a3-aus-27

Pigface (Carpobrotus) is a succulent groundcover that grows on sand dunes along the Australian coast. Describe four features of pigface that help it survive in hot, dry, windy coastal conditions. (4 marks)

Fleshy leaves store water and have a thick cuticle that reduces water loss [1]; a low, trailing growth habit reduces exposure to wind and heat [1]; stems root at the nodes, so the plant anchors itself in shifting sand [1]; it spreads vegetatively along the ground, allowing it to colonise and hold dune sand after disturbance [1].
bio12a3-aus-28
Describe how the water-holding frog's cocoon helps it survive a long dry period in inland Australia. (2 marks)

The frog sheds layers of skin that harden into a cocoon around its body while it sits in mud [1]; the cocoon reduces evaporative water loss from the skin, so the water stored in its body lasts longer [1].
bio12a3-aus-29
Some desert shrubs have silvery, hairy leaves. The hairs reflect sunlight and trap a layer of humid air against the leaf surface. These features are best classified as
physiological
reproductive
structural
behavioural

The hairs and the silvery surface are physical features of the leaf, so they are structural. The reflected light and trapped humid air reduce heat gain and water loss. Physiological adaptations are internal processes such as producing concentrated urine, and behavioural adaptations are actions such as sheltering.
bio12a3-aus-30
The greater bilby of arid central Australia has large ears with many blood vessels close to the skin. The main function of these ears is most likely to
lose body heat from the blood vessels in the ears, helping the bilby regulate its body temperature
detect predators from a long distance, as the ears of an owl do
store water in the blood vessels of the ears during dry periods
display the ears to attract mates, as in many other mammals

Large, well-vascularised ears act as radiators, releasing heat when the bilby is hot. Hearing is a real function of the ears, but the blood vessels point to heat exchange. Blood vessels in the ears do not store water, and display is not the main role of these ears.
bio12a3-aus-31
Explain how torpor helps the mountain pygmy-possum survive alpine winters when food is scarce. (2 marks)

Torpor lowers the animal's body temperature and metabolic rate, so it uses much less energy [1]; this allows it to survive on stored body fat and limited food through the cold winter months when food is scarce [1].
vce-bio12-au-c1
Some Banksia species release their seeds mainly after a fire. This is an advantage because:
Fire kills all seed-eating animals permanently, so every seed survives
Seeds land on cleared ground with less competition and nutrients from ash
The seeds must be cooked before birds can eat and disperse them
Fire increases soil moisture, so seedlings never run short of water
This serotiny times germination for when conditions favour seedlings. Eucalypts use epicormic buds and lignotubers to regrow after fire.
vce-bio12-interdependencies-and-keystone: bio12a3-inter-1
A keystone species is best defined as a species that
is the most abundant species in an ecosystem
has a disproportionately large effect on ecosystem structure relative to its abundance
is always the top predator in a food web
is found only in one ecosystem

A keystone species has an effect on community structure that is far larger than its numbers would suggest. Removing it causes big changes. Keystone species are often predators but do not have to be: ecosystem engineers and pollinators can also be keystone species.
bio12a3-inter-2

Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, gaining protection, while the anemone gains nutrients from clownfish waste and protection from some predators. This relationship is an example of
parasitism
commensalism
mutualism
amensalism
Both species benefit (+/+), so this is mutualism. In commensalism one species benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0). In parasitism one benefits at the other's expense (+/−).
bio12a3-inter-3
In south-eastern Australian kelp forests, removing a predator of sea urchins led to a large increase in sea urchin numbers and the loss of most kelp. This chain of effects is best described as
a trophic cascade
competitive exclusion
primary succession
biomagnification

A trophic cascade happens when a change at one trophic level (fewer predators) spreads through the food web: urchins increase and graze down the kelp. Biomagnification is the build-up of toxins up a food chain, which is a different process.
bio12a3-inter-4
Mistletoe attaches to eucalypt branches and extracts water and nutrients from the host. The relationship between mistletoe and its host is
mutualism
commensalism
parasitism
predation of a herbivore

Mistletoe takes water and minerals through haustoria while the host gets no benefit, so it is parasitism (+/−). Mistletoe is a hemiparasite because it still photosynthesises, but its relationship with the host is still parasitic. Its berries and nectar do support many birds and insects.
bio12a3-inter-5

Dingoes have been suggested as a keystone species in parts of arid Australia. In areas where dingoes are controlled, red fox and feral cat numbers increase and small native mammal numbers decline. Which explanation best fits these observations?
Dingoes compete with small native mammals for food
Dingoes suppress fox and cat numbers, reducing predation pressure on small native mammals
Foxes and cats are prey of small native mammals
Dingoes spread disease to foxes and cats only when their numbers are low

Dingoes kill and scare away foxes and cats (mesopredators). When dingoes are removed, mesopredators are released, they increase and they prey more heavily on small native mammals. This is mesopredator release, a form of trophic cascade.
bio12a3-inter-6
Describe the difference between interspecific and intraspecific competition, and give an example of each in an Australian ecosystem. (3 marks)

Intraspecific competition is competition for limited resources between individuals of the same species, e.g. male red kangaroos competing for mates, or eucalypt seedlings of one species competing for light; interspecific competition is competition between individuals of different species for the same resource, e.g. introduced European honeybees and native bees competing for nectar and tree hollows, or rabbits and native herbivores competing for grasses.
bio12a3-inter-7
Flying foxes (fruit bats) feed on the nectar and fruit of many native trees. Explain why flying foxes could be considered a keystone species in Australian forests. (3 marks)

Flying foxes pollinate the flowers of many native trees (e.g. eucalypts) as they feed on nectar; they disperse seeds over long distances, often tens of kilometres, which helps regenerate forests and maintain gene flow between fragmented patches; because many plant species depend on them and, in turn, many other animals depend on those plants, losing flying foxes would have a disproportionately large effect on forest structure.
bio12a3-inter-8

A food web contains the following feeding relationships: grass → grasshopper → magpie; grass → kangaroo → dingo; grasshopper → skink → kookaburra. Predict and explain the effect on the skink population if a disease greatly reduced the grasshopper population. (2 marks)

The skink population would decrease; grasshoppers are the skinks' food source, so less food would lead to lower survival and reproduction of skinks (and they may face greater predation pressure as kookaburras have less alternative prey).
bio12a3-inter-9
Barnacles attach to the skin of a whale and filter plankton from the water that passes the whale. The whale is neither helped nor harmed by the barnacles. This relationship is best described as
parasitism
commensalism
mutualism
competition
The barnacles benefit while the whale is unaffected, which is commensalism (+/0). Mutualism would require the whale to benefit too, and parasitism would require the whale to be harmed.
bio12a3-inter-10

A eucalypt releases chemicals from its leaves that stop seeds of other plant species from germinating in the soil beneath it. The eucalypt gains nothing and is not affected by this. The relationship is an example of
mutualism
parasitism
amensalism
commensalism
One species is harmed while the other is unaffected, which is amensalism (−/0). Commensalism is the reverse pattern, where one species benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0).
bio12a3-inter-11

Lichens are made of a fungus and an alga living closely together. The fungus supplies water and minerals, and the alga supplies sugars made by photosynthesis. Both partners gain from the relationship. This relationship is best described as
parasitism
commensalism
competition
mutualism
Both partners benefit (+/+), which is mutualism. Parasitism would mean one partner benefits at the other's expense, and commensalism would mean only one partner benefits.
bio12a3-inter-12

A fan-tailed cuckoo lays its eggs in the nest of a thornbill. The cuckoo chick is raised by the thornbill parents, who feed it at the expense of their own young. This relationship is best described as
parasitism
competition
commensalism
mutualism

The cuckoo benefits at the thornbill's expense (+/−), which is brood parasitism, a form of parasitism. Competition would involve both species using the same limited resource, which is not the main pattern here.
bio12a3-inter-13
A powerful owl hunts and eats ringtail possums, killing each one it catches. The relationship between the owl and the possum is best described as
commensalism
predation
mutualism
parasitism
The owl kills and eats the possum, so the owl benefits and the possum is harmed (+/−), which is predation. Parasitism involves a parasite living on or in a host that is usually not killed quickly.
bio12a3-inter-14
Which statement best distinguishes an indicator species from a keystone species?
An indicator species is always rare, while a keystone species is always common
An indicator species is a predator, while a keystone species is a producer
The presence or absence of an indicator species reflects environmental conditions, while a keystone species has a large effect on community structure relative to its abundance
An indicator species can live in only one ecosystem, while a keystone species is found in many

An indicator species shows the condition of an environment, such as lichens reflecting air quality, but removing it does not usually reshape the community. The other statements wrongly link these terms to abundance, feeding role or range.
bio12a3-inter-15
Which example best describes an ecosystem engineer?
a koala that feeds on eucalypt leaves
a dingo that hunts kangaroos
a fig tree that is the most abundant plant in a rainforest
a wombat whose burrows provide shelter for many other species

Ecosystem engineers physically change the habitat, and the wombat's burrows create shelter used by many other species. Feeding on leaves or hunting does not change the habitat, and abundance alone does not make a species an ecosystem engineer.
bio12a3-inter-16
Which organism is a decomposer?
a fungus breaking down a fallen eucalypt log
a green turtle grazing on seagrass
a koala feeding on eucalypt leaves
a dingo hunting a kangaroo
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil. The turtle, koala and dingo all eat living organisms, so they are consumers.
bio12a3-inter-17
The competitive exclusion principle predicts that two species with identical niches
will always evolve to use different niches
will both increase in population as resources become more available
cannot coexist indefinitely in the same place, and one is eventually eliminated
will coexist in equal numbers

Two species using exactly the same resources compete directly, so the less competitive species is eventually eliminated. Niche partitioning, which evolves over time, is how species avoid exclusion, so it is not the prediction of the principle.
bio12a3-inter-18

Two bird species feed on the same insect prey in a eucalypt woodland. Over time they are observed feeding in different parts of the trees, with one feeding on the bark and the other in the canopy. This most likely reflects
interspecific competition that has caused one species to become extinct
mutualism between the two species
a trophic cascade caused by a predator
reduced competition through resource partitioning

Feeding in different parts of the trees reduces the overlap in the resource used, which is resource partitioning, and this lowers competition. Extinction is not described, the birds are not benefiting each other, and no predator is changing lower trophic levels.
bio12a3-inter-19

In a grassland, grass captures 20 000 kJ of energy. Grasshoppers eat the grass, and lizards eat the grasshoppers. Using the 10% energy transfer rule between each trophic level, how much energy is available to the lizards?
200 kJ
20 kJ

About 10% is passed on at each level, so 20 000 kJ becomes 2 000 kJ for the grasshoppers and then 200 kJ for the lizards. The value of 2 000 kJ is only one transfer, and 20 kJ wrongly applies a third 10% transfer.
bio12a3-inter-20
A rainbow lorikeet feeds on nectar and pollen from flowering eucalypts. In the food chain eucalypt → rainbow lorikeet, the lorikeet is best classified as a
producer
primary consumer
secondary consumer
decomposer

A primary consumer eats producers, so a bird that feeds on plant nectar and pollen is a primary consumer. Producers make their own food, secondary consumers eat other animals, and decomposers break down dead matter.
bio12a3-inter-21
In the notation used for species interactions, a relationship shown as (+/0) means
one species benefits and the other is harmed
both species are harmed
one species benefits and the other is unaffected
both species benefit

The + shows that one species gains a benefit and the 0 shows that the other is unaffected, which is commensalism. A (+/−) pattern means one species benefits while the other is harmed, and a (+/+) pattern means both benefit.
bio12a3-inter-22
Define the term trophic level. (1 mark)
The position an organism occupies in a food chain or food web, based on its feeding relationship and source of energy [1]
bio12a3-inter-23
Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels. (2 marks)

At each trophic level about 90% of the energy is lost, mainly as heat from respiration, and so is not passed on to the next level [1]; by the top level too little energy remains to support a viable population of consumers [1]
bio12a3-inter-24
Describe how mycorrhizal fungi and eucalypts are interdependent. (2 marks)

The fungal hyphae extend the tree's root system, increasing the absorption of water and mineral nutrients such as phosphorus for the tree [1]; in return the tree supplies the fungus with sugars produced by photosynthesis [1]
bio12a3-inter-25
Explain why a common and widespread species is not necessarily a keystone species. (2 marks)

A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on community structure relative to its abundance, so a common species is only a keystone if its removal causes major changes to the community [1]; many abundant species can be replaced by other species, so their loss would have only small effects on other organisms [1]
bio12a3-inter-26
Explain the difference between predation and parasitism. (2 marks)

In predation, the predator kills and eats its prey, so the prey is harmed immediately [1]; in parasitism, the parasite lives on or in the host and gains nutrients from it while usually not killing it quickly [1]
bio12a3-inter-27
Cane toads have toxic skin secretions. Predict and explain the effect of cane toads on a native predator, the northern quoll, and on a prey species of the quoll. (3 marks)

Quolls that eat cane toads are poisoned and die, so the quoll population declines [1]; with fewer quolls, predation pressure on the quoll's prey, such as insects and small vertebrates, is reduced, so prey numbers are likely to increase [1]; changes in the prey population may then affect other species that depend on the prey or compete with it [1]
bio12a3-inter-28
Termites build mounds and tunnels in the soil of many Australian ecosystems. Explain how termites can act as ecosystem engineers, and describe one effect this has on other species. (3 marks)

Termites physically change the environment by moving soil and building mounds and tunnels, which alters soil structure, drainage and the distribution of nutrients [1]; these structures create shelter and habitat for other invertebrates and small animals [1]; if termites were removed, these species would lose their shelter and could decline [1]
bio12a3-inter-29

Algae in a pond capture 60 000 kJ of energy. Water fleas eat the algae, small fish eat the water fleas, and a kingfisher eats the small fish. Using the 10% energy transfer rule, calculate the energy available to the kingfisher. Show your working. (3 marks)
Water fleas receive 10% of 60 000 kJ = 6000 kJ [1]; small fish receive 10% of 6000 kJ = 600 kJ [1]; kingfisher receives 10% of 600 kJ = 60 kJ [1]
bio12a3-inter-30

A disease kills most of the seagrass in a meadow that provides food and shelter for dugongs, green turtles, juvenile fish and prawns. Explain the effects of this loss on at least three populations in the meadow, and describe one flow-on effect on the wider ecosystem. (4 marks)

Dugongs and green turtles lose their main food source, so their survival and reproduction decline [1]; juvenile fish and prawns lose their shelter and nursery habitat, so their numbers fall [1]; larger predators of these fish and prawns lose prey and may also decline [1]; reduced seagrass means less sediment is trapped and stabilised, increasing turbidity and harming other organisms such as filter feeders and corals [1]
bio12a3-inter-31

Fig trees in Australian rainforests depend on fig wasps for pollination. Each wasp species lays its eggs only inside the flowers of one fig species, and the developing wasps are housed in the fig, which also depends on the wasps to carry its pollen. This relationship is best described as
parasitism, because the wasp lays its eggs inside the fig flowers
commensalism, because the wasp benefits and the fig is unaffected
predation, because the wasp eats the seeds inside the fig
mutualism, because the wasp and the fig both benefit and depend on each other to reproduce

The fig provides a brood site and the wasp pollinates the fig, so both partners benefit (+/+), which is mutualism. Parasitism and predation would each harm one partner, and commensalism would leave the fig unaffected.
vce-bio12-ks-c1
Sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze on kelp. If otters are removed from an area, the most likely result is:
Kelp forests grow larger
Urchin numbers fall
No change, because otters are a small part of the ecosystem
Urchin numbers rise and kelp forests decline, reducing habitat for many species
A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem far larger than its abundance suggests.
vce-bio12-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-i: bio12a3-ik-1
Cultural burning practised by many Aboriginal communities typically involves
large, intense fires lit in the hottest, driest part of summer
small, cool, patchy fires lit at particular times of year, creating a mosaic of burnt and unburnt areas
burning only after every tree in an area has died
fires lit only to clear land permanently for agriculture

Cultural burning uses low-intensity, cool, patchy fires, often in the cooler months or early dry season, guided by Country, plants and animals. The resulting mosaic cuts fuel loads, protects fire-sensitive species and supports regrowth of food plants.
bio12a3-ik-2
Which is the most likely ecological benefit of a mosaic of patches burnt at different times?
It removes all habitat for small mammals
It reduces fuel loads and provides refuges and a range of habitat ages for different species
It prevents any plant from flowering
It increases the likelihood of large, uncontrollable wildfires

Patches of different ages break up continuous fuel, so the risk of large, intense wildfires goes down. They also give animals unburnt refuges to shelter in and fresh regrowth to feed on, which supports biodiversity.
bio12a3-ik-3
Seasonal calendars developed by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, such as those of the Gulumoerrgin (Larrakia) people around Darwin, are based on
the four European seasons of spring, summer, autumn and winter
detailed observation of local indicators such as weather, flowering of plants and animal behaviour
the phases of the moon only
randomly assigned periods of equal length

These calendars come from long-term observation of local environmental cues, such as winds, rain, plants flowering and animals breeding or migrating. They often recognise more than four seasons, and the cues signal when to hunt, gather or burn.
bio12a3-ik-4
Fish traps such as those at Budj Bim in south-west Victoria, built by the Gunditjmara people, show that Aboriginal peoples
relied only on chance encounters to catch eels
used detailed knowledge of the short-finned eel's life cycle and seasonal movements to build sustainable aquaculture systems
introduced eels from overseas
drained wetlands to farm crops

The Budj Bim system of channels, weirs and ponds was built to trap and hold short-finned eels (kooyang) during their seasonal migrations. It is among the world's oldest aquaculture systems and reflects detailed ecological knowledge. Budj Bim is World Heritage listed.
bio12a3-ik-5
Which statement best describes how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge can contribute to modern ecological management?
It is only of historical interest and not relevant today
It replaces the need for any scientific monitoring
Working with Traditional Owners combines long-term, place-based knowledge with scientific methods, for example in ranger programs and fire management
It can be used without consultation once recorded in books

Traditional knowledge is built from observing particular places over thousands of years. Combined with scientific monitoring in partnership with Traditional Owners (for example Indigenous ranger programs and savanna burning), it improves land and sea management. Using this knowledge needs consultation and respect for cultural and intellectual property.
bio12a3-ik-6
Explain how cultural burning can reduce the impact of large bushfires and support biodiversity. (3 marks)

Cool, low-intensity burns at the right time remove understorey fuel such as dry grass and leaf litter, so later fires have less fuel and are less intense; burning in small patches creates a mosaic of different-aged vegetation that acts as firebreaks and gives animals refuges; regrowth after burning provides fresh food for herbivores and promotes germination of fire-adapted plants, maintaining a diversity of habitats and species.
bio12a3-ik-7

Give an example of how Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander peoples use observations of one species to indicate the timing of a change in another species or in the environment, and explain why such indicators are biologically reliable. (2 marks)

Example: in parts of south-eastern Australia the flowering of certain wattles signals that fish such as mullet are running or that eels are moving (accept other valid examples, e.g. flowering of a plant indicating turtles or dugong are fat and ready to hunt); such indicators are reliable because both species respond to the same seasonal environmental cues (e.g. temperature, day length, rainfall), so their life cycle events happen at consistent times relative to each other.
bio12a3-ik-8

Torres Strait Islander communities manage the harvest of dugong and green turtles. Suggest two ways that traditional knowledge and practices can contribute to the sustainable use of these species. (2 marks)

Knowledge of breeding seasons, feeding grounds and population changes guides when and where hunting occurs, avoiding times when animals are breeding; community-based management plans and cultural rules limit how many animals are taken and which individuals (e.g. avoiding pregnant females or young), helping keep populations stable.
bio12a3-ik-9
Traditional Ecological Knowledge held by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is best described as
knowledge built over many generations through close observation of particular places and passed on through language, stories and practice
a set of general scientific principles developed in universities and then applied to Country
knowledge limited to spiritual beliefs, with no practical ecological content
a fixed list of plant and animal names recorded by early European explorers

Traditional Ecological Knowledge is cumulative and place-based, built up over many generations and transmitted through language, stories and practice. The idea that it is purely spiritual ignores its detailed, practical information about species and seasons, and it is not a fixed list recorded by early explorers.
bio12a3-ik-10
Many savanna Traditional Owners burn early in the dry season rather than late in it, mainly because early, cooler burns
produce the hottest fires, which clear the ground most thoroughly
reduce the fuel that would otherwise feed larger, hotter late-season wildfires and their greenhouse gas emissions
are the only type of fire that will spread through dry grass
allow fire to spread into closed forest so that new growth appears

Early dry season fires are cooler and patchy, so they leave less fuel for the hotter, larger wildfires that tend to occur late in the season. The idea that the hottest fires clear ground best is a common mistake, because intense fire damages habitat and is not the goal of cultural burning.
bio12a3-ik-11
Some cycad seeds are toxic if eaten raw. Aboriginal peoples in northern Australia prepared them by soaking or leaching the seeds in water before eating them. The main purpose of this step was to
ferment the sugars so the seeds taste sweeter
soften the seed so it could be cracked more easily
remove water-soluble toxins before the seed was eaten
reduce the protein content so the seed would store for longer

The toxins in cycad seeds dissolve in water, so leaching removes them and makes the seed safe to eat. Fermentation and softening can be part of other food preparation, but neither removes the toxins, which is why they are not the purpose here.
bio12a3-ik-12
An Indigenous Protected Area is best described as
land that the federal government leases to Traditional Owners for grazing
a national park in which all human use, including cultural burning, is banned
a commercial fishing zone that Aboriginal people may use only for ceremonies
land or sea country that Traditional Owners have voluntarily dedicated for conservation, managed under their own plans and knowledge

Indigenous Protected Areas are voluntarily dedicated by Indigenous landowners and managed for conservation and culture, often in partnership with governments. The national park option is wrong because these areas actively include cultural land management such as cultural burning.
bio12a3-ik-13
When gathering seed from a native grass or bush food, Traditional Owners often leave some of the seed on the plant. Why does this practice support sustainable use?
the remaining seed allows the plant population to regenerate and still feeds wildlife
plants cannot be harmed by any harvest, so the amount taken does not matter
seed left on the plant always rots, so harvesting everything prevents waste
harvested plants produce more seed each year because of the damage

Leaving seed lets plants regenerate and provides food for birds and other animals. The claims that plants cannot be harmed, or that damage boosts seed production, are not sound grounds for sustainable harvest.
bio12a3-ik-14
In many Aboriginal kinship systems, particular plants and animals are linked to certain people, which can lead to
a rule that every species must be eaten at least once each year
obligations to care for those species, which can limit when and how much of them is taken
the belief that species can be bought and sold within families
the view that people should never intervene, because species always look after themselves

Kinship and totem relationships can carry responsibilities to care for and protect particular species, so people may limit when and how much they take. The idea that species are bought and sold describes a commercial system that is not part of traditional management.
bio12a3-ik-15
Some Aboriginal groups managed food plants such as yams not only by collecting them but by tending the plots. Which practice best illustrates this?
digging up every tuber in a patch and leaving no plant material behind
avoiding a patch entirely so that the plants are never disturbed
replanting parts of the tuber and returning later, so the patch can supply food in future seasons
importing non-native crops to replace the native yams

Tending a patch by replanting and returning to it increases future harvests and keeps the food supply sustainable. Clearing a patch completely undermines future yield, and importing non-native crops is not part of traditional management.
bio12a3-ik-16
Many Australian plants have seeds or buds that respond to fire. How can a patchy, cool burn increase the abundance of such species?
fire kills every seed in the soil, so the species must regrow only from roots
fire makes the soil acidic, which these species require to grow
fire permanently removes all competing plants, so the species never face competition again
heat and smoke can trigger germination or resprouting, and reduced competition gives these species room to grow

Smoke and heat can break seed dormancy or stimulate resprouting in many fire-adapted species, and reduced competition helps seedlings establish. The claims that fire kills all seeds or changes soil acidity are common misconceptions and do not describe how these species respond.
bio12a3-ik-17
Why do many Traditional Owners keep fire out of rainforest margins during burning?
rainforest is fire-resistant and benefits from hot, intense fire
hot fire can kill fire-sensitive rainforest plants and the animals that depend on them
rainforest plants produce oils that make fire spread faster into the forest
rainforest trees need fire to open their seed pods

Rainforest edges contain many fire-sensitive species, so a hot fire can destroy them and the animals that rely on them. The idea that rainforest is fire-resistant is a common mistake, because its margins are often damaged by fire.
bio12a3-ik-18
In arid Australia, people can locate water by observing seed-eating birds such as finches and pigeons. Why is this an effective indicator?
the birds store water in their crops and release it near the surface
these birds must drink daily, so they fly to water in the early morning and late afternoon along predictable paths
the birds only nest near water, so any nest reveals a nearby spring
the birds feed only on water plants that grow in standing water

Many seed-eating birds need to drink every day, so their flights to water at dawn and dusk show the direction and distance to water. The claims about storing water in crops, or nesting only near water, are not supported as reasons for this method.
bio12a3-ik-19
Traditional Owners can find the nest of a native stingless bee (sugarbag) in a hollow tree by
listening for buzzing from inside tree trunks, mainly at night
searching for the largest flowering eucalypt in the area and cutting into it
watching the foraging bees and following their flight lines back to the hollow
assuming the nest is in the closest tree to the nearest flower

Foraging worker bees fly in fairly direct lines between flowers and their nest, so following their flight paths can lead to the hollow. Cutting into trees harms the colony, and the other options are guesses that do not track the bees.
bio12a3-ik-20
A tracker wants to judge how recently an animal passed through sandy ground. Which evidence is most useful?
whether the edges of the print are sharp or crumbled, and whether wind, rain or dew has altered it
the exact length of the animal's stride, which shows its age
the colour of the soil inside the print
the total number of tracks in the area, since more tracks always mean a more recent visit

Sharp, unweathered edges and an undisturbed surface suggest a recent track, while wind, rain or dew soften and fill it in over time. Stride length mainly indicates the animal's size and gait, not its age, and the number of tracks says nothing about when a single track was made.
bio12a3-ik-21
When scientists want to publish Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander knowledge about a species, why is consent from the knowledge holders important?
the knowledge belongs to the people who hold it, and some may be culturally restricted or sacred
knowledge is only protected when it is written down in a government report
scientific journals will not publish any knowledge that comes from oral sources
consent is needed only for knowledge about animals, not plants

Traditional Owners hold cultural and intellectual property rights over their knowledge, and some of it may be restricted by cultural law. The idea that knowledge is protected only when written down is a misconception, since much traditional knowledge is oral and still belongs to its holders.
bio12a3-ik-22
Coastal Aboriginal communities often plan shellfish gathering around the lowest tides. What is the main ecological reason for this?
high tides push shellfish into shallow water where they are easily caught
the sea is calmer at low tide, so shellfish stop moving and can be collected
shellfish only breed during high tides, so low tides are the safe time to harvest them
the lowest tides expose intertidal shellfish that are otherwise underwater and hard to reach

Low tides expose intertidal shellfish, making them accessible and reducing the effort needed to collect them. The claims about high tides pushing shellfish into shallow water, or about breeding timing, are misconceptions about how shellfish behave.
bio12a3-ik-23
Define the term 'Caring for Country' in the context of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land management. (1 mark)
The ongoing responsibility of Traditional Owners to look after land, sea, plants, animals and cultural places, using their knowledge, law and practices [1].
bio12a3-ik-24
Explain why ecological knowledge built up over many generations in one place can be valuable for managing that place. (2 marks)

It is based on long-term, direct observation of changes in species, seasons and water that short-term records would miss [1]; it captures local species interactions and environmental cues, so management can be tailored to that specific area [1].
bio12a3-ik-25

A ranger team plans to reintroduce cultural burning on a property where dense shrubs have built up after decades without fire. Outline three steps the team could take to plan the burns safely and sustainably. (3 marks)

Consult the Traditional Owners and use their knowledge of timing, weather and seasonal indicators to choose when to burn [1]; assess fuel loads, wind and humidity, prepare firebreaks, then burn cool and in small patches [1]; monitor the results and plan a mosaic of burns of different ages over time to maintain habitat diversity [1].
bio12a3-ik-26
Explain why the Sea Country approach involves Torres Strait Islander and Aboriginal people in marine management rather than relying only on scientists. (2 marks)

Sea Country includes the reefs, waters and animals that are part of people's culture and identity, so people hold detailed local knowledge of changes [1]; involving them gives management a basis in their rights, responsibilities and long-term care, which supports compliance and continuity [1].
bio12a3-ik-27
Discuss how cultural burning can help reduce greenhouse gas emissions from northern Australian savannas. (4 marks)

Early dry season burns are cooler and patchy, so they reduce the fuel available for later fires [1]; this reduces the area burnt by late-season wildfires, which are hotter and more extensive and release more greenhouse gases in total [1]; savanna burning projects led by Traditional Owners can earn Australian Carbon Credit Units under the Emissions Reduction Fund for emissions avoided [1]; patchy burning also protects large trees and other vegetation that store carbon, so less carbon is lost [1].
bio12a3-ik-28
In arid Australia, people dug soaks in the sand of dry creek beds to reach water. The soaks worked because
dew condensing on the sand overnight collected in the hollow
rain falling on the sand was stored there for several years
underground water flows beneath the dry creek bed, close enough to the surface to reach by digging
seasonal floodwater filled the hollow and never drained away

Water moves through the sand and gravel beneath dry creek beds, so digging reaches it where it lies near the surface. Dew and rain stored in sand are not reliable sources, and floodwater does not stay in a hollow for long.
bio12a3-ik-29
Explain why cultural burners often light fires so that they move into the wind (backing fire) rather than with it. (2 marks)

A fire moving into the wind spreads slowly with a low flame height, so it burns at lower intensity and is easier to control [1]; the cooler fire consumes less of the canopy and understorey, leaving unburnt patches and reducing the risk of large, hot wildfires later [1].
bio12a3-ik-30
Explain how stone fish traps on the Barwon River at Brewarrina could catch fish while leaving many fish free to continue upstream. (2 marks)

The stone rows (weirs) funnelled fish into pools and enclosures as water levels fell, so fish could be caught when they were concentrated [1]; openings in the traps let smaller fish and many others pass upstream, which supports continued breeding and a sustainable catch [1].
vce-bio12-ak-c1
Which best describes Aboriginal cultural burning practices?
Large, hot fires lit across whole regions at the peak of summer to clear all the undergrowth
Burning the same small area every week of the year to keep the ground completely bare
Cool, low-intensity, patchy burns timed by seasonal indicators, reducing fuel and promoting new growth
Fires lit only to clear land for growing crops, with no link to the seasons or Country
Mosaic burning creates a patchwork of habitats and lowers the risk of intense bushfires; it is based on deep knowledge of Country.
vce-bio12-challenge: vce-bio12-challenge-1
Compare the surface area to volume ratios of cube-shaped cells with sides of 10 µm and 20 µm, and explain what this means for the larger cell.
10 µm: 600 ÷ 1000 = 0.6 µm⁻¹. 20 µm: 2400 ÷ 8000 = 0.3 µm⁻¹. The larger cell has half the surface per unit of volume, so it exchanges materials (O₂, nutrients, wastes) relatively more slowly.
Show both calculations, then link the result to diffusion.
vce-bio12-challenge-2
Potato cylinders are placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations. Their mass does not change in 0.3 M sucrose. This suggests that:
The solute concentration inside the potato cells is about equal to 0.3 M sucrose
No water moves into or out of the cells at all in any of the solutions
Sucrose enters the cells in 0.3 M solution, balancing the water that leaves
Potato cells are impermeable to water, so their mass never changes
In an isotonic solution water moves in and out at equal rates, so there is no net change in mass.
vce-bio12-challenge-3
Give three differences between mitosis and meiosis.

Mitosis: one division, two daughter cells, diploid, genetically identical, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four cells, haploid, genetically different (crossing over and independent assortment), producing gametes.
Pair each difference: number of divisions, number and ploidy of cells, genetic identity, purpose.
vce-bio12-challenge-4
Two plants with genotype AaBb (genes unlinked) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to show both recessive traits?
vce-bio12-challenge-5
Two affected parents have an unaffected child. The condition is most likely:
Recessive
Dominant
Y-linked
Caused only by the environment
Both parents must be heterozygous for a dominant allele to have an unaffected (homozygous recessive) child. Recessive affected parents could only have affected children.
vce-bio12-challenge-6
Compare how the nervous and endocrine systems send signals.

Nervous: electrical impulses along neurons and neurotransmitters at synapses; very fast, short-lived and precisely targeted. Endocrine: hormones carried in the blood to cells with receptors; slower, longer-lasting and often widespread.
Compare mode of transmission, speed, duration and targeting.
vce-bio12-challenge-7
Cancer cells typically keep dividing because they:
Divide only by meiosis, which has no checkpoints
Lack DNA, so no signals can stop them dividing
Have extra mitochondria that drive constant division
Ignore cell-cycle checkpoints and avoid apoptosis
Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle (proto-oncogenes and tumour-suppressor genes) remove normal limits on division.
vce-bio12-challenge-8
A colour-blind man (X-linked recessive) and a woman who is a carrier have a child. What is the probability that the child is a colour-blind daughter?
XᵇY × XᴮXᵇ. Daughters receive Xᵇ from the father, so half of daughters are XᵇXᵇ. P(daughter) × P(colour-blind | daughter) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
vce-bio12-challenge-9
Which statement about a keystone species is correct?
It is always the most common species, so removing it leaves the most empty space
Removing it causes large changes in the ecosystem, even if it is not the most abundant
It is always a producer, because every food web depends on its energy
Removing it has little effect, because other species quickly take its place
Keystone species are defined by their impact, not their number.
vce-bio12-challenge-10
Explain the difference between negative and positive feedback, with one example of each.

Negative feedback reverses a change to restore a set point (for example, insulin lowering high blood glucose). Positive feedback amplifies a change (for example, oxytocin increasing contractions in childbirth).
Name the direction of change and the purpose of each loop.

X.title: Glucose: membranes, insulin and diabetes
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Glucose enters most body cells by facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins in the plasma membrane.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain why glucose needs a protein to cross the plasma membrane, but oxygen does not.
pieces.answer: The phospholipid bilayer has a hydrophobic (non-polar) interior. Glucose is a large, polar molecule, so it cannot pass through the bilayer and needs a carrier protein. Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it diffuses straight through the bilayer.

steps.working: Glucose is large and polar, so it cannot cross the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and needs a carrier protein.
Oxygen is a small, non-polar molecule, so it can diffuse directly through the bilayer.

pieces.mistake: Saying glucose is 'too big for the pores'. The key reason is that the inside of the bilayer is hydrophobic and glucose is polar.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain why facilitated diffusion does not need energy from ATP.
pieces.answer: It moves glucose down its concentration gradient, from high to low concentration, so it is passive.

steps.working: Facilitated diffusion moves molecules down their concentration gradient, so no energy from ATP is needed.

pieces.mistake: Confusing it with active transport. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and uses ATP.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Using the stimulus–response model, describe how blood glucose returns to its normal level after a meal.
pieces.answer: Stimulus: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect the rise and secrete insulin. Insulin causes body cells (such as liver and muscle cells) to take up glucose, and the liver converts it to glycogen, so blood glucose falls back to normal.

steps.working: The rise in blood glucose (stimulus) is detected by beta cells in the pancreas, which respond by secreting insulin into the blood.
Insulin makes target cells such as liver and muscle cells take up glucose, and the liver stores it as glycogen, so blood glucose falls.

pieces.mistake: Naming glucagon. Glucagon is released when blood glucose is low and raises it.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain why this is an example of negative feedback.
pieces.answer: The response (a fall in blood glucose) counteracts the original stimulus (a rise in blood glucose), bringing the level back towards normal.

steps.working: The response reverses the change that triggered it: high blood glucose leads to a response that lowers blood glucose.

pieces.mistake: Saying it is negative because something decreases. Negative feedback means the response opposes the original change, whichever direction it was.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the beta cells. Explain why, without treatment, blood glucose stays high after meals.
pieces.answer: With no beta cells, little or no insulin is produced. Without insulin, body cells do not take up glucose and the liver does not convert it to glycogen, so glucose stays in the blood.

steps.working: Destroyed beta cells mean little or no insulin is secreted.
Without insulin, cells do not take up glucose from the blood and the liver does not store it as glycogen, so blood glucose remains high.

pieces.mistake: Describing type 2 diabetes. In type 2, insulin is produced but cells respond poorly to it; in type 1, insulin is not produced.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Insulin is a protein made inside beta cells and released into the blood. Name the organelles that make it, and describe how it leaves the cell.
pieces.answer: Ribosomes (on the rough endoplasmic reticulum) make insulin. It is packaged by the Golgi apparatus into vesicles, which fuse with the plasma membrane and release it by exocytosis.

steps.working: Ribosomes, attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, synthesise insulin.
Vesicles from the Golgi apparatus carry it to the plasma membrane and release it by exocytosis.

pieces.mistake: Saying insulin leaves by diffusion. Proteins are too large; they are secreted in vesicles by exocytosis.

X.title: Coat colour in guinea pigs
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: In guinea pigs, the allele for black coat (B) is dominant to the allele for white coat (b).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Give the genotype of a white guinea pig.
pieces.answer: bb

steps.working: White is the recessive phenotype, so it only appears when both alleles are recessive: bb.

pieces.mistake: Writing Bb. A guinea pig with even one B allele is black.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Two heterozygous black guinea pigs are crossed. Use a Punnett square to find the expected ratio of phenotypes in their offspring.
pieces.answer: 3 black : 1 white

steps.working: Each parent is Bb and makes B and b gametes. The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
BB and Bb are black and bb is white, so the expected phenotype ratio is 3 black : 1 white.

pieces.mistake: Giving the genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) when the question asks for phenotypes.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: A breeder has a black guinea pig of unknown genotype. Describe a test cross to find its genotype, and the results that would show each genotype.
pieces.answer: Cross it with a white (bb) guinea pig. If any offspring are white, the black parent is Bb (about half the offspring would be white). If all of a large number of offspring are black, the parent is very likely BB.

steps.working: Cross the black guinea pig with a homozygous recessive (white, bb) guinea pig.
If any white offspring appear, the parent must be Bb (expected ratio 1 black : 1 white); if all of many offspring are black, it is most likely BB.

pieces.mistake: Crossing it with another black guinea pig. A test cross uses the homozygous recessive so the unknown parent's alleles show directly in the offspring.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain two ways in which meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from each other.
pieces.answer: Crossing over: in prophase I, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments, giving new combinations of alleles. Independent assortment: in metaphase I, each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up in a random orientation, so gametes get different mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes.

steps.working: Crossing over in prophase I exchanges sections between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, recombining alleles.
Independent assortment in metaphase I: homologous pairs line up randomly, so each gamete receives a different combination of chromosomes.

pieces.mistake: Naming mutation or fertilisation. The question asks how meiosis itself creates variation.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Guinea pig body cells contain 64 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a guinea pig gamete.

steps.working: Gametes are haploid (n), with half the diploid number: 64 ÷ 2 = 32.

pieces.mistake: Giving 64 or 128. Meiosis halves the chromosome number.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: A population of wild guinea pigs lives among dark volcanic rocks, and most of them are black. Explain how a black coat is a structural adaptation in this environment.
pieces.answer: A black coat is a physical feature that camouflages the guinea pig against the dark rocks. Predators are less likely to see it, so it is more likely to survive and reproduce.

steps.working: Coat colour is a physical (structural) feature; a black coat blends in with the dark rocks.
This camouflage makes black guinea pigs harder for predators to see, increasing their chance of surviving and reproducing.

pieces.mistake: Saying the guinea pigs turned black in order to blend in. Individuals do not change their coat colour to suit the environment; the feature helps those that have it survive.

X.title: Cells that divide, specialise and die
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Body cells divide by mitosis, while bacteria divide by binary fission.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Describe what happens during interphase.
pieces.answer: The cell grows, makes organelles and proteins, and replicates its DNA (S phase), preparing to divide.

steps.working: The cell grows and produces organelles and proteins (G1 and G2).
DNA is replicated during the S phase, so each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

pieces.mistake: Calling interphase a resting phase. The cell is very active, especially in copying its DNA.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: List the stages of mitosis in order and describe what happens in metaphase.
pieces.answer: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. In metaphase, chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres.

steps.working: Order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
Metaphase: chromosomes line up along the cell's equator, with spindle fibres attached at the centromeres.

pieces.mistake: Describing anaphase (chromatids separating) as metaphase.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain how apoptosis normally prevents tumours, and how a failure of apoptosis can lead to cancer.
pieces.answer: Apoptosis removes damaged or abnormal cells by programmed death. If the signals fail, damaged cells survive and keep dividing, forming a tumour.

steps.working: Apoptosis is programmed cell death that removes damaged or unneeded cells.
If apoptosis fails, abnormal cells survive and divide uncontrollably, which can form a tumour (cancer).

pieces.mistake: Saying cancer cells die more often. Cancer involves cells that avoid death and keep dividing.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Compare embryonic and adult stem cells.
pieces.answer: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (can become almost any cell type) and come from early embryos; adult stem cells are multipotent (limited to related cell types) and are found in tissues such as bone marrow.

steps.working: Embryonic stem cells: pluripotent, from early embryos.
Adult stem cells: multipotent, found in tissues such as bone marrow, giving rise to a limited range of cells.

pieces.mistake: Describing only one type. A comparison needs both.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one cell, how many cells are there after 2 hours?

steps.working: 2 hours = 6 divisions, so the number of cells is 2⁶ = 64.

pieces.mistake: Adding instead of doubling (1 + 6 = 7). Each division doubles the number of cells.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Explain why binary fission is simpler than mitosis.
pieces.answer: Bacteria have no nucleus and usually a single circular chromosome, so there is no need for the stages of mitosis or a spindle.

steps.working: Prokaryotes have a single circular chromosome and no nucleus, so the DNA is simply copied and separated as the cell splits.

pieces.mistake: Saying bacteria have no DNA. They have DNA, just not inside a nucleus.

X.title: Staying warm and staying hydrated
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: On a cold winter morning, a hiker sets out without a jacket.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Use the stimulus–response model to describe how the hiker's body responds to the cold.
pieces.answer: Stimulus: falling body temperature. Receptors: thermoreceptors in the skin. Control centre: the hypothalamus. Effectors: skeletal muscles (shivering) and arterioles in the skin (vasoconstriction). Response: heat is produced and conserved, so body temperature rises back to normal.

steps.working: Stimulus (drop in temperature) detected by thermoreceptors in the skin.
The hypothalamus, the control centre, sends signals to effectors.
Effectors respond: skeletal muscles shiver to produce heat, and skin arterioles constrict to reduce heat loss.

pieces.mistake: Naming the brain as the receptor. Receptors detect the stimulus; the hypothalamus processes it.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain how vasoconstriction reduces heat loss.
pieces.answer: Less blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface, so less heat is lost to the surroundings.

steps.working: Narrowed arterioles send less warm blood to the skin surface, reducing heat loss by radiation and conduction.

pieces.mistake: Saying the blood vessels move away from the skin. They narrow; they do not move.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: A lizard basks on a warm rock in the morning. Explain why this is a behavioural adaptation for an ectotherm.
pieces.answer: Ectotherms rely on external heat to control body temperature. Basking is an action that raises the lizard's body temperature so it can become active.

steps.working: An ectotherm gains most of its heat from the environment rather than from metabolism.
Basking is a behaviour (an action), and it warms the lizard so that its enzymes and muscles work efficiently.

pieces.mistake: Calling it a structural adaptation. Structural adaptations are physical features; basking is a behaviour.

pieces.text: Later, after hiking for hours without drinking, the hiker's urine is small in volume and dark in colour.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain the role of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in this response.
pieces.answer: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the high solute concentration of the blood; the posterior pituitary releases ADH, which makes the kidney's collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and less, more concentrated urine is produced.

steps.working: Dehydration raises blood solute concentration, detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, and the posterior pituitary releases ADH.
ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and urine is concentrated.

pieces.mistake: Saying ADH increases urine production. ADH reduces it by increasing reabsorption.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Describe two structural adaptations that help desert plants reduce water loss.
pieces.answer: For example: a thick waxy cuticle; sunken or fewer stomata; small or needle-like leaves.

steps.working: First adaptation, for example a thick, waxy cuticle that reduces evaporation.
Second adaptation, for example sunken stomata, fewer stomata, or reduced leaf surface area.

pieces.mistake: Describing behavioural or physiological responses. The question asks for structural features.

X.title: Challenge: running a marathon in the heat
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Sam runs a marathon on a 32 °C day. His body temperature starts to rise, he sweats heavily, and he drinks little water during the race.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Using the stimulus–response model, identify the stimulus, receptor, control centre and effector involved in Sam's sweating.
pieces.answer: Stimulus: rise in body temperature. Receptor: thermoreceptors (skin and hypothalamus). Control centre: hypothalamus. Effector: sweat glands.

steps.working: Correct stimulus and receptor.
Correct control centre and effector.

pieces.mistake: Naming the skin as the control centre.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain how vasodilation of skin arterioles helps Sam lose heat.
pieces.answer: Arterioles widen, so more blood flows near the skin surface, and heat is lost to the surroundings by radiation and convection.

steps.working: More blood flows through capillaries near the skin.
Heat is transferred from the blood to the environment.

pieces.mistake: Saying blood vessels move closer to the skin.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Sam loses a lot of water as sweat. Explain how his body reduces water loss in urine.
pieces.answer: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect concentrated blood. The posterior pituitary releases more ADH. ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

steps.working: Osmoreceptors detect a rise in blood solute concentration.
More ADH is released by the posterior pituitary.
More water is reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, giving concentrated urine.

pieces.mistake: Saying ADH makes the kidneys produce more urine.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Late in the race Sam's blood glucose falls. Explain how his body responds.
pieces.answer: Alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon, which stimulates liver cells to break down glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood.

steps.working: Glucagon is released by alpha cells.
The liver converts glycogen to glucose, raising blood glucose.

pieces.mistake: Saying insulin raises blood glucose.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why the responses in parts b–d are examples of negative feedback.
pieces.answer: Each response reverses the change that triggered it, returning conditions towards the set point.

steps.working: The response opposes the original change.

pieces.mistake: Saying 'negative' means the response is harmful.

X.title: Challenge: tracing an inherited condition
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Anna and Ben are both unaffected, but their daughter Chloe has a rare inherited condition. Their son David is unaffected.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain how this information shows that the condition is recessive and is not X-linked recessive.
pieces.answer: Two unaffected parents have an affected child, so the allele must be hidden in the parents (recessive). If it were X-linked recessive, Chloe's father Ben would have to be affected, but he is not, so it is autosomal recessive.

steps.working: Unaffected parents with an affected child: recessive.
An affected daughter with an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive.

pieces.mistake: Saying it must be X-linked because only one child is affected.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Give the genotypes of Anna and Ben (using A and a), and the probability that their next child is affected.
pieces.answer: Both Aa; 1/4 (25%)

steps.working: Both parents are heterozygous, Aa.
Aa × Aa gives 1/4 aa.

pieces.mistake: Thinking that because they already have an affected child, the next is less likely to be affected.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: What is the probability that David, who is unaffected, is a carrier?

steps.working: He is AA or Aa; among unaffected offspring the ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa, so P(Aa) = 2/3.

pieces.mistake: Answering 1/2, which ignores that David is known to be unaffected.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: During which stage of meiosis do the A and a alleles separate? Explain.
pieces.answer: Anaphase I, when homologous chromosomes (each carrying one allele) move to opposite poles.

steps.working: Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate.

pieces.mistake: Answering anaphase II, when sister chromatids separate.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why a karyotype would not detect this condition.
pieces.answer: A karyotype shows chromosome number and large structural changes; a change in one gene's allele is far too small to see.

steps.working: Karyotypes show only whole chromosomes, not individual gene sequences.

pieces.mistake: Saying karyotypes only work on adults.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: A treatment greatly reduces Chloe's symptoms. Has her genotype changed? Explain.
pieces.answer: No. The treatment changes her phenotype by altering the environment of her cells; her alleles are unchanged and can still be passed on.

steps.working: Phenotype changes; genotype does not.

pieces.mistake: Saying treatment cures the allele.
